#6827. Bazaar’s Thanksgiving Outfit Guide

How to be the best-dressed guest at the dinner table

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Thanksgiving calls for comfort, but it’s also an opportunity to show off your fashion prowess to relatives you haven’t seen all year. Focus your sartorial efforts from the waist up. Ruffled skirts and statement shoes won’t earn compliments while you’re seated, but artful jewelry pieces, interesting layers, and trending prints certainly will.

The 12 Thanksgiving outfits below will fast-track you to the evening’s best-dressed list, whether you’re hosting a casual get-together or attending a more formal affair.

Prioritizing comfort doesn’t have to be overt. This printed wrap dress from the Senegalese brand Diarrablu will earn you compliments while allowing for subtle fit adjustments throughout the evening.

A casual Thanksgiving gathering is the perfect place to test-drive this season’s sweatpant-jeans hybrids. Elevate your laid-back bottoms with a buttery cashmere knit and Tory Burch’s new Bunny Knot bag, and no one will be able to tell the difference.

A tonal Thanksgiving outfit in fall’s trending olive green reads sophisticated without the added effort. Chestnut-brown bags and boots make a reliable pairing for olive-colored skirts and dresses. Complete your look with classic stud earrings, which will serve you well during the holiday party season.

Deep wine-red tones work especially well for holiday gatherings. Add interest with on-trend details like croc embossing and fringe trims. Then, top your monochrome burgundy look with a classic tan Burberry coat.

Draped sleeves and flowy skirts can prove a hassle while cooking, so consider your pre-dinner tasks when choosing an outfit. Stick with comfortable pieces that allow you to move around easily. This playful La DoubleJ apron is worth planning your look around if you’re fully in charge of this year’s meal.

Hill House Home’s range of coordinating dresses is perfect for those hoping to snap Christmas-card photos while waiting for the turkey to cook. Minimalist shoulder bags, flats, and hoop earrings give your holiday outfits timeless appeal.

A wisely layered look will keep you at a comfortable temperature while prepping side dishes over a hot stove, then easily transition to watching a quick game of flag football in the backyard. An androgynous button-up can peek out from under J.Crew’s retro Rollneck Sweater in the morning, then act as a solo layer on a warm afternoon.

Even the most casual gathering can be a stylish affair. Éterne’s cashmere sets are just as comfortable as any sweatsuit but look much more put together when paired with luxe accessories, like suede flats and a tennis necklace.

Here’s one way to master plaid for fall. Style a checked button-up with coordinating trousers and keep the rest of the look comfortable and chic with elevated basics and a cozy scarf coat.

A sleek charcoal gray is an unexpected complement to richly textured brown suede jackets, boots, and bags. Mixing multiple mocha tones makes this trending fabrication feel even more elegant.

If you’re feeling extra festive this year, consider accessorizing with a statement necklace, such as this sculptural Sézane necklace. It may help fill awkward silences and give you and your mother-in-law plenty to talk about while preparing this year’s turkey.

Employ corduroy textures for a seasonal take on a Canadian tuxedo. Then, complete the autumnal palette with dark-wash denim, saddle leather, and tan suede. Those Frame swing trousers will be a useful addition to your work wardrobe, which you can style in a multitude of ways throughout fall and winter.

#6821. Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

Microsoft is introducing new tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

In a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

"Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

One of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

Microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

Microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

The company is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. New capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

That initiative introduces plans for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

"Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

Project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

Taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The company is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

Phillips said AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

#6815. Cisco Intros Privileged Infrastructure Access for People and AI Agents

Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

In a recent blog post, Cisco's Matt Caulfield described a system that uses cryptographic identity to connect an administrator or agent to the infrastructure needed for a particular task. Access is governed by short-lived privileges, with session recording providing a record of the work performed.

"If there is no work being done, no privilege exists," Caulfield wrote. Cisco positions the offering as a way to bring identity controls directly into infrastructure operations while reducing dependence on static credentials, shared secrets, and broad access.

The announcement follows Cisco's previously announced Teleport partnership and its Infrastructure Identity concept, which connects the identity of a person or machine with the resources it can access, the actions it performs, and the permissions governing those actions.

Caulfield described a gap between the controls organizations apply to workforce applications and those used to administer network infrastructure. Companies have invested in single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and risk-based controls for application access, he wrote, but those protections often do not follow an engineer logging into a router or switch.

Instead, infrastructure access may depend on long-lived credentials, shared accounts, or separate policy systems. According to Cisco, that separation makes it harder to enforce least privilege and establish which person or system performed a particular action.

The company illustrates the problem with an administrator updating hundreds of switches during a maintenance window. If some updates fail, the administrator needs to troubleshoot before the window closes. The permissions available to handle that work, however, may cover more infrastructure and remain active longer than the task requires.

Traditional privileged access management can reduce risk through credential vaulting and rotation, Caulfield wrote. But he argued that operational friction can undermine those controls when teams create exceptions to complete urgent work. Those exceptions can leave credentials and privileges usable after the immediate need has passed.

Cisco's stated objective is to give infrastructure teams a consistent route to the devices they manage while providing security teams with policy enforcement, temporary permissions, and a record of activity. The company describes operational convenience as part of the design, rather than treating access governance solely as a credential-management problem.

Privileged Infrastructure Access makes access an on-demand action, according to the announcement. Cryptographic identity establishes the actor, and the resulting connection provides only the privileges needed to complete the task. Those privileges expire when the task concludes.

For customers using Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) and Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+), the offering can draw on existing policy and device context to govern access to Cisco routers and switches. Cisco says customers can extend the same access model to other infrastructure, including servers, Kubernetes clusters, and cloud resources.

#6812. Maura Higgins Seemingly Responds to Harsh Fan Feedback After Her “Toughest” Week on ‘DWTS’

“Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay. I’m only human,” she wrote, in part.

Maura Higgins is opening up after tackling her Disney Night choreography as Tinker Bell on Dancing With the Stars. The Love Island alum got candid in a lengthy statement she penned alongside a carousel of behind-the-scenes photos from Monday night’s episode after fans criticized her performance in Team Slaytopia’s group number.

“This week was definitely one of the toughest I’ve had so far. I was really unwell, running on very little energy and trying to learn two dances, but I gave it absolutely everything I had,” she started her message, adding that she had no previous dance experience before joining DWTS.“I wanted to challenge myself, step outside my comfort zone and give something completely new my absolute best & that’s exactly what I’m trying to do every single week. I’m learning, I’m making mistakes, I’m pushing myself and I’m growing along the way!! Some weeks will be better than others, and that’s okay,” she continued, adding, “I’m only human.”She insisted she wasn’t sharing the message for “sympathy or to make excuses, but simply to share a little of the reality behind the scenes.”

The Traitors star uplifted her pro partner and “biggest support throughout this journey,” Mark Ballas, before seemingly addressing harsh feedback from viewers who criticized her “low energy” performances in both of her numbers this week.

“Genuinely what is up with maura tonight…she was the clear weak link of that team dance,” one person wrote, while another added, “i'm going to be very honest with you i genuinely think maura did by far the worst of any celebrity tonight and the judges were just distracted by how good of a show mark is able to put on that they didn't notice lol.”

Per her message, Maura seems to be focusing on those who continue to uplift and support her throughout the competition.

“To everyone who continues to support me, encourage me and cheer me on, please know how much it means,” she wrote toward the end of her statement. “You genuinely give me the strength to keep going, especially on the harder days. Your kindness never goes unnoticed.”

She then closed her post by expressing how “grateful” she is to still be in the running for the iconic Mirrorball trophy.

Based on that alone, I tink she’ll be just fine either way!

#6805. Survey Finds 84% of Organizations Reported at Least One AI-Related Incident in the Past Year

Companies are running into problems as they give artificial intelligence more control over critical business applications, with 84% reporting at least one AI-related incident in the past year, according to a new survey from identity security firm Delinea.

The company's 2026 Application Access Governance report found that some organizations have experienced incorrect financial transactions and AI actions they couldn't trace or explain. The findings raise concerns about whether enterprises have enough oversight of AI systems that can make decisions and take actions on their own

The findings are based on an independent survey of 1,000 senior finance and finance technology leaders in the United States and United Kingdom. The AI-specific analysis included 879 respondents whose organizations use the technology in critical business applications.

The report found that 35% of surveyed organizations have deployed AI agents capable of taking actions within business applications. However, only 11% of organizations using AI said their governance and security controls were keeping pace with deployment.

Delinea also found gaps in centralized visibility into agent deployment and permissions, including who owns agents and who approved their use.

Some respondents reported segregation-of-duties conflicts involving AI, while others identified agents that continued operating after the employees who deployed them had left the organization.

The research also highlighted gaps in monitoring access across business systems. Only 46% of respondents said they continuously monitor and manage cumulative access risks across applications.

Those gaps can make it difficult to identify segregation-of-duties conflicts, in which a person or agent has permissions across systems that should be kept separate.

Despite those issues, 95% of respondents said they were confident their access controls would withstand scrutiny in an external audit.

However, 26% reported access-related audit findings that had recurred in consecutive years, while 25% said some findings had remained unresolved for three or more years.

Only 22% of organizations had a single named owner for each application, with ownership tracked in one system of record.

Meanwhile, 60% reported an increase over the past two years in the number of critical applications operating outside the scope of access governance or Sarbanes-Oxley Act compliance.

The findings highlight the oversight challenges associated with giving AI agents authority to act within business systems, particularly when organizations cannot consistently identify who owns an agent or trace its actions.

Frank Vukovits, chief security scientist at Delinea, said organizations remain responsible for the actions AI agents take within their systems.

"When an agent can approve a transaction or change permissions, the business owns the outcome. You need to know what every agent can do, who owns it, and who approved it, before an auditor asks or your financials are misstated," Vukovits said.

For the full report, go to the Delinea site.

Network-provider trust concerns are impacting enterprise AI plans, with AI and data-driven projects the most affected initiatives among respondents reporting disruption, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

CrowdStrike's latest Threat Hunting Report traces a multiyear shift from conventional intrusions toward attacks that exploit trusted identities, cloud services, AI systems, and software dependencies.

Video game designers spend an enormous amount of time studying what keeps people engaged when something becomes difficult. They have become very good at helping people persist. Schools should pay attention.

A new report from Caylent, an AI-focused Amazon Web Services Premier Tier Services Partner, found that enterprises are already moving agentic AI beyond pilots and into production environments. #6799. What Does Non-Acnegenic Mean, Exactly? Dermatologists Break Down the Skincare Term

And I thought I knew all the acne buzzwords...

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

When I was a young girl in the early 2000s, there was always a bottle of that iconic blue Cetaphil Gentle Skin Cleanser in my parents’ house. It was probably the only thing I washed my face with for the first 10 years of my life. But what stuck with me the longest (and perhaps was an early sign that I was destined to be a beauty editor) was that, right under the product name, the label said “non-comedogenic.” This new word perplexed me. I vividly remember trying to figure out how to pronounce it as I washed my face every evening, finally asking my mom during my very short nighttime skincare routine. She told me how to say it and what it meant in a way that a 7 year old would understand, and that was that. I was all up to speed.

Fast forward two decades later, and I’m sitting here, perplexed once again, as I learn about a new-to-me, related-to-non-comedogenic term: non-acnegenic. I’ve been seeing the word pop up here and there when it comes to an acne-friendly skincare routine, but I had to know, what actually makes it different from non-comedogenic? Is it a marketing buzzword, or is whether or not a product is non-acnegenic really important to pay attention to? I had far more questions than 7-year-old me, so I turned to two dermatologists to explain everything.

Let’s start with some good news: The definition of non-acnegenic is honestly pretty straightforward. “Non-acnegenic means a product has been formulated and tested so it won’t trigger acne breakouts, including the red and inflamed bumps and pustules most people picture when they think of acne,” says board-certified dermatologist Mona Foad, MD.

If you have acne-prone skin and/or are currently trying to figure out how to get rid of acne, Dr. Foad calls it “one of the most useful labels you can look for.” This is because brands “typically test these products on people with acne-prone skin over several weeks with a dermatologist evaluating the skin for any new breakouts,” she explains.

However, using a non-acnegenic skincare product isn’t a 100 percent guarantee that it won’t cause a breakout, unfortunately. “Think ‘less likely to invite a breakout,’” says board-certified dermatologist Mona Gohara, MD. This label means the product is unlikely to cause or worsen acne, but there’s no way for a brand to promise that result for everyone.

Non-acnegenic and non-comedogenic are different—but there’s plenty of overlap, Dr. Gohara says. Non-comedogenic, as you may already know, means that a product “is designed not to clog pores,” says Dr. Foad, who notes that a comedone is the technical term for a clogged pore. “Non-comedogenic addresses clogged pores, while non-acnegenic addresses the full picture of acne, including inflammation.”

Here’s what I found really interesting: “A product can avoid clogging pores and still irritate the skin enough to trigger inflammatory breakouts,” says Dr. Foad. Just because a product is non-comedogenic doesn’t mean you won’t get a breakout after using it. But that doesn’t mean using a non-comedogenic product can’t be helpful in avoiding acne, either. “Clogged pores are the starting point for acne, so preventing them is the first line of defense,” Dr. Foad explains. “When a product carries this label, the brand is claiming that its formula won’t block your pores and set the stage for breakouts.” Think of it this way: Acne-prone skin wants protection from potential pore cloggers and acne triggers alike. So, if you’re shopping for acne-prone skin, Dr. Foad recommends looking for products that are both non-comedogenic and non-acnegenic.

Oh, and another important thing to note: “Neither means the product actually treats acne,” says Dr. Gohara. Remember, these labels just mean that you’re putting skincare or makeup on your face that is less likely to set off a breakout.

As discussed above, non-comedogenic and non-acnegenic do have accepted definitions in the beauty industry. But there’s one super important caveat: Just like any non-medical claim on an over-the-counter beauty product, neither of these terms is regulated by the FDA. “This is one of the biggest sources of confusion I see,” says Dr. Foad. Because the FDA doesn’t define or regulate either of these, “there’s no standard test brands are required to use,” she says.

What does that mean, exactly? “One company might test a product on dozens of acne-prone volunteers over several weeks, while another might rely on ingredient lists alone,” explains Dr. Foad. “That’s why these labels are a helpful starting point, not a guarantee.” Your best bet is to look for brands that are transparent about their clinical and consumer testing, so you can review those and decide for yourself if a product looks promising enough to buy.

There’s no one magical ingredient that automatically makes a product non-acnegenic, but these are often used in products meant to support acne-prone skin:

Again, the inclusion of these ingredients doesn’t guarantee you won’t break out after using them. If you have an allergy or sensitivity to anything on this list, you should avoid it.

On the flip side, here are some ingredients to avoid, as they can trigger breakouts and clogged pores:

In general, for those who are acne-prone, “I’d steer them away from heavy, oil-based foundations, concealers, and facial balms,” says Dr. Gohara. Instead, look for lightweight foundations and other makeup products that don’t contain the ingredients above.

Of course, anyone who’s acne-prone, oily, or combination may want to ensure their beauty products are non-acnegenic. But beyond that, “they’re also essential for patients using prescription acne treatments like tretinoin or benzoyl peroxide, which can be drying and require a moisturizer that won’t undo their progress,” says Dr. Foad.

While pimples are often associated with teenagers, you may also benefit from non-acnegenic products as you age: “I also see many women dealing with hormonal acne in their 30s and 40s, and through perimenopause and menopause, when breakouts can appear for the first time in years,” she adds.

#6797. Reggie Dinkins Is Still the Funniest Show on TV

Tracy Morgan and Daniel Radcliffe return for season 2 of their hilarious NBC sitcom somehow even wittier than before.

It’s a gross exaggeration to say that television is a lost art, but we can maybe agree that it has changed. Big-time. But sadly, not all of it is for the better. The binge model pigeonholes every show into a novel, scriptwriters tragically factor in second-screen doomscrolling, and the half-hour situational comedy has been driven to near extinction. Which is why I thank the television gods for The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins and then thank them again that it’s back so soon.

Still sharp, still absurd, and still just plain funny, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins proves sophomores aren’t always in a slump, with a new season that picks up from season 1’s high point. “More of the same” isn’t bad news here, and if the series can keep pace, we might have a proper TV MVP when other sitcoms can’t make the cut.

Season 2 of Reggie Dinkins, which premiered November 2 on NBC, catches up with Daniel Radcliffe’s anguished auteur, Arthur Tobin, as he documents the show’s hero, Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan). Dinkins is a disgraced football superstar, and he’s hell-bent on rehabilitating his public profile. Arthur still lives in the Dinkins’ crowded New Jersey mansion that also houses Reggie’s levelheaded ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), their son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), Reggie’s younger fiancée Brina (Precious Way), and Bobby Moynihan as Rusty, Reggie’s freeloading BFF who is too integral to the family’s cohesion to kick to the curb.

This season, Arthur grows ever closer to the Dinkins clan, despite his own hyperawareness of his documentary ethics violations. (Episode 2 of this season at last interrogates how compromised the in-progress project has been since the start.) Most of the ensemble, Radcliffe and Morgan included, exists in a sort of stasis—this is a network sitcom, after all—but it’s Precious Way who shines as the much-improved standout of the bunch.

Formerly “just” the younger woman in Reggie’s life last season, Brina has grown into the soul of the show. Along with Way’s buoyant charisma, there’s a newfound depth to Brina that wasn’t present in her before. I’ll admit, I thought she was grating at first blush, and I was ready to write her off as a shallow antagonist who didn’t seem involved with Reggie or the family in earnest. But in season 2, she’s evolved into a phenomenal supporting player who instantly brightens the room and contrasts beautifully with the others, most of all Radcliffe’s flummoxed British artiste. (A throwaway gag involving her “Voice Bucket Challenge” had me cracking up at my desk.) It’s a mere single component upgrade we’re talking about here, but it elevates Reggie Dinkins to a much higher degree this time around.

Jalyn Hall, too, grows in his once-thankless role as Reggie and Monica’s teenage son, Carmelo. Through a new overarching storyline involving a forbidden romance, which becomes a linchpin for most of season 2’s first half, Carmelo crystallizes in his specific variant of “Blerd” that is more refreshing than derivative. He’s not just “The Geek,” as you’d find in most sitcoms. He’s fluid enough to perform the function without killing the buzz.

The first four episodes of the season, provided to the press, keep up season 1’s winning formula—22-minute-sitcom hijinks that unfold against an airy atmosphere with well-timed punchlines. Daniel Radcliffe and Tracy Morgan further assert their powers as TV’s unlikeliest duo, and I can’t get enough of them. I pray there are yet more improbable excuses to ensure multiple seasons of a single documentary’s production. Sure, the rhythms are familiar now, but it’s welcome fun. Reggie Dinkins is a potent reminder of what television used to be and what it still can be if we’re brave enough to let it.

#6796. How to Choose a Graphic Print Bag That Won’t Go Out of Style

Exploring the power of pattern through the lens of Dior’s Cigale.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A printed accessory can bring color, dimension, and personality to an outfit without requiring much else. The key is finding a design that works with the clothes you already own, suits your daily needs, and feels relevant beyond a single season. Dior offers an interesting case study, particularly when it comes to houndstooth, a motif closely associated with the house’s history and Christian Dior’s use of menswear-inspired fabrics in women’s fashion. The Dior Cigale bag, Mini Lady Dior Bag, and Bow bag give us a starting point for exploring the appeal of graphic prints and what makes a patterned accessory a worthwhile long-term purchase.

A graphic print should have enough character to stand out, but it should also work with the clothes you already wear. Houndstooth has a strong geometric pattern that can look just as good with denim as it does with formal, more tailored styles. If you prefer something more playful, a colorful or embellished design can make a familiar outfit feel different.

The bag’s shape and construction matter, too. Consider its size, how you plan to carry it, and whether the materials suit your lifestyle. A bag you intend to use regularly should be practical enough for your routine, with craftsmanship that holds up to frequent wear. The Cigale, for example, has a sculptural silhouette inspired by the architectural lines of a 1952 Christian Dior gown. That connection to couture gives the design a distinct identity, while its silhouette offers something to consider beyond the print alone.

A graphic print bag can work with a range of outfits, particularly when its colors complement the rest of your wardrobe. A black-and-white houndstooth pattern, for instance, pairs naturally with neutral knitwear and sharp separates. More colorful prints can coordinate just as well, provided you give them room to stand out.

The simplest approach is to keep the rest of your outfit relatively restrained. A printed bag can add interest to a white shirt and trousers or break up an all-black look without requiring a complete wardrobe overhaul. If you prefer a more coordinated outfit, pick up one of the bag’s colors in your shoes or another accessory. You don’t need to match everything. Just a little repetition is enough to make the look feel deliberate.

No accessory is immune to changing tastes, but some patterns have been around longer than others. Houndstooth, for one, predates Dior, but the designer incorporated it into his collections alongside other fabrics traditionally associated with menswear. He used these materials in women’s suits and dresses, pairing their masculine character with silhouettes that emphasized the female form. The brand continues to revisit houndstooth, including on the Cigale bag.

If you’re buying a graphic print bag to carry for years, think about whether you’ll wear it with more than one or two outfits. A pattern that works with your everyday wardrobe will get more use than one that calls for a specific look. It’s also worth considering whether you like the bag’s shape on its own. Trends come and go, but a bag you enjoy carrying for reasons beyond its print has a better chance of staying in rotation.

Start with the clothes you already wear. A graphic print bag can add interest to everyday staples like straight-leg jeans, a simple knit, and loafers, or bring some personality to office staples like tailored trousers and a crisp shirt. For dinner, try one with a black dress or a streamlined suit. The idea is to let the print add something to your outfit without making getting dressed more complicated.

You can mix prints, too. A fine stripe or small check can work with a bolder graphic, especially when the colors complement each other. If the combination feels too busy, simplify the rest of the look. With the Cigale, clean lines and structured tailoring can play off its sculptural shape. And remember, the bag doesn’t need much competition. A few well-chosen pieces will let it stand out without overwhelming the outfit.

A graphic print can draw you to a bag, but the details are what make it worth the investment. Look closely at the stitching, hardware, lining, and finish. The materials should feel appropriate for the price, and the construction should hold up to regular use. Consider how the print is worked into the design, too. The pattern should feel like part of the bag, not an afterthought.

With Dior, the appeal also lies in how the house approaches familiar motifs. Its graphic patterns are part of a broader design vocabulary, reinterpreted through changing silhouettes, materials, and embellishments. That gives the Cigale context beyond its appearance alone. Ultimately, a bag’s value comes down to what it offers in design and execution, not just the name on the label.

#6786. Was There a Fall on ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Disney Night, or Was It on Purpose? Dancer Diego Pasillas Speaks Out!

Dancing With the Stars delivered a truly epic series of performances during Disney Night, including a packed opening number complete with a Newsies segment. And the whole thing was so well-choreographed that one of the dancers fell over and recovered so flawlessly that everyone thought it was on purpose.

While there was some debate from fans online, turns out this fall was, in fact, a fall. Dancer Diego Pasillas confirmed as much on Instagram, saying “You guys. I just ate it on national television.” He then did an example of the correct move, recreated his fall, and said “the show must go on.”

Diego’s comments were filled with praise and support from his fellow Dancing With the Stars cast members, including Hailey Bills, who wrote “BUT THE WAY YOU GOT UP,” and Val Chmerkovskiy who commented, “Bro you shablammed it and then shamblammed it in the air.”

Reminder: pro Adele Zaikman had to unexpectedly skip Disney Night due to being sick, and The Sun reports that her absence “left producers and dancers racing to rework multiple performances,” with the rehearsals “becoming even more chaotic” since she was booked for three different dances.

“She had to drop out very last minute, so that mixed with the week already being one day shorter has been really hectic behind the scenes,” a source said. “Multiple troupe members are going to fill in for her. The opening number was the big one. The other two she just had a tiny part, so it wasn’t as big of a deal to fill. But the troupe has been practicing all Monday before showtime.”

In other words, this was a slightly last-minute routine without a lot of practice time!

#6785. The Best Dressed Celebrities at the CFDA Awards

All decked out in their favorite American designers

At most awards shows that we cover—the Oscars, the Golden Globes, the Grammys—fashion is a secondary concern for the judges and nominees. At the CFDAs, however, the entire evening is dedicated to the American fashion industry, and, much to our annual delight, the attendees always dress with that in mind. Last night’s wardrobe selections were not dominated by European fashion houses (or celebrity contracts). Instead, guests seized the opportunity to celebrate American talent, much of which is based here in New York, with collections equally worthy of a spot on the red carpet.

Take, for instance, Mona Tougaard in a sweet, colorblocked look from Lii by Zane Li, who was nominated in the emerging category this year. Or actress Sydney Lemmon, who wore a long-sleeved, button-front black sheath worn just undone enough to reveal a pair of red, bedazzled panties underneath, created by Emily Dawn Long, another emerging nominee. And then there was returning nominee—and winner!—Colleen Allen, who outfitted guest Gracie Abrams in a strapless, twisted, black velvet gown.

Those who represented the larger American brands leaned into a more relaxed approach to dressing. Emily Ratajkowski wore a simple black sweater paired with a low-rise orange skirt and black boots from Tory Burch. Elle Fanning showed up in a dusty pink slip beneath a floor-length leather trench from Coach by Stuart Vevers. (Each was nominated for awards: womenswear and accessory designer, respectively.)

And then came Anthony Vaccarello, nominated for International Designer of the Year, swanning in from Europe with his high-glam, gold-foiled posse. Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, Rosé, and Anja Rubik each wore a look from his megawatt Spring 2027 collection, which was almost entirely blanketed in gold. But they still managed to retain some semblance of casual American ease with bomber jackets layered over knee-length skirts and bedazzled, midriff-baring two-piece sets.

All in all, it was a very well dressed celebration of the country’s fashion industry, so picking our favorites was difficult. But ahead, we’ve rounded up the best-dressed guests of the 2027 CFDA Awards.

Zac Posen transformed classic denim waistbands into sculptural eveningwear.

There’s no denim without Demi. At tonight’s 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City, Demi Moore stepped out in a tongue-in-cheek GapStudio look that redefined the meaning of denim-on-denim.

Designed by Zac Posen, Moore’s custom gown centered on a series of indigo denim waistbands stitched one atop another to form a corseted shape. The bodice featured a halter neckline with folded-over ends, while the low-waisted maxi skirt had a long slit and a slight train.

Moore completed the look with suede pumps, diamond drop earrings, and, of course, a fully denim handbag created by the brand’s executive director of accessories, Reed Krakoff.

Later in the evening, the actress presented the Innovation Award to Richard Dickson and Zac Posen on behalf of Gap Inc. Dickson and Posen, naturally, both wore denim too.

While sculptural and evening-ready, Moore’s gown put a distinctly American spin on the evening’s “American Black Tie” theme. Plus, denim is woven into the fabric of American style—and Gap’s DNA, too.

“Denim is at the heart of Gap’s identity, and I wanted to explore its function in an entirely new way for my dear friend Demi,” Posen said in a statement. “By deconstructing the familiar details of a classic jean and reimagining them through the lens of elevated eveningwear, we created something sculptural, unexpected, and distinctly GapStudio.”

#6777. The Best Mini PCs to Buy in 2026

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

These high-performing, small-footprint models will clean up your workspace.

Tiny computers are nothing new. I know you have one in your pocket right now—that is, if you’re not reading this on it already. The smartphone proved that computers can be anything, and anything can be a computer. Even putting aside the smartphone and the laptop, desktops have been getting smaller and changing form over time. The mini PC (sometimes also called a NUC) is a term that’s getting a lot of use lately, but it’s for something that’s more or less existed for decades: a small, prebuilt computer.

Traditionally, a PC runs Windows, but you can find Linux-based and MacOS-based mini PCs too. Of course, Apple makes its own in the form of the Mac Mini, probably the most popular one on the market. The original version debuted back in 2005, proving my point that these are nothing new, and has made its way into millions of homes without needing anyone to utter the words “mini PC.”

Point is, if you’re looking for something with the capability of a desktop without wanting a space-hogging tower, this is what you need to be looking at. Whether you need a machine for school, work, or gaming, these are the most capable desktops that come in shockingly small packages. These four machines are the best mini PCs to buy right now.

Starting off, it’s the 2026 Mac Mini. For the average person, you can start and stop the shopping journey here. If you want a compact home computer and you’re already deeply embedded in MacOS and Apple’s ecosystem, it’s hard to resist the simple appeal of the Mac Mini M6. It’s unassuming, smaller than a cable box and about the size of your internet modem. Ninety percent of the time, it’s as quiet as either of those too, despite being a fast mid-range computer optimized for AI workloads (more so than any generation before it). In terms of connections, you get a full stack; three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an HDMI port, and an Ethernet port in the back, as well as two USB-C ports and a headphone jack in front. More than plenty for all your accessories.

Like I said, this is a mid-range Mac. It’s just as suited for a home office as the main family computer in the living room. For something with professional level capabilities (we are all professionals, but I’m talking video editing, software development, any 3D model rendering), you’ll want the one with the M5 Pro chip instead. As always, with either of these, the biggest downside is Apple’s walled garden. You can’t upgrade the RAM or storage capacity like you can with other PCs, and Apple isn’t afraid to charge an arm and a leg for the versions that come with extra.

If you’re in both a time and money crunch, this is the kind of computer you want. For less than $400, it’s a Windows-capable machine with 16 gigs of RAM that can output to up to three 4K displays at a time. And unless you are pushing its processing power, it stays cool and relatively silent. It’s got all the ports you’d want—USB, HDMI, DPI, headphone jack—plus two high-speed USB-A ports in the back. These are decent for when you have large files to transfer, but they admittedly pale in terms of speed compared to a Thunderbolt port.

At the price it’s currently at, this is also cheaper than any gaming console out there. Not even as powerful as a Nintendo Switch (the old one), but it can run Minecraft and other casual or indie titles with little trouble.

If your job or home business requires running more and more local AI models (as many do), you might want a mini PC designed with these workflows in mind. Plus, it has every kind of port you’d want and more. With HDMI, USB, Thunderbolt, Ethernet, even an SD card slot and Copilot button, it’s fully kitted out for even the more niche uses.

It’s not a perfect solution. This machine will struggle with more intensive tasks and you’ll hear about it. For its size and light frame (it’s easily mountable to a monitor stand), though, it’s nothing to sneeze at.

Any machine can run some video games, but if you’re the type who considers gaming your hobby of choice, and you need something to play all the latest releases in 4K, well, then you need something as dedicated as you. For a reasonable price tag (trust me, it is), you’re getting a powerful PC with an RTX 5060 graphics card and 32 gigabytes of RAM. For the completely uninitiated, that’s a mid-range 2025 dedicated graphics card—sure to run any modern game, but when it comes to more demanding titles you just may have to choose to prioritize either frame rate or visuals.

Beyond gaming, this is a capable machine due to the decent GPU. And for those who don’t want to tinker at all, the G1 Pro offers three default modes to quickly swap between. Swap from Office to Gaming when it’s time to play, or go into Beast mode when you’re really trying to throttle the machine and get the most out of it.

The real reason to get something like this over a console or Valve’s Steam Machine is that it’s upgradeable. The storage and RAM can both be swapped out for newer or higher-capacity options. It’s not a full-on PC, though. With the CPU and GPU, you’re stuck with what is on board.

#6775. All the Highlights From Lagos Fashion Week 2026

The 16th edition of Lagos Fashion Week celebrated sustainable circularity and local talent.

The spring/summer 2027 fashion month may have come to a close in the major cities, but it’s just getting started everywhere else. Over the course of this past weekend, designers and industry insiders came together in Lagos, Nigeria, for the 16th edition of Lagos Fashion Week. Workshops, panels, and presentations focused on sustainability and local talent, alongside a strong lineup of emerging designers and Nigerian household names. Above all else, the designers demonstrated a commitment to craft and heritage. As Aisha Ayensu, the designer behind Christie Brown, said during a panel discussion on day one: “It is necessary to build a sustainable relationship with African artisans, because the success of any African fashion brand relies on the craft people.”

Global favorite Orange Culture (which has shown internationally at New York and London Fashion Weeks) kicked off the season in the city. Curious about the other moments that happened during Lagos Fashion Week? Read on for some of the designers to know from the new season.

Founded in 2015 by Segun Aladejana, Sevon Dejana puts an emphasis on high-drama evening wear with a sculptural, artistic nod. Think: gowns covered in explosive florals and feathers, but sculpted in an unusual way, with a modernist take on traditional haute couture shapes. The label is for the bold, and there is certainly no lack of embellishment or color, as was the case for the new collection presented on the runway for the new season.

Hertunba puts an emphasis on African craft with experimental, sculptural silhouettes. Founder Florentina Agu started taking dressmaking classes at the age of 13, and officially started her line in 2020. The brand makes a point of employing (and training) local women to sew and weave and also reduces waste. 90 percent of Hertunba’s excess materials are repurposed into handcrafted interior décor like rugs and throw pillows, or are pieced together into new, wearable pieces.

Designed between Lagos and London, PiiLLz and PoiZn takes a slow fashion approach to maximalism. Designer Ifeoma Umenyiora creates pieces that embrace stripes, sequins, and feathers, always with a focal point on color. The label maintains its local craft by offering bespoke tailored gowns and other pieces, all made on-site in its atelier in Lagos.

Launched as a sustainable, gender-neutral line by Adedamola Adebayo, most of Bornstar Nigeria’s pieces are made of fabric that is manufactured locally in Nigeria. The brand’s relaxed tailoring is a colorful new take on Nigerian style. Details like intricate beadwork, crochet, and tassels accent the streamlined, tailored separates, and accessories, like chunky bags, are also strong.

Founded in 2021 by designer Adedayo Ilori, Dimeji Ilori upcycles old pieces to create new garments that are collaged, cut, bleached, and transformed into new tactile wonders. Texture is definitely at the center of the aesthetic. Think: a fluffy hat and matching trims or dresses fully embellished with cowrie shells, as shown above.

#6772. The 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards Celebrated Fashion’s Next Generation—and Its Icons

Rachel Scott, Ralph Lauren, and Colleen Allen were among the night’s top honorees.

Often called the Oscars of American fashion, the CFDA Fashion Awards lived up to the billing last night, drawing a starry crowd to the American Museum of Natural History. The ceremony, now in its 45th year, recognized the designers and creatives shaping the direction of American fashion, from established names to independent newcomers.

Before guests headed inside the museum halls, they stepped onto the red carpet to channel the evening’s dress code, “American design excellence,” where many of the evening’s nominees and honorees were well-represented. ELLE cover star Mona Tougaard wore a punchy primary-color look by Zane Li of LII, who was nominated in the American Emerging Designer of the Year category. Demi Moore and Lupita Nyong’o chose to rework American wardrobe classics in custom GapStudio. And Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, Rosé, and Anja Rubik glimmered in gilded Saint Laurent looks from Anthony Vaccarello’s final collection for the brand. (Vaccarello was honored with the International Designer of the Year Award.)

Then, Thom Browne, the CFDA’s chairman of the board of directors, started the ceremony with powerful opening remarks: “American fashion is at the center of the world and at the center of the spirit of our time,” he said. “It’s never been more important to tell important stories.”

Browne handed the reins off to host Keke Palmer, who delivered a major fashion moment in 1970s Bob Mackie previously worn by Raquel Welch, to begin awarding the evening’s most anticipated prizes. Rachel Scott was crowned American Womenswear Designer of the Year, her second time earning the prize, while Ralph Lauren, set to celebrate 60 years in business in 2027, won American Menswear Designer of the Year.

In her speech, Scott issued a call to action that was especially poignant ahead of the midterm elections. “In a world where independent and marginalized voices are systematically quieted, I feel extremely lucky and very, very responsible,” she said. “And we have a lot of work to do, starting tomorrow morning.”

Colleen Allen, beloved by the New York fashion scene for her bewitchingly feminine but powerful designs, won the coveted Google Shopping American Emerging Designer of the Year Award, while Ana Khouri took home Accessory Designer of the Year for her sculptural jewelry and gravity-defying ear cuffs.

Also included in the programming were a series of special honors, including Tory Burch’s Positive Change Award, Peter Marino’s Fashion Icon Award, and Inez and Vinoodh’s Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award.

#6768. How Her Love of Vintage Changed Writer Keli Goff’s Life

Her collection, which has given new life to some of the great Black designers, is now a museum show.

When Keli Goff began purchasing vintage, it was a way to put together stylish looks for her new job within her budget. But over the years, as her interest grew, collecting became a way of connecting to the stories of Black designers unrecognized during their lifetimes. Goff, a writer who has been on the staff of shows including Being Mary Jane and And Just Like That, now owns work from major fashion figures like Patrick Kelly, Isaia Rankin, Stephen Burrows, and Ann Lowe, together making up one of the biggest private collections of work by Black designers. This month, the Houston Museum of African American Culture presents “Collecting in Color: Highlights from the Keli Goff Collection,” which was curated by John Guess and Danielle Finnerman. It’s the first major exhibition focused on her collection, and some of the pieces will be donated to the Bard Graduate Center’s Study Collection.

Goff’s interest in fashion design has intersected with her writing career in interesting ways. The estate of legendary costume designer Edith Head chose Goff to adapt her story for a biopic. “It’s all so surreal. I obviously have admired Edith’s work as long as I can remember, so my collection bringing this project into my life is a dream come true,” she says. Last year, Goff completed studying to become an art appraiser. She now consults in the art and auction sphere in addition to writing.

“People have been fascinated by my collection,” Goff says. “It’s a bit rare to see, frankly, collectors in this space like me. I mean like me in all sorts of ways, not just as an African American woman, but an African American woman who’s not from a privileged background. It’s important to me that I’m not the last one like me in these spaces.”

Goff spoke to ELLE about the joy of working with a museum in her Texas hometown, the old movies that inspired her love of vintage, and the designers she wishes everyone knew.

It really started by watching old movies with my mom and watching her dress up [when I was] a little girl. When I show friends old photos of her, people are always thinking, “Oh, she looks like a movie star or very Diana Ross-esque.” We would watch old movies, especially Imitation of Life and things from that era, the real glamour, the golden age of Hollywood. She would always say, “Look at the dresses, look at the dresses,” and I would. I really fell in love with old movies, which I do believe is part of how I ended up becoming a writer.

But also, I really fell in love with vintage clothes. I moved to New York and didn’t have a lot of money, and vintage was not trendy and didn’t cost thousands of dollars like it can be today. For one of my earliest jobs, I had to go to fancy events, but I had no money. I bought a couple of pieces from the ’60s at a flea market. I remember being at this event, and all these women who obviously had a lot more money to spend on clothes, asking, “Who’s this by? What boutique did you buy this at?” And I was like, “Oh, I got it at a flea market on Avenue B.” I think they thought I was joking.

I wrote a piece for The Daily Beast several years ago about the most influential Black designers in history. It was one of the most memorable pieces I’ve written. I don’t think at the time I was aware of how profoundly it impacted me, but I learned how many seminal Black American designers died of AIDS in a really short window of time. Willi Smith, one of the first Black designers to achieve major crossover commercial success in department stores, died. And so did Isaia Rankin and then Patrick Kelly. What I took away is that so much history was lost, but I also think about how different the future of American fashion might be today because these were really trailblazing and hugely influential.

They weren’t just influential Black American designers, but hugely influential American designers. Isaia Rankin basically had invented athleisure wear. It was his idea that you should be able to go from a coffee shop to a gym to the club. [He made] one of the first pieces by a Black designer I acquired online. I’ll never forget that the person selling it said, “This belonged to my aunt. Apparently, this guy used to be somebody,” which I just think is the saddest thing. He had this profound impact and then had been largely forgotten.

During the pandemic, when everyone worked from home with too much time on their hands and easy access to shop online, I ended up acquiring quite a bit, in part because a lot of the brick-and-mortar stores, particularly in Europe, were really struggling. They were so reliant on tourist foot traffic, and so a lot of them started selling online [for the first time]. And so there were a number of French boutiques I started acquiring pieces from, including some Patrick Kelly pieces that still have the original store tags from the 1980s, which I won’t remove. Those I won’t wear. The rest of them I wear when they fit. As life goes, they don’t always fit forever.

I’ve become friendly with Patrick Kelly’s widower, Bjorn Amelan, who’s a lovely, wonderful man and the keeper of Patrick’s legacy. It is important to me, when possible, to try to maintain relationships with the people I view as keepers of the legacies because I see my collection as serving the legacy of the designers. The pieces don’t belong to me. They belong to our wider community because they’re a part of our lived history.

The really cool thing is how many people I’ve met along this journey who have not only become cheerleaders but actually reach out to me about pieces. Writer Jill Kargman has become a friend and she gifted me a vintage Stephen Burrows dress. She said, “It belongs in your collection,” which is just the coolest thing ever.

I’m from Houston, and we have the Houston Museum of African American Culture here. We’re living in a really interesting time where people are having conversations about the politics of diversity, but one of the things that’s cool about fashion is that people of different political persuasions were like, “I think this collection’s really cool. I read an article about your collection, I ended up ordering a book about Elizabeth Keckley, or I ended up going down a rabbit hole about Ann Lowe.” At this moment, to be able to do an exhibition like this in my hometown felt particularly poignant.

Melanie Lawson has been a legendary anchor in Houston for decades. She was asked what she’s going to do in retirement, and she said that her husband, John Guess Jr., was the CEO of the Houston Museum of African American Culture. I sent him a note about how much Melanie inspired me and then mentioned my collection.

It was just kismet. They’ve actually never done a fashion exhibition. It was a real gamble. But what I so appreciated is that they had the same vision that, in a time in which our world is so divided, it’s really beautiful when you can find pieces of art that people can come together around.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

The cutthroat lawyers of All's Fair provide more than just fashion inspiration and captivating plot twists. Each character also embodies one or more zodiac signs. Together, the power players of Grant, Ronson, & Greene represent the 12 signs’ best traits—and some of their not-so-nice ones, too. Aries is assertive, ambitious, and impulsive. They go after what they want, even if it means being the bad guy. And if nobody wants to join them, they’ll do their own thing. The first sign of the zodiac, Aries is ruled by Mars, the planet of war—a fitting influence for their ability to turn any courtroom into a battlefield.

A born romantic who yearns for a life of luxury—that’s the earth sign Taurus. But it’s not all red roses and dreamy silk gowns. Taurus also shows determination and a serious work ethic; the sign is known for its stubborn pursuit of goal.

Gemini is the hyper-intelligent sign of communication. They not only find out information, but strategically choose how and when to reveal it. Gemini loves to make a statement, whether with what they say or what they wear.

Cancer feels everything fully, and their big heart can often lead them to form bonds with unexpected people. At the same time, their mood can also cause drama. Like Emerald, this water sign’s empathetic nature makes it easy to relate to others and understand where they’re coming from—even if their lives and personalities are totally different.

Scorpio is all about power—who has it, who wants it, and how to use it. The most ambitious sign of the zodiac, Capricorn will stop at nothing to get what they want. Hard-working and intelligent, they’re more motivated by material gains than intangible ideals. As the sign of innovation, Aquarius loves nothing more than breaking with tradition and setting out independently. When the old ways don’t work, they create a new way. Aquarius is also quite independent; they’re often more comfortable alone rather than relying on others.

Pisces is the last sign of the zodiac, a placement that gives it wisdom. They often find themselves in a mentor role, inspiring the younger people who follow in their career footsteps. #6765. Jamaica Revisited: A New Expression of Caribbean Luxury

Sandals Resorts elevates its robust amenities across the properties of its home island.

There are places in the sun that are just a little more special than the rest. Jamaica is one of them, with powder-sand shores lined with luxury resorts; a dense, verdant interior laced with waterfalls and coffee farms; waters that range from the lightest turquoise to the darkest navy; and a distinctive cuisine layered with spice. The beaches are spectacular and the natural wonders such as the crystalline YS Falls and the winding Martha Brae River are just that—full of awe and adventure.

The Taíno name for Jamaica is Xaymaca, which translates to “the land of wood and water”—and few descriptions capture the island more distinctly. For Sandals Resorts, that ethos has inspired a homegrown luxury. Born in Jamaica more than four decades ago, the brand remains deeply rooted in the island’s familial spirit, personality, food, and topography, even as its properties continue to evolve beyond their birthplace. The result is an immersive travel experience shaped by beaches, lush mountains, local flavors, deep culture, and the people who make Jamaica an unforgettable destination.

From the energy of Montego Bay and Ocho Rios to the sweeping coastline of Negril and the more tranquil pockets of the South Coast, the seven Sandals resorts across Jamaica each offer distinct ways to settle into the island. Across the collection properties, accommodations function as private retreats within a bigger resort experience. Swim-Up Suites allow guests to slide directly from the terrace into the water. Private pools create an aquatic world unto themselves. And on the Caribbean Sea, the Overwater Butler Villas turn a quiet resting place above the water into a pampered vacation lifestyle.

This year, a trio of properties are entering significantly new chapters following gorgeous reimaginings. The iconic comebacks promise renewed accommodations, including new Swim-Up suites, and new dining options. Cocooned by nature thanks to its setting beside a 500-acre preserve, Sandals Jamaica South Coast reopens November 18, with Overwater Butler Villas and the brand’s first Two Queen Junior Suites—perfect for friend-group travel. One month later, December 18 sees the return of Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, introducing a redesigned pool, Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay features newly refreshed accommodations, which are luxurious cocoons. Some days the hardest decision you make might be whether to head for the beach, dine at your favorite restaurant, or remain in your robe exactly where you are.

At Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, the resort where the brand first began, renewed ocean-view suites promise an impressive vantage point to view the gorgeous ocean. The new Bay Roc Rum Club embraces the music and rum culture that’s part of the fabric of Jamaica and the Caribbean.

Nearby, the former Sandals Jamaica Royal Caribbean emerges as Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with a unique resort experience centered around the sea and water. The new SkyPool Suites will feature a private plunge pool with an infinity edge that’s cantilevered from a large open air terrace, allowing guests to swim while enjoying uninterrupted views of the white sand and aqua waters below.

Further south, the secluded Sandals Jamaica South Coast offers ultra-luxury villas, including detached overwater villas arranged in a heart shape over the calm lagoon. Each comes equipped with see-through glass floor panels, outdoor overwater hammocks, and private boat dock access for the ultimate ocean-to-door service.

Jamaican food rarely arrives without presence. Scotch bonnets bring the heat, pimento adds the spice, and jerk carries the intensity of wood and smoke long before the plate lands on the table. That sense of heritage is part of the experience at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with Suppa, a new restaurant inspired by the island ritual of Sunday dinner. The menu celebrates familiar Jamaican flavors in savory dishes, stews, and curries served in a casual, supper-style setting made for sharing plates around the table. The adjoining Keynote Rum Bar features a soundtrack of the island’s legends in a laid-back lounge drenched in warm leather and rich tones, plus an extensive Caribbean rum selection.

The waterfront Buccan at Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay brings a different kind of fire. This open air space is where meats, seafood, and veggies are cooked over an open hearth and served at family-style tables set by the ocean. The well-received concept first debuted at the lush and secluded Sandals Saint Vincent, nestled in its own private cove, and is now arriving in Jamaica.

Visiting Sandals Jamaica South Coast, every beach day can start with Jamaica’s renowned Blue Mountain coffee and island pastries at BLŪM before afternoons stretch into hours at The Jerk Shack, enjoying must-have Jamaican jerk chicken, jerk pork, fish in foil, and other heritage-style comfort snacks. At the newly arrived Butch’s Island Chop House, excellent steak dinners and perfectly chilled martinis are on the menu.

Arguably one of the greatest luxuries while on a getaway is not having to weigh every decision. Sandals’ all-inclusive model is built around freedom. Not only are meals, snacks, and drinks included, but so are many of the resort experiences that turn a beach trip into an adventure, such as snorkeling, paddleboarding, kayaking, and daily diving for certified scuba divers, as well as classes to become PADI certified. Back on land, guests can move from the beach to an active day at the tennis and pickleball courts. For the golf lover, a day at Sandals Ochi, Sandals Dunn’s River, and Sandals Royal Plantation in Jamaica also include complimentary greens fees at Upton Estate Golf & Country Club in the green hills above Ocho Rios.

All-inclusive leaves room for every traveler to have their own version of the Caribbean holiday. One guest may spend the morning beneath the surface of the sea and the afternoon learning pickleball, then indulging in fresh sushi and sashimi. Another may decide the day’s only pursuit should be moving from a suite to a lounge chair, then being served jerk chicken or just-out-the-oven pizza beachside.

For all of Jamaica’s waterfalls, rivers, lagoons, beaches, and mountains, the element travelers often cherish most is a feeling of welcome. The ease of a conversation with the butler, the waiter who remembers your daily coffee order, the laugh with the bartender that extends a quick interaction into a memory, the recommendation to try a local dish, visit a secluded beach or a local shop or market that might have otherwise been missed is waiting in Jamaica.

That kind of Jamaican hospitality at Sandals cannot be engineered by simply refreshing a pool or designed into a new suite. It comes from people knowing how to welcome guests to their home. At Sandals Resorts, the flavor, the memorable landscapes, and the contagious Jamaican warmth makes visitors feel less like they simply arrived at a destination—and more like they’ll be welcomed back again and again.Book your Jamaican getaway today at sandals.com.

#6758. 17 Candidates Who Made History in the 2026 Midterms

From Gina Hinojosa to Peggy Flanagan, these soon-to-be senators, representatives, and governors broke barriers in races across the country.

Democrats took control over the House of Representatives and the Senate in a sweeping midterm election that saw voters reject President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidates and policies.

Amid the “blue wave,” numerous candidates made history as they won—becoming the first of their background, or their gender, to hold the office. While many of them “avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters’ rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded,” notes the Associated Press. With the Democrats’ victory, too, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries will likely become the first Black Speaker of the House.

“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, told the AP. “For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy. These wins are because of them.”

While the majority of these politicians are Democrats, two Republican governors also made history last night—Marsha Blackburn, who became the first woman elected to serve as governor of Tennessee, and Bryon Donalds, who is set to become Florida’s first Black governor. Ahead, 17 soon-to-be senators, governors, and members of the House of Representatives who also claimed a historic “first” in the midterms.

Dr. El-Sayed became the first Muslim American elected to the Senate. “I’m not running to be the first Muslim anything,” El-Sayed told CNN. “I just want to be a really, really great senator for my state.”

Pappas became the first openly gay male Senator upon winning his election in New Hampshire.

Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, is set to become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate. (She could be joined by Alaska’s Mary Peltola, of the Yup’ik tribe, but that race has not been called yet.)

Turek, two-time Paralympic gold medalist for Team USA (with the wheelchair basketball team), was elected in Iowa. He will become the first Senator to have been a Paralympian, and the first Senator with spina bifida.

Not only did Bottoms become Georgia’s first Black and first female governor, she is the first Black woman to be elected governor of any U.S. state.

“Tonight should remind us all that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person,” Bottoms said in her victory speech. “It’s been defined by all of us, and I will be a governor for everyone in this state.”

Becerra, the former United States Secretary of Health and Human Services, was elected the first Latino governor of California.

Hinojosa was elected the first Latina governor of Texas. She will also be the first Democratic governor of the Lone Star State in more than three decades.

Haaland, former United States Secretary of the Interior, will be the first Native American woman governor. “Tonight, in our nation’s 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” she said last night.

Haaland, of Pueblo Indian descent, is no stranger to making history: She was the the first Native American cabinet secretary.

Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor of Ohio and the state’s first Jewish governor.

Crowley will become the first Black governor of Wisconsin. He actually dropped out of the race over the summer, but rejoined at the urging of the outgoing Democratic governor.

Former Senator Klobuchar will become the first woman to be governor of Minnesota.

With Stratton’s victory in the senate race in Illinois, the state will now be represented by two women of color—the first time in U.S. history both senators from a state are women of color.

Kiros’s victory in Colorado’s first district was history making in numerous ways: At 29, she is the first Gen Z woman elected to the House, and Colorado’s first Black woman representative.

Dr. Andrews, a pediatrician, became the first woman ever elected to the U.S. Senate from South Carolina.

Nevada’s Attorney General is poised to become the first Black governor of the state.

Dr. Hamawy, a retired U.S. Army combat surgeon, will be the first Muslim representative from New Jersey.

Valdez, citizen of Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo, is set to become the first female Native American member of Congress from New York.

Emily Burack (she/her) is the Deputy Digital Editor for Town & Country, where she covers entertainment, celebrities, the royals, and a wide range of other topics. Before joining T&C, she was the deputy managing editor at Hey Alma, a Jewish culture site. Follow her @emburack on Instagram, Twitter, and other social media platforms.

#6756. Reckoning With Borat, 20 Years Later

Last month, I sat in a packed-to-the-gills movie theater to experience the latest release from a controversial comedian whose work regularly blurs the line between docu-reality and narrative fiction. I am, of course, referring to Ali G: Who Iz I?—the cinematic return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s once-and-still-somewhat-beloved durag-doffing titular character.

Before the film was unceremoniously dumped on Prime Video last week, I managed to snag a ticket to the only New York City screening that wasn’t totally sold-out, booking a seat—last row, tucked in an alcove of the theater—with the intention of isolated note-taking and (gasp!) the occasional phone-glance should the movie prove tedious. The recliners next to me were eventually claimed by a gentleman decked in a very Ali G-esque skull cap and wraparounds, who unleashed a deafening “BOOYAKASHA!” after Nicole Kidman’s AMC intro.

Cohen’s brand of confrontational cringe comedy continues to attract a level of interest, thanks in part to a certain mustached-and-mankini’d Kazakh journalist. The cultural explosion that was Borat! Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (has any movie title so padded the word count?) turns 20 years old this week, and it remains a curious artifact of the 2000s: impossibly dated and slightly better than you might remember, even as its creator’s talent has slowly and unmistakably eroded.

If you were just old enough to purchase a ticket to an R-rated movie in 2006, Borat felt like a truly out-of-nowhere phenomenon in terms of mass impact. But the character, armed with little more than a shabby suit and an aggressive cheer, emerged from Cohen’s cult favorite Da Ali G Show, which ran for one season on BBC’s Channel 4 in 2000 before making the leap to HBO in 2003. Alongside Ali G and the gay Austrian fashion correspondent Brüno, Borat Sagdiyev was just one of the many personalities Cohen regularly deployed in the thorny thickets of gotcha-mentary, trading in culturally oblivious and antisemitic observations supposedly inherited from his Kazakh homeland, often to the shock and dismay of his unsuspecting subjects.

These fool-me-once hijinks weren’t necessarily groundbreaking, even for HBO’s then-provocative late-night programming. Several years prior, The Chris Rock Show engaged in similar man-on-the-street shenanigans (once, he polled residents of NYC’s notoriously hate-crime-prone Howard Beach region about renaming a street after Tupac Shakur). But segments in which Ali G addressed Buzz Aldrin as Buzz Lightyear, or the one where Borat led a bar full of Arizonans in a rousing chorus of “Throw the Jew Down the Well,” were practically reverse-engineered for virality in the internet’s pre-social-media infancy, and the appeal of Cohen’s approach—how far will he go, and will ordinary folk follow him?—was easy to understand, regardless of the visceral discomfort it may have generated.

Straying from the sketch-based format of Da Ali G Show, Borat embraced a loose narrative structure, with its titular inquirer setting out for America to make a documentary on the country’s social peccadilloes with the intent of eventually romancing Pamela Anderson. If you want to get highfalutin about it, the plot itself situates Borat within the legacy of films about Europeans attempting to understand America—a small-but-fascinating subgenre that includes Paul Verhoeven’s fairytale-cum-nightmare Showgirls, the post-hippie pessimism of Michaelangelo Antonioni’s Zabriskie Point, and Kristoffer Borgli’s social-mores rom-dramedy The Drama.

Don’t get it twisted, though: Borat was and still is best enjoyed as a showcase of physical comedy and inflammatory non sequiturs. It’s no less funny in 2026 to watch a grown man wash his face in a toilet bowl, or gesture toward a tortoise while sincerely asking, “What type of dog is this?” The scene in which an etiquette coach attempts to guide Borat through the intricacies of comic timing is itself an excellent study in comic timing; the notorious full-frontal hotel chase sequence between Borat and his producer Azamat (portrayed by steadily-working character actor Ken Davitian) is a marvel for its sheer escalation alone. This stuff killed in a massive Northern New Jersey movie theater when I was 19, and it still kills from the confines of my couch 20 years on.

Unlike much of Cohen’s subsequent work, Borat is not an explicitly political film. Nonetheless, a good deal of its “GREAT SUCCESS!”—$262 million in box receipts off an $18 million budget, with a Best Actor Golden Globe for Cohen himself—is undoubtedly owed to a different sort of comic timing. The film came out in the throes of George W. Bush’s second presidential term, with the US mired in two wars abroad and a hell of its own making. Americans were thirsty for easy targets to shoulder the blame and, if possible, provide some cheap laughs in the process.

Their thirst was quenched in the form of Borat’s many unsuspecting subjects. Some of this was low-hanging fruit: Borat telling a group of feminists to smile more, or acting like a literal bull in a china shop amidst Confederate memorabilia. But the film’s more sensational material depicted rough corners of the American psyche long hidden in plain sight. Most memorably, Borat encounters a group of rowdy frat boys who huff about white pride and express dismay at the abolishment of slavery before engaging in a viewing of Anderson’s infamous leaked sex tape with ex-husband Tommy Lee.

Not everyone was displeased at their portrayal, though. Joe and Miriam Behar, the Jewish couple who offered Borat and Azamat room and board, were good-natured in a 2006 interview with the Boston Globe. For her part, Miriam shrugged off Borat’s naked antisemitism. “To me it's an anti-Muslim movie, not anti-Jewish, because Kazakhstan is mostly Muslim,” she offered.

Behar’s observation underlines the casual bigotry that otherwise stains Borat. The film’s portrayal of Kazakh culture is undoubtedly offensive, and provoked mixed reactions from the country’s government for years to come. For what it’s worth, Cohen pushes back—intentionally or not—on anti-Muslim sentiments during the film’s rodeo sequence, in which Borat tells a particularly racist attendee that he is indeed “not Muslim.”

But given the post-9/11 climate into which Borat was launched, the implications of a foreign correspondent from a majority-Muslim country espousing antisemitic and misogynistic viewpoints are crystal-clear, and Cohen himself seems too smart to sincerely profess a lack of awareness as to how this might be received. It doesn’t help that his subsequent projects resulted in exponential escalations of offense: 2012’s more narratively-focused The Dictator spared no quarter when it came to stereotypes of Arab culture, while the astoundingly homophobic Brüno, from 2009, was loaded with gags about anal sex and resulted in an out-of-court settlement with a Palestinian grocer who was falsely credited as a former terrorist in the film itself.

After 2016’s box-office bomb Grimsby, which is most notable for the allegations of on-set sexual harassment co-star Rebel Wilson later brought toward Cohen, his work went in a more explicitly political direction. There was his 2018 docu-satire series Who Is America?—two episodes of which featured writing and directing contributions from Nathan Fielder—and 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a second-verse-same-as-the-first sequel which earned several Oscar nominations and brought a truly bizarre “October surprise” to that year’s presidential election involving actress Maria Bakalova, Rudy Giuliani, and the former New York City Mayor’s pants zipper.

Both of those films were more explicitly message-y than they were riotously funny. Cohen’s latest, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is neither, carrying the all-too-familiar stink of a comedian insisting that their capacity to offend amounts to protected speech. At 55, Cohen is clearly not as willing to submit himself to the ragdoll physics he once deployed; in its place is an often-sullen-looking Ali G, his dreads now gray, weighing the merits of cultural appropriation and sparring with a DEI coordinator about the origins of the durag. The entire affair is belabored and depressing.

It made me think of the Who Is America? character Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, a send-up of Rachel Dolezal-flavored liberals in the form of a Berkeley professor who dons dashikis and keffiyehs. Early in the film, he rages against Ali G’s culturally appropriative ways to a majority-Black community meeting in Oakland. “We don’t care!,” shouts one participant. In hindsight, it’s as much an expression of exhaustion with the dictates of capital-D discourse as it is a referendum on Cohen’s confrontational method, which now yields far less interesting insights about the national psyche than it did when Borat arrived on American soil in 2006.
