#6726. The Real-Life Diet of John King, Who Hides Mini Protein Bars Behind the Magic Wall on Election Night

Nobody white knuckles Election Day the way John King does. Since 2008, CNN’s chief national correspondent has spent his midterm and presidential elections in wizard-like command of the Magic Wall—the omnipresent interactive map that drills into granular data from county to county as votes trickle in. (This year it will also include stats that show whether the cost of gas, rent, or groceries have increased or decreased in specific precincts.) The so-called charthrob has also completed some especially long shifts—working back-to-back 12- to 16-hour days during the 2020 presidential election, when results took about a week to tabulate. This year, to prepare for the midterms, he’s been traveling nonstop between battleground states, interviewing sources to stay on top of the national mood. “The way to be at my best on election night is to actually do the homework by visiting those places in the year and a half or so leading up to the election,” he says.

That is no easy task, given the 63-year-old dad of three also lives with multiple sclerosis. To keep his symptoms in check and his head cool as results pour in, he’s created a disciplined regime that includes hitting the gym no matter how little sleep he gets, keeping a mental map of healthy places to eat in flyover country, and occasionally giving himself time to sightsee—or stare at a wall. GQ spoke with King a week ahead of Tuesday’s races to learn how he keeps steady amid the chaos.

John King: All this year, I’ve been on the road, on average, about two weeks a month for the midterm cycle. And we started obviously late last year. You have to do that. This last week is particularly grueling. Normally we go out and we do one state and we travel into say, North Carolina. We were there for three days. We went to Texas and we were there for four days, three nights. The schedule’s pretty busy on those days, but you have a little bit of breathing room and you can make time for a hotel gym and you can search a little bit to find a better restaurant that might have a few actual salads or fresh fish on the menu. This week, we’re doing five states in five days.

That included working until about 10 o’clock on Monday night and then having to catch a 6 a.m. flight Tuesday morning. It included last night wrapping at about 8 o’clock in Detroit and having to drive four, four and a half hours into central Ohio to be here today. On those days, you’re not really in control of your schedule. Your schedule is in charge of you. You just have to be somewhere at a certain point the next day. So everything is driven by that.

So can you fly there? If not, you have to drive there. And in those situations, if you’re talking about trying to keep a healthy diet, that becomes a pretty tough challenge. You’re driving past the McDonald’s and the Burger Kings and the Culvers and you’re thinking, Oh, wow, that looks great. And you shouldn’t go anywhere near it.

Sometimes you do. Sometimes you do because you decided you deserve a treat. Sometimes you do because you have no choice. My philosophy about that is, like anything in life, if you indulge, then you just have to pay the price on the other end. So that means having yogurt and granola for breakfast and some berries, and that means making sure you get to the gym.

I’m psychotic about the gym. In part because I have multiple sclerosis and I have some mobility challenges sometimes. At the end of just about every day, I get what the doctors call MS fatigue. You get headaches and your legs are very heavy. And so I have found in dealing with this that if I exercise in the morning, it really helps me. And so the other day, when we had that 6 a.m. flight, even though I didn’t get to bed until 11 at night, I got up at 2 in the morning and went to the hotel gym.

I’m trading sleep for exercise, which if you do that over 10 days, two weeks, you’re going to pay a price for it. But we’re doing five states in five days. It’s going to be pretty grueling anyway. We had an early start this morning. We had to be to a farm pretty early, and so I was at the hotel gym at 5:30 in the morning. That’s just part of my routine.

That depends on how much time I have. If I can, I work out for about 90 minutes in the morning. Every gym is a little different. Some hotels are great, some hotels are in-between. The hotel we stayed in last night was a bit of a time warp. The equipment was pretty old. If there’s a recumbent bike, I obviously have either emails from overnight to read or news articles to read or things to write. So I’ll spend 30 minutes or so on a recumbent bike, where I’m pedaling to get my body warmed up and I’m also doing some work, reading and communicating about the day ahead.

And then I get on the treadmill for a little bit. I’m not a runner, but I can jog a little bit, or do incline treadmill just to get my heart rate up a little bit, and then try to do a little bit of light weights if I have the time.

You do what you can. I’m pretty set in that I bike because I have to do some administrative stuff and that’s easiest on the bike. And then I get on the treadmill where I just try to listen to music and zone out a little bit. And if I can, I’ll do a quick circuit of some light weights because if you just do cardio, that one beer you have at the end of the night stays with you. So you got to do the weight.

I don’t usually write scripts or anything, but I will write to people back in Washington who are asking me questions. Or if I’m trying to find somebody on trips like this, a lot of stuff we do on the fly. I’ll occasionally write graphics. If I know I need to write a graphic or in the middle of a process, if we’re editing a piece, the editor might send me a graphic that they’ve done, What do you think? I’m not trying to write my actual scripts for pieces. Sometimes I tweak them, but if I tried to write them from scratch on a bike, I would lose my mind.

You have no choice. If I’m going to get my exercise in, at least part of that, it’s going to have to include some work time.

Yes. When I travel. I started this when I covered the White House—I covered the White House for 10 years—especially on international trips where you’re living on local time wherever you are in the world, but our CNN programming is on US time. I would have what I call the 20-minute rule where no matter how tired I was, if I was in a cool place around the world or even in the country, I just tried to get outside of the hotel for 20 minutes of me time. And so if you’re in Paris, you take a walk and stare at the Eiffel Tower.

I remember the Bush-Putin trip to Estonia where Bush said he looked into Putin’s soul. That became a big controversy. I remember after that day—we were on television all day and it was a big day—just walking around and looking at the architecture. The Berlin Wall had come down. We were a decade past that or more. But in a lot of those countries, you’d have this fabulous European architecture, like you’re in Paris or like you were in Prague, and then across the street would be this horrible concrete structure that the communists built.

And so that’s how I learned. I’m a kid who grew up in Dorchester, Massachusetts. My family had no money. We never traveled. So I have this enormous gift of this job that sends me everywhere. And so I really think it’s important both for the curiosity part of it, but also I have a lot of work to do, but I’ll actually be more efficient at my job if I take 20 minutes to just say, “Wow, this is a cool place. Let’s enjoy it.”

I don’t think of myself as someone who meditates, but do I sit still sometimes and listen to music. I try to keep up with the books my son in high school is reading. Sorry, CNN, sorry, politics, sorry, campaigns. I’m filing you away for 15 or 20 minutes. That’s absolutely critical to mental health.

I try to pack a carry-on on this trip because we’re out for five days. Plus, on the tail end of it, I have to go to New York City because my daughter lives in New York City and she just got engaged and we’re having a celebration for her on Saturday night.

Thank you. It’s a really amazing time. And of course, it all comes in a tornado, but that’s fine. But I have to bring a suit and I have to bring some other clothes. And as I said, my exercise is important, so I have to pack gym stuff. So usually I think of myself as a very efficient, tight packer so that I can have a carry-on bag, just so, number one, they can’t lose it. And number two, you can keep moving faster. But on this trip, I actually have to check my bag because I’m on the road for six days and then I’m going to New York for two more. I don’t like checking a bag, but so be it. I have to do it on this trip.

I operate on East Coast time all the time. I get tired. I wouldn’t really even call it jet lag because I try to keep my body on East Coast time and my brain on East Coast time because that’s who I report to. After international trips, I’ll get jet-lagged, but exercise is important, number one. I drink too much coffee, and so on a long trip, that can get to you. Your body gets a little jittery if you have a little bit of jet lag. You try to sleep when you can. One thing I was never good at until campaigns is napping. Now I can take a 20-minute nap. There was a time in my life I could not nap. I can take a 20-minute nap now, which helps you sometimes when you need to. But I’m just trying to think of the last time I had really profound jet lag. I can’t have jet lag, I guess.

Yeah. I’m not allowed. My work doesn’t allow me normally, so I just bull through it. That doesn’t mean I don’t get tired. This trip is going to be grueling. I’ll get to New York on Saturday and I’ll have three or four hours before my daughter’s dinner and I’ll need to get to the gym, but I’m also betting I’ll stare at a wall for a few minutes and just be like, Whoa. But I don’t dwell on it because I can’t.

It gets hard on the hotel menu. Most hotels now at least will have a yogurt parfait or at least yogurt. There’s a very wide—what do we want to call it?— quality control or quality between the different kind of hotels you stay at.

We’ve been to Wisconsin several times. There’s a hotel called The Trade in Wisconsin we always stay at and they have a spectacular yogurt granola parfait bowl. I know in the morning I’m going to have a nice, healthy breakfast. Other places, it’s a challenge and you can’t find it or you just have no choice. So you grab the bacon, egg and cheese sandwich and that means I’m having a salad for lunch.

Then when you’re on the road, like last night, we were driving here, we had a four-and-a-half-hour drive, so you stop at a random gas station in small town America and you’re a little hungry. I try to grab the almonds, not the potato chips. Luckily, I’ve never been a sugar person, so I’m not going to drink soda that has sugar in it. I don’t even really drink diet soda. But on the road, it’s mostly water and coffee. And then, I’d be lying if I didn’t say I’m very happy if I could find a cold beer at the end of the day.

Yesterday, we had fantastic Middle Eastern food in Dearborn, Michigan. Just a chicken salad, falafel. And we’ve been back there a couple times. There are a couple other places where we know of these small businesses, just some local person has started, just a place where they just have salads and healthy smoothies. When we’re in those towns, we go back to those places because we’re grateful they’re there and they help us reset the bad-road-food meter.

If I’m in Kansas City, I’m going to Arthur Bryant’s barbecue, and that is full of sodium and it’s not good for you, but it’s amazing.

Part of it, especially since my MS diagnosis, I know that I’m going to get tired. I may have issues with both my leg and my hand functions. You learn a lot more from your struggles than you do from your successes, and I’m much more aware of my body on a daily basis, even on a minute-to-minute basis of how I’m doing and what are my challenges at the moment. Hydration is critically important.

On election night, I might be standing for 16 hours. It’s probably closer to 12, but it might be 16. If you go back to 2020 when we had the election that went on all week, we didn’t call the election until Saturday. I was on my feet for 14 or 15 hours the first night, and then 12 hours the next day, and then 12 hours the day after that. That was a huge challenge.

That week was the longest. I’ve been on the road for campaigns covering candidates where it’s event, bus, presidential campaigns, you’re going from state to state. So it’s event, bus, plane, event, bus, plane, event, bus, plane. They’re handing you a box. You don’t even know what’s in it, but you eat it. Because it’s the only food you’re going to get for the next 10 hours.

In the studio, I’m standing on my feet the whole time, but I have access to cold water. Somebody can get me a coffee. If you’re on television, you’re just asking for it if you try to eat a salad or anything like that because it’s going to get in your teeth and you don’t have time to go down the hall. You just don’t. You’re on live television. So I get little tiny mini protein bars and put a few of them behind the Magic Wall. And if I feel like I just need a little energy boost, I’ll eat those. I drink more coffee than I should, but coffee will help me when I need a boost. And then when I’m done, I can go to sleep. I can have a Nespresso after dinner and go to bed. My colleagues hate me because of that.

When I am sometimes challenged by the MS issues I have, it’s when something surprising happens and I’m not prepared for it. And then an hour into having to do something that I didn’t know I was going to have to do, I might think, Wow, my legs are jello, or having, they call it MS brain. It’s like a foggy brain issue sometimes.

But I know the election is Tuesday. A lot of people ask me, “Why are you going on the road for five days? You don’t need to do that.” I do need to do it. Professionally, I need to do it. Physically, I will pay a price for this, but I know that. And so you just prepare for it.

The human brain is amazing. I don’t pretend to understand it, and MS has a lot of mysteries, but from when I was first diagnosed to now, I can prepare myself for something and I’ve been able to get through it, knock on wood, which is my skull.

I was diagnosed in 2008, and so we’ve had many big election nights since then, and I’ve gotten through them, and I’ll get through this next one. And then when it’s over, I will collapse. I’ll go home and I’ll fall into bed and I’ll sleep. But if I have to get up in four hours and do it again, I will. I’ve just trained myself to do that.

I work out a lot so that I stay fit physically and that I have good stamina. I’m 63 years young, as I like to say, so it’s important anyway that you stay more physically fit and more active in your body. Part of that is preparation.

In 2020, I was having issues with my hands, and my hands have to navigate a touchscreen Magic Wall. It’s hard for me to explain because you can’t see it, but the few people who have been around me when I’m having some struggles could see it. I have to watch more closely. I have to follow my hand because I can’t trust it to get where it’s going to go because it’s not connected to my brain.

I don’t know what’s in front of you right now, but if you have a notebook or a glass of water, you see it and you reach for it and then you stop looking. You don’t watch your hand anymore. You know where your hand’s going, your hand knows where it’s going. It picks up your phone. It starts typing on your keypad. Sometimes I have to watch my hands. I have to watch my hand pick it up, and then I have to check to make sure I have a good grip on it because I can’t feel my fingers.

I can’t feel the extremities. And so I will squeeze something extra tight. Sometimes, if you watch me on television, if my feet seem abnormally wide in my gait when I’m walking, that means I’m having balance issues and I spread my legs a little bit. To the naked eye, nobody sees that. If you’re around me all the time, you might say, “John’s walking a little weird today.”

MS is really cruel to some people. MS sucks for me. MS challenges me, but I have been able to manage it thanks to good doctors and thanks to personal discipline. I call it my visitor. If my visitor is active on any given day, my attitude is, okay, well, I can’t kick you out, so I have to figure out how to deal with you, and you just do it.

As much as I can. And then, if I have to come back at it the next day like I did in 2020, I was going home and getting three or four hours sleep, and maybe I could’ve had five or six hours sleep, but I know that I have to do that 45 minutes or 50 minutes of exercise to be able to function. So I have to cut my sleep short to get the exercise. That’s the way I have to do it to function. I’m able to get through it. Could I do that for a month? I hope I never have to answer that question. I was able to do it for a week in 2020. 2024, you’re still doing stuff the days after the election. We just didn’t have that long drawn out uncertainty.

I do not have trouble falling asleep. Even when I’m having a pretty good MS week, I have never had trouble sleeping. When my brain knows I’m done, I’m off the set, I’m in my office, I’ve had whatever post-action meeting I have to have, my brain tells me, “You’re done.” That means I’m going to find a bed, and I will sleep. I’ve been blessed so far, and I assume this will continue, that when I need to get back at it, I just get back at it.

Attitude is everything, especially if you’re tired or you’re struggling or things aren’t going well. Could I give you a list of complaints about my life? Could I give you a couple of complaints about where I work? Of course I could. Everybody can. As somebody who sometimes goes down to the gym in the basement of our office, why isn’t the office gym a little better? I mean, get over yourself. I think attitude is everything.

I say this as a sinner. When I was initially diagnosed, I was taking that out on other people sometimes. There were times when it was either the stress of work—this can be a stressful business sometimes—or the stress and the fear. I was being a grumpy person, not being a good colleague. If you feel that, take a walk, get away and just have a good attitude. In traveling the last two years, when you see the struggles that working families are going through across this country right now, I’ve always considered myself to be the luckiest person in the world. And when I feel myself starting to complain, I just give myself a whack in the head and say, “Dude, get over it.”

Attitude is incredibly important. That’s not a hack. It’s not a secret. It’s not a supplement, but look yourself in the mirror every morning and just go to it. Live your day in a way that you can look yourself in the mirror at the end of the day, and hold the gaze.

In Real-Life Diet, athletes, celebrities, and other high performers talk about their diet, exercise routines, and pursuit of wellness. Keep in mind that what works for them might not necessarily be healthy for you.

#6725. Louisa Jacobson’s Suited Streetwear Couldn’t Be More Different From Her Gilded Age Character’s Style

From corsets to bustles to floor-length skirts, the womenswear of the Gilded Age was known for many things. But Louisa Jacobson’s frayed raw hems and buckled collars were certainly not in the ladies’ 1880s style guides.

While doing press in New York City for the fourth season of her smash HBO historical drama The Gilded Age, Jacobson showed us a bit of her own street style... and it was a far cry from the looks that her character, Marian Brook, has donned on the very same streets.

Leaning instead into a bit of menswear, rather than the pastel gowns we’ve come to expect from her on-screen alter-ego, the actor experimented with suiting and modernized tailoring, thanks to the help of her stylist, Edward Bowleg III.

Last Monday, Jacobson turned to Mel Usine for a light-gray set from the label’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. Composed of a frayed, collarless jacket and matching inside-out skirt, the ensemble offered an unfinished, deconstructed look you’d have never seen during the 1883 Metropolitan Opera House opening.

It was layered over a black-trimmed white tank with a skinny red tie wrapped around her waist, and paired with peep-toe heels.

The next day, the actor pushed things even further, wearing a black-on-black monochrome look from Commission’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. This one was all about the buckle accents, with a zip-up blazer topped with a belted collar and little capri leggings trimmed with the same detail. In between was a pleated skirt, and for shoes, Jacobson wore pointed-toe pumps over calf-high socks.

Later in the day, Jacobson was a proper Calvin Klein girl—seen in Hudson Square wearing a dark-clay satin blazer and matching trousers with a heather-gray jacket over both. Her little nude ballet flats featured a contrasting reflective strap, and she grabbed a shoulder bag before heading out for an afternoon of press.

In an age of constant method dressing, it appears Jacobson is doing things her way.

#6724. Blake Lively Makes a Big, Bold, Blue-Sequin Return to the New York Party Scene

With the holiday season fast approaching, Blake Lively is certainly back in her element. Lively stepped out in New York City to attend the holiday collection launch of jeweler Brent Neale at Majorelle in the Upper East Side, making a sparkling return to the party circuit.

The actor and beauty founder donned a midnight-blue sequin minidress from Chanel’s fall 1994 collection. The strapless archival number featured a scalloped, petal-like neckline, with black satin bows running down the fitted bodice. She paired it with a black leather Chanel bucket bag, black Christian Louboutin Bis Un Bout pumps with transparent panels and ankle straps, and glittering statement earrings and rings by Brent Neale. Her blonde hair was swept into glossy, side-parted Hollywood waves. Serena van der Woodsen, is that you?

The Gossip Girl alum, whose on-screen alter ego was rarely one to shy away from a fabulous party and who, IRL, famously styles herself, has long shared that affinity for dressing up. The appearance marks a return to the spotlight for Lively, who has kept a relatively low public profile in recent months. She was last widely photographed at the FIFA World Cup final in July, where she took a decidedly more casual approach to dressing, supporting Argentina in a blue-and-white striped shirt, jeans, and a white tank top.

But party season is where Lively really shines. Her wardrobe is a veritable sweet shop of candy-colored dresses, high-shine fabrics, extravagant embellishments, and accessories with a sense of humor and novelty. Recall that bedazzled Judith Leiber pepperoni pizza bag, or the martini-shaped clutch she carried during the Another Simple Favor press tour. There have been rainbow Ashish tweeds, sequined Stella McCartney denim, and plenty of vintage treasures, including a turquoise 1960s sequin dress worn to a Tiffany & Co. event. Even her holiday wardrobe last December ran the gamut from frothy, angelic white to full-blown Mrs. Claus red.

This latest outing finds Blake Lively returning to some of her favorite sartorial territory, and the holiday party season has only just begun.

#6723. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reimagines the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; and Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up.”

Elsewhere, Grace Winfrey looks to Italian good-luck charms for the colorful “Poppy Fortuna”; Robinson Pelham checks into “Suite 96” to celebrate 30 years of bold jewelry; Le Vian brings Georgian-era romance to Jared with a new collection of warm-toned diamonds; and Wempe puts traditional goldsmithing at the center of “au:thentic,” inspired by the humble jump ring. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back.

For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Reimagined for today in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier’s ‘Trottola’ Takes on a New Form

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Reimagines the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s Latest Collection Is All About Good Fortune

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign reimagines jewelry as the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection reimagines historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

#6721. Chris Rock on Directing an A24 Movie and ‘Crying Like a Bitch’ in Therapy

Chris Rock enters a room a bit diffidently, like he’s feeling out what’s inside, making quiet observations about the world around him that sometimes tip over into jokes and sometimes don’t. Because today we’re meeting on the 24th floor of the World Trade Center, I will not repeat the jokes. He looks around at the setup for the interview, which is being filmed: lights and cameras and microphones everywhere. “I just shot a movie with, like, three people,” he says. “It was much lower-budget than this.”

That movie is Misty Green, Rock’s fourth feature as a director. It’s about an actress named Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar, who has talent and who has had success but who cannot quite get out of her own way. Rock identifies and he doesn’t. “I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie,” he says—including Misty’s best friend, played by Anna Kendrick, who is mostly there to crack jokes and report on her own unsatisfying romantic life. The film is a portrait of Hollywood that is dystopian but not cliché; Misty goes through hell, much of it of her own making, but her talent never dims. It has a lived, almost casual quality that belies Rock’s grasp of his craft: At 61, he hasn’t lost his eye for the telling, damning detail or hypocrisy, but there is also a warmth here, a genuine love for his characters. With Misty Green, you can feel both Rock’s lifetime of experience making things for audiences, and also something new—and more finely observed emerging.

All clothing, tie, and sunglasses by Tom Ford. Pocket square by Charvet.

Misty Green is part of a growing tradition in Rock’s work, including the previous film he directed, 2014’s Top Five, about the highs and lows of show business—something Rock has also chronicled, in exacting autobiographical detail, in his past two comedy specials: 2018’s Tamborine (which is about, among other things, Rock’s divorce) and 2023’s Selective Outrage (about, among other things, his encounter with Will Smith at the 2022 Academy Awards ceremony).

Rock has been at times the most famous man in all of comedy. His 1996 special Bring the Pain was a cultural phenomenon on a level few humans will ever experience. But as a director, he has increasingly been drawn to smaller ’70s-style character studies of people making an earnest attempt just to figure out themselves and their demons. “I’d love to make Man on Fire or something,” he says. “It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay.”

This interview has been condensed and edited; watch this cover story—an episode of GQ’s One More Question—above or on YouTube, and listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

Chris Rock: No, no. We’re going to be good. I think.

“How’d you get started?” “Were you funny in school?” Stuff like that. Whatever. I get it. You guys have a job. I’m not Harry Styles. Sometimes it requires a reintroduction.

I mean, it’s a thing you worry about every day. Am I still funny? Well—you don’t worry about being funny. You worry about being professionally funny. On a world-class level. I always had a joke: If I ever did a talk show, I’d do a morning show. I wouldn’t do a late-night show. Because I would only have to be funnier than Al Roker. You know what I mean? Al’s lovely, but I think I could take him in a joke-off.

You guys have a job, and the job is to get clickbait and things you can turn into controversy, and what’s the headline that has nothing to do with the actual article.

I mean, it’s your job, though. You might have better intentions, and I appreciate your interest. But a lot of what I read, it’s like: “Oh okay.” People want to talk about your personal life. I get it. We’re in a gossipy culture. We live in a world where Andy Cohen is Norman Lear and Ryan Murphy is Steven Spielberg. That is the world we live in. So people want gossip. We’re righteous people that follow nine commandments. And the one commandment we don’t follow is Thou shall not spread false witness. We are all about spreading false witness now. That is the world we live in. And that’s what journalism, or at least entertainment journalism, has become. Not that everything’s false, but it is definitely amplified to create sides, no matter what the issue is. How’s that? How am I doing?

Some of it is I got divorced. Nobody has a successful divorce, so that takes time. Then once it’s done, okay, you’re not sitting on the money you had before, so now you got to really make some money. So you go on tour, or two tours. So there was a lot of stand-up. There was a lot of getting my life together. You got a pandemic, you got a bunch of nonsense going on there.

I was not a great husband. I watched a lot of porn. I don’t watch porn anymore. I haven’t watched porn in five, six years.

It’s not anything I’m proud of, but it’s something I had to go through. It’s like you watch a Marvel movie, and the guy, he has to test his powers. You know what I mean? Every Marvel movie, man or woman, they have to test their powers. They’re assholes. They get these powers and they’re assholes, and they’re racing trains and they’re lifting up ocean liners and they try to go to the sun, then they crash down because they realize they’re not God. And then they start helping people. I tested my powers. I definitely realized I wasn’t God or anywhere near him, and I was severely humbled, as I should have been.

It’s basically Bring the Pain to Kill the Messenger. That’s one guy. Tamborine’s the beginning of a new guy. And that guy’s in fucking pain in Tamborine. That guy is damn near—Tamborine’s like the blues, man. Where Selective Outrage is like—there’s some pain in that one. Well, there’s a lot of pain in that one, but Tamborine is like: What have I become? [Starts singing Johnny Cash’s cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Hurt.”] Goes away, in the end. I’m Johnny Cash with Rick Rubin, singing about my empire of dirt. That’s Tamborine. Tamborine is the fucking blues.

Yeah. I’m not one for a hint. You got to tell me exactly what the fuck you want. You have to tell me exactly what the fuck you mean.

A friend just kind of blurted it one day. You ever have somebody say something and you’re like, “Okay, let me get this looked into”? And it’s before Tamborine, but around that time. So I’m already quitting porn. You know what I mean? I’m already in a place where, “Okay, what the fuck’s wrong with me?” And I got a cognitive assessment test. And it’s like eight hours of testing to basically see—it’s the kind of thing you would get if you were bipolar or something. So it’s a lot of testing, and that’s what they came up with.

It made me realize how insensitive a lot of my behavior was throughout the years. Because it’s weird. I’ve got a friend who always says, this is a side joke, but he says, “When a schizophrenic sees a famous person, they go, ‘Ha, see? Told you!’ ” Mental illness and celebrity—it’s a weird combination there, because you think people are reacting a certain way because of celebrity. Because it’s this weird thing that you can’t quantify. So I used to just blame everything on celebrity. It’s like, “Oh, we’re not connecting because I had a chronic unique-ism.” I thought I was so fucking unique.

But also, okay, what are the symptoms? Black-and-white thinking. It’s an advantageous thing to have if you’re a comedian, black and white. Catastrophizing, great. You know what I mean? When you see one of those specials—okay, the average comedian, or even above average, probably does 40 shows before they record a special. And maybe they did 20 club things before this, so that’s 60 times onstage. My average special, I’ve gone onstage over 250 times. So I’m working it. It looks like I’m just, “Oh my God, he’s got this great insight.” But it’s like, “Yo man, I’m grinding this stuff.” Also, I have a hard time picking up on social cues, but I have a weirdly accurate ear. I can pick up on things in my ear. Sometimes I can pick up on a cue, but I can’t decipher it. I don’t know what just happened for a week, and I’m like, “Oh, that’s what she meant. Oh, that’s what he was trying to say.” It’s like my mind is working on the case. It just can’t solve it at that moment. Does that make sense?

Well, yeah. We do have this thing where everybody’s like—they brag about their therapy. Put it this way, my personal life wasn’t what I wanted it to be. And I’ll leave it at that. And that’s my relationship with everybody. So yeah, I went in there crying like a bitch. Like: What the fuck is going on?

You never come out. It’s an ongoing thing. You know what I mean? You’re always an alcoholic. So it’s a combination of therapy and what I have, NVLD, nonverbal learning disorder. So I have a person that helps me with that, and I have another therapist. I mean, it’s okay.

I mean, it’s not like a threat or anything. I’m just saying it’s okay. Whatever happened happened. Everybody saw it. I don’t really like talking about it. By the way—any awards show.

Yeah. Something happened. It wasn’t cool. And I would like to move on. I would like to—I had a nice career before it, and I know there’s a part of that that’s going to follow me the rest of my life. I got jokes. I got scripts. I got movie scripts. I got TV shows. I’m writing a book. I’m doing shit. I have a plethora of art I’m trying to get out, and that’s what I want you to pay attention to, not some crazy night.

I don’t get a lot of stuff. I honestly don’t. I mean, I probably get more offers as a director, to tell you the truth, than as an actor. It’s weird. When you’re really famous, it works for you and it works against you. So you got name recognition, but you also have people thinking they know what you can do and thinking that there’s a ceiling on your talent. So you got to fight that. The hardest thing you can do in show business is change perception. Reinvention is the hardest thing. So it’s kind of relatively easy to get famous, in the sense that it’s twice as hard to become a new person that is already famous. You know what I mean? The John Travolta that was on Welcome Back, Kotter, that was probably easy compared to the guy that did Pulp Fiction. Like: Wow, I got to change everybody’s perception about who I am. I don’t get a lot of offers, but it’s okay.

They don’t really make comedies anymore. Not like they used to. I don’t want to be [cast in the role of] the judge. Plus, I’m at this weird place. People are like, “How old is he?”

I’m older than Morgan Freeman was in Shawshank. I’m older than Danny Glover was in Lethal Weapon. You know what I mean? So it’s like: “Is he the guy, or is he like Michael Douglas in Ant-Man?” Like: You go get him, Antie.

Hey, I’ll do it. I’ll shine Michael B. Jordan’s guns. “All right. They’re ready. They’re ready.” I don’t give a fuck. If that’s where I am now, you got to make these adjustments. I’m just trying to stay in the league, man. So I don’t get 25 shots anymore. Now I’m just boxing out. I’m playing good defense. Come in off the bench.

Oh, I totally identify. I mean, I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie. So I’m her, I’m the agent, I’m my character. I’m Anna Kendrick, even. I’m everybody in there. And yeah, Misty’s going through what I just said. It is hard when people actually think they know who you are to give you another chance, to think you’re worthy of another chance. And she doesn’t make it easy for herself. You know what I mean?

I mean, not to that extent. But here’s the thing about self-destructive behavior. Can you be nice while you’re doing it? Some addicts are better than others. I’ve never been that guy. I’ve never been poison on a set. I would even say, and I say this about most actors, 40, 50 percent of your work’s going to be from friends, from people just going, “Hey, you know who’s really cool to hang out with? Chris.” You know what I mean?

I’ve been in that audition. And then Kadeem Hardison walked in the room. You’re like, Kadeem! When I write a Hollywood thing—and I’m not trying to diss anybody—I’ve actually worked jobs. Most of my friends that work in show business have never worked a fucking real job. And if they worked a real job, they were working their way through college, knowing good and well they weren’t going to be there [forever]. So they never really thought the job was going to be their life. So when I write Hollywood, I’m still writing the guy that worked at Red Lobster. I’m writing the guy that loaded trucks at the Daily News. These are jobs that I had. It’s not a Hollywood thing. It’s an everywhere thing.

Why’d I cast myself? I don’t know. I guess I could have given it to somebody. I did think about it. It’s just like, “Eh, it’s not that time yet.”

You know what? It was like a quick on-set thing, basically, so I’m not the same guy in Top Five. A lot of directors, a lot of Black directors, have this hat uniform. They have a hat, and the hat’s got the name on it. So it’s Spike. It was the Hughes brothers. It was Matty Rich. There’s this uniform in being a Black director sometimes. It’s my homage to Robert Townsend and Reggie Hudlin and Malcolm Lee, and all these guys.

I mean, a little. I had a brother who struggled with alcohol, yes. It’s a lot of other people I’ve met. We just have so much mental illness now. And there’s something about—it’s weird. When you’re the sibling of somebody like that, or even my brother, your friends, everybody around you, only sees the drunk person, only sees the manic schizophrenic person, but you always see the person you grew up with. You still remember this brother that was like your best friend, and you don’t give that up. No matter what behavior you see, you’re just holding on [to] all the hope in the world that you can get that brother back. And that’s what Misty goes through. A lot of people are like, “Well, just leave him.” It’s like, “Nah, man. You didn’t know him like I knew him.”

I know some dead people. I know a lot of dead people. How old are you?

I’ll give you about 12 years, 15 years. You start losing the people that just don’t eat right. Just as simple as that. It’s not even the addicts who start going. And it’s not even that they OD; it’s just at some point your body can’t fight this fight anymore. So [in your] 50s, you start losing people. You start losing people to natural causes sometimes. It’s crazy.

There’s a weird statistic I read a long time ago. Of the 45 presidents, like 35 of them lost a father or a parent early in life. It makes you grow up. It’ll make you or break you. So yeah, it sobered me up somewhat. My father died in ’88; ’90, I’m on SNL. You know what I mean? So it’s like, Get serious, figure it out. It’s time to figure it out.

I was successful, I guess. But you got to also remember, at that time, all of us were in the shadow of Eddie Murphy. That’s what success was.

How do I explain it? I bought a house a year and a half, maybe two years before, bought a carriage house in Brooklyn, and I couldn’t afford it. And so I just had to get onstage a lot, and I had to work every gig. You ever read the Gladwell book? The Beatles basically just did more shows than everybody. So it was the Beatles, the Kinks, all these other bands. And the Beatles had the worst boss. The Beatles just did way more shows than everybody. We try to make it into this mythical thing. It’s kind of the same thing, man. I bought a house, and I had to fucking get onstage. Two things happened. I had to get onstage to pay for this house, but I also, privately anyway, I had quit show business in a sense.

I had given up because I’d done CB4, I’d done New Jack City, I’d been on SNL, and I was like, “Okay, I’m going to just be a comedian.” Not that there was any shame to it, but my goal was to be George Wallace. George Wallace is a great comedian, and I love George Wallace because all he did was stand-up and he had a real schedule in his life. Most comedians have no schedule, right? George Wallace works from here to here. He goes on vacation these months of the year. I kind of, in the back of my mind, always wanted a family, always wanted kids. So that was my goal. I do this special, and it’s hard to even explain. The world went crazy.

Here’s a funny story. I got Bring the Pain. I have a VHS of Bring the Pain. I left my agent, and I left my manager, but I have Bring the Pain. Now nobody knows what it is. It’s very similar to Dre and Snoop walking around with The Chronic, trying to get a deal. And by the way, it’s around the same time. So I go to this agent. I’m not going to say his name, whatever. He’s made up with me since. I still got a little ego, and I’m like, “Hey, I’d like you to be my agent.” I give him the Bring the Pain tape. He watches it. He says, “It’s okay.” He goes, and I quote, “I got too many Black guys.” He said, “I got too many Black guys.” Whatever. Cut to two months later, Bring the Pain airs and it’s like this big thing. I’m on Oprah, I’m on 60 Minutes, and that agent calls me back, “Hey. I’ll handle you for 5 percent.”

I thought about it, but then I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t do it. I got too many Black guys. A guy actually said that to me.

Bigger & Blacker is bigger than Bring the Pain. It’s like, what if Bad sold more than Thriller? I got a nice body of work. I’m fine with Head of State, I’m fine with I Think I Love My Wife, [which are] the two films before Top Five, but I think I could have been more serious about directing. That’s the only thing I would say. I never let my ego mess up my stand-up. Every special, I put a ton of work into. Kill the Messenger, I remember Mike Nichols calling me and he said, “I like it, but you got onstage too much. It’s like: You worked it too much. And I can see at points you’re a little robotic. You don’t need to work it that hard.” But yeah, I was learning a lot of things on the fly. I didn’t know anything about money. Lorne Michaels said to me a long time ago, “Everybody loses their first money. But if you’re talented, you’ll make more.” I knew nothing about just the dynamics of fame and how it affected the people around you and all that stuff. It was a lot.

No, I’m not doing it for money. I mean, I’ll make money off of it, but the thing with Misty Green, what I realized when I did Top Five, it’s like: This is my lane as a filmmaker. I’d love to make Man on Fire or something. I would love to make fill-in-the-blank big-budget movie and have this big-budget Rush Hour–esque idea. Those guys are really good at that. It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay. A little movie is what I should probably be doing, and it’s where my interest is. And some of those other movies I did was kind of me trying to get famous.

Robert De Niro’s like 84. He’s got a little baby. He’s my man. He’s got literally a two-year-old or something. I mean, I never plan too much ahead. I’m just trying to get as much work done as possible. Having kids that are grown, it seems like I got a little more time on my hands. So hopefully that results in more work. I’m probably going to direct more. I don’t know how much [more] stand-up I’m going to do.

I got like six, seven specials, man. That’s a lot. So I don’t know. I’m not announcing anything or anything, but if I do it, I want to do it right. In sports, especially in football, they always talk about separation. “Can he get separation?” You know what I mean? “Yeah, he’s fast, but is he fast enough? Can he get separation?” And that’s the way I feel, like, as far as stand-up. As long as I can get separation, I’ll do it. Yeah, I’m going to write. That’s basically what it boils down to. Wake up, write. That’s it. Just write, write, write, write, write. Get it all out. ✦

#6719. What to Read, Watch, and Listen To According to the Spring 2027 Collections

Our extensive analyses of the spring 2027 season now contine into the broader realm of culture. This, on the heels of decoding the trends—both what to where and how, clocking the art influences, and highlighting trenchant quotes from the reviews.

One way to fill in the six-month lag between the close of the season and the arrival of clothes in stores is to go deeper into designers’ inspirations. The list below collects the books, movies, and tracks that inspired the spring 2027 collections.

The French philosopher Michel Foucault, the Bloomsbury writer Virginia Woolf, and the photographer Bettina Rheims all make more than one appearance here, as does Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet, a perennial fashion fave. You might want to take a listen to the 1972 Italian song written in gibberish that was the soundtrack to Fendi’s show or rewatch the romantic idyll that is Merchant Ivory’s 1985 film A Room With a View (based on E.M. Forster’s novel), which was Simone Rocha’s touchstone for the men’s collection she presented at Pitti Uomo. And how fitting that Valentino’s show, presented in a library, should include a sheer tulle pullover, the equivalent of a glossy book cover. Alessandro Michele had been ruminating on a concept put forth in the book Black Swan.

“The astounding Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève played host to Alessandro Michele’s latest Valentino show. For the occasion, Michele produced a sort of bibliography of imagined books, complete with descriptions, made-up authors, and phony ISBNs. Among the many creative titles were A Garden of Small Errors, Elsewhere Is a Precise Place, and The Social Life of Velvet. In the copious show notes, he talked up the value of an ‘anti-library’ of unread books (a concept lifted from the Lebanese American scholar Nassim Nicholas Taleb), comparing the enormous potential such a trove contains to a closetful of unworn clothes.

‘Even the garments that we will never wear, no differently than those books sitting unopened on our shelves, still speak to us of the lives we could have lived. Not as regrets, but as promises,’ Michele wrote.” —Nicole Phelps

“‘I read that book called Foucault in California,’ Tron said before the show. ‘It’s about him experimenting with LSD in Death Valley, and basically this idea of the desert as a space for expanding consciousness, experimenting, also disillusion.’ From there, he said, came ‘American desert psychedelicism, Jim Morrison, sexuality, Joan Didion, Walter De Maria’—a collision between the strictures of French intellectual thought and the psychic expansiveness of the American West.” —Luke Leitch

“Pay Per View was a collection about the slippery, sensual business of being watched—and what happens to the self when we know there is an audience. Zinko had been reading Michel Foucault on Jeremy Bentham’s panopticon: the circular prison structure in which inmates cannot know at any given moment whether the guard at its center is observing them, and therefore start to regulate their own behavior. ‘Modern society revolves around live-streaming and social media, and it forces us to behave as if we are constantly being perceived,’ she said.” —Anna Cafolla

“She had been reading Women Who Run With the Wolves, Clarissa Pinkola Estés’s 1992 bestseller about reconnecting with an instinctual female power. In Ahn’s home of Tokyo, the tension between the expectations of society and the pull of nature is palpable: ‘Japanese people are really in their heads, especially in the city, because there are so many unwritten rules we need to follow. Because of that, the city is like a well-oiled machine, and everything is functioning, but when you’re in it, I feel like it drives all that energy up to your head.’” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“For her spring 2027 collection, Lost to Virtue, Laura Gerte explored the deconstruction of femininity’s moral ideals. Her starting point was research into Dadaism and the work of artist and poet Mina Loy, whose feminist manifesto, written in 1914, framed female ‘virtue’—or rather virginity—as a patriarchal tool of control. Published only decades later, the text still felt radical enough to hint at just how provocative it must have been in its own time.

‘One of the manifesto’s central ideas is the destruction of virtue. For generations, the idea of female morality has been used to keep girls and women small, forcing us into predefined roles. And we don’t want that anymore,’ Gerte said after the show.” —Valerie Specht

“Dushane Noble is tapped into the ongoing discourse around taste as a social signifier. Can taste be acquired like wealth or commodities? (Tech bros sure think so.) Is it just something else to be flattened by the algorithm?

Status and Culture: How Our Desire for Social Rank Creates Taste, Identity, Art, Fashion, and Constant Change by W. David Marx informed Noble’s spring 2027 collection. ‘[Marx] talks about this idea of status-seeking being the quiet engine behind taste and culture—that what we see as cool or good taste is really status,’ Noble explained.” —Hannah Jackson

“The designer built her spring 2027 collection around Florian Illies’ book, 1913: The Year Before the Storm. ‘It was about how all the European artists and thinkers and scientists at that moment were living their life as if there was no tomorrow,’ the designer explained. ‘There was really this sense of creativity and how they were working together that was really inspiring to me; there was something that felt so parallel to the time that we live in today.’” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“For their [10th-] anniversary collection, the duo drew inspiration from the recently published book Modestadt Berlin by historian Gesa Kessemeier; through years of research, she documented the flourishing fashion scene of prewar Berlin and highlighted long-forgotten names such as Joe Strassner, Johanna Marbach, and Uli Richter.” —Kerstin Weng

“‘If you know me, you know that I'm obsessed with a thing that’s just for a thing,’ said Daniella Kallmeyer. That thing this season was a book about traditional Japanese packaging titled How to Wrap Five Eggs. The cover art, which features eggs gently crocheted together, became a bit of an obsession for its structural discipline and textural intrigue. It captures when an obsession becomes a meditative practice, and in the Kallmeyer world, that inevitably becomes a collection. Sharp eyes hopefully caught the bright flash of eggs nestled in their crocheted carrier swinging against a trench-length blouson-bottomed coat.” —Alexandra Hildreth

“His latest he dubbed Remnants and Relics, and very good it was too: a time-traveling 400-year odyssey with an Orlando-type character who gathers up a wardrobe of foppish, high-buttoned ivory suiting with a Death in Venice vibe to it. ‘The collection is based on the Virginia Woolf character,’ Mario Keine said after his show, ‘but it’s also a development of last season’s, which was based on the Enlightenment’—the 18th-century movement where fearful superstition gave way to rational, empirical knowledge. ‘Today we’re also looking for knowledge, even though we’re meant to have it all because it’s on our phones.’” —Mark Holgate

“Home as a shelter was the genesis of Marco Rambaldi’s spring 2027 collection. From a reference to Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own, the Bolognese designer developed the concept of a space where anyone who enters can express themselves freely, without any judgment.” —Alberto Calabrese

“‘One can do without meat, but cannot live where there is no bamboo; lacking meat merely leads to weight loss, whereas lacking bamboo means losing peace of mind.’ This poem by the Song dynasty scholar Su Shi became a guiding reference for this knockout IM Men collection, which was all about bamboo.” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“This season he’s been thinking about The Little Mermaid, and related with the metaphor of looking up toward the surface. This wasn’t a Disneyfied ‘Part of Your World’ expression, but one that in typical Yusho fashion drew on the original story’s darker themes: the pain of walking on one’s feet in an unfamiliar world, the realization that the seawater running down the mermaid’s cheeks was really tears, and maybe the hint of regret at making a choice that can no longer be reversed.” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“Many models wore floppy white cloche hats, which Murakami said referenced Shiroi Boshi (The White Hat), a Japanese children’s story. The premise is too convoluted to summarize here, but the point Murakami was making was one of beauty in abstraction. ‘It’s about dissolving the boundaries between the real world and fantasy,’ he said. ‘That’s how I view memory, after all. We might casually look at things like the sky, or a coat hanger’—he gestured to one in the room—‘but the images we’ve built up in our minds are often slightly twisted or blurred at the edges. I feel there’s immense value in being able to sense and appreciate those kinds of nuances.’” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“The collection was entitled Skin and based around the idea of an outer surface continually shed, renewed, and rewritten, with the phoenix, specifically Osamu Tezuka’s Phoenix, providing the central image of rebirth.” —Luke Leitch

“She started, she said, from reading the play The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant. It’s a reference, with its woman fashion designer as a central character that has inspired many for years; yet Dujancourt took it in her own way. Drawing on her experience of synesthesia, the visual suggestion of the title triggered her to create a ‘tears library’—strings of lace and crochet, representing ‘despair, grief, pain, and relief.’” —Sarah Mower

“Susan Fang has been in the midst of designing costumes for M. Butterfly, an opera by Huang Ruo showing at the La Monnaie - De Munt in Brussels next year. Naturally, the plot of M. Butterfly has been top of mind for Fang, though rather than lifting references directly from the story to inform her spring collection, she looked to holistic moods and feelings. Specifically, the ‘imagined worlds people create around love,’ as she explained at a preview.” —Alice Cary

“The invitation was a wedding announcement: that of Ippolita and Antiogu, in Alghero, ‘the midday after St. John’s night.’ …the collection’s title hid another layer: ‘A Midsummer Midday Wedding’ nodded to Shakespeare, whose midsummer comedy ends with the wedding of Theseus and Hippolyta, Ippolita in Italian, while Antiogu is the Sardinian form of Antioco.”—Giorgia Feroldi

“Casa Susanna, a photo book chronicling the lives and loves of a group of midcentury men who dressed as women at a country retreat in the Catskill Mountains, was Joseph Altuzarra’s starting point for spring. Something about Susanna Valenti and her friends’ expressiveness served as an unlock for Altuzarra. ‘I just love how joyful it was,’ he said. ‘I really wanted the collection to feel joyful, to be all about color and this idea of freedom.’” —Nicole Phelps

“Isabel Marant is the quintessential Parisian brand, but for spring creative director Kim Bekker found her inspiration a world away, in LA. There, she came across a ’60s book of photographs by Sam Haskins showing women bathed in hazy light, dressed or undressed. ‘The colors were almost translucent,’ Bekker said.” —Tina Isaac-Goizé

“‘I started from a very simple idea—to continue exploring an Italian way of life defined by authenticity, quality, and a natural relationship with objects,’ Matteo Tamburini said. Simplicity, however, is seldom simple. Tamburini’s point of departure was Viaggio in Italia, Luigi Ghirri’s seminal 1984 photographic project, which offered a new way of seeing the country: attentive rather than sentimental, curious and slightly raw rather than steeped in clichés.” —Tiziana Cardini

“Inspired by Modern Lovers (1990), photographer Bettina Rheims’s portrait series exploring the performance and plurality of gender identities, Yanagawa subtly disrupted his signature tailoring—blazers and suits cut long or cropped—with conventionally feminine gestures: lace peeking from sleeves, mesh tulle, crushed velvet, glossy patent finishes, and shorts designed to resemble skirts. Altercasting completed the picture with models that looked lifted straight from Rheims’s photographs, slicked-back hair included.” —Valerie Specht

Charlotte Knowles and Alexandre Arsenault “will be celebrating their brand’s 10th anniversary next year, and found themselves returning to a central source of inspiration for their graduate show at Central Saint Martins: the French photographer Bettina Rheims’s landmark book Chambre Close, which featured images of women undressing across a series of cheap, anonymous hotel rooms. ‘We’ve been feeling nostalgic about where we started, and we thought it would be an interesting exercise to think about how we see things now, versus how we saw them back then,’ Arsenault said at a preview. Added Knowles: ‘All the women in the book are in different stages of undress, so we translated that into the collection quite literally: a lot of deconstruction and layering. We also took inspiration from the colors and went a little more zingy with the palette. It’s really about our twist on femininity.’” —Liam Hess

“‘I always try to go with a little bit of romance and beauty, but I always try to give it this grunge element,’ Hillary Taymour said at a preview. The designer carried over some 18th-century loveliness (see the opening ruffled moiré cape) from the not-for-sale collection she presented at Copenhagen Fashion Week, and introduced medieval (see the plaid printed sequined fabric that is a stand-in for chain mail) after watching Heath Ledger and Shannyn Sossamon in A Knight’s Tale on the flight back. ‘My whole goal is to make everything big and voluminous and as light as possible,’ said Taymour.” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“For spring 2027, his 11th season, he felt the urge to connect back to the brand’s foundations, in part as a response to his father’s recent passing. ‘There’s a more somber tone,’ he said. Miles Davis and Tupac Shakur served as touchstones, as did the movie Ichi the Killer and the Japanese actor Takeshi Kitano.” —Max Berlinger

“Wong Kar-wai’s In the Mood for Love was the starting point for Patrick McDowell’s spring ’27 collection, titled Love. It’s also the designer’s partner’s favorite film. In it actress Maggie Cheung wears 21 cheongsams of different prints. It was one of those prints McDowell translated into the green stripe silk material that was the protagonist of the show, taking inspiration from the film’s dominant hues of red and green.” —Electra Kostoni

“There was a whiff of the 1980s, she said, in the Hawaiian shirts (the print based on the one Leonardo DiCaprio wears in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet and a picture of Bruce Willis), and cropped, garment-dyed, coated-nylon cargo jackets in Miami Vice hues.” —Max Berlinger

“Dsquared2’s Dean and Dan Caten went deeper into Italian-ness for their spring 2027. In fact, the duo drew on the Mediterranean folklore of southern Italy, exploring religious symbolism through a spicy lens. Crosses and holy references, along with religious-inspired tattoos, were at the core of this season, with nods to Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet.

This was especially evident in the gangster-inspired atmosphere, a choice that showcased Dsquared2’s propensity to mix up very different references, often rooted in pop culture.” —Alberto Calabrese

“The starting point was Green Snake, Tsui Hark’s 1993 film starring Maggie Cheung and Joey Wong, a modern retelling of the ancient Chinese legend of the white snake. For designers Samuel Yang and Erik Litzén, the duo behind the label, there was no shortage of material to shed and reassemble.” —Tiziana Cardini

“While gestating the collection, Rocha returned to the 1985 Merchant Ivory movie adaptation of Forster’s book, reacquainting herself with an Oscar-winning suite of Edwardian costume design by Jenny Beavan and John Bright almost as exquisitely realized as Florence itself. ‘This is my Irish man and he’s arrived in Florence and become the main character,’ she said of a designed ensemble that was inhabited by multiple character studies.” —Luke Leitch

“Opening with sharp tailoring and an elegant Dalmatian print on skirts and blouses, it read like something Cruella de Vil would have worn had she been a Wall Street big shot in the ’80s.

Instead, it was the much cooler 1982 cult classic Smithereens that Reid Baker and Inês Amorim were inspired by, which also informed the bold punky checks that were mixed in, all finished off with leather driving gloves and wraparound statement sunglasses that lent a sleek edge.” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“‘I always tell the Los Angeles story, the rock and roll, something sunny and optimistic,’ Amiri said backstage. ‘But one night I watched American Gigolo, and I saw Los Angeles in a very dark way, a seductive way.’ From there, he was sketching out a script involving a cast of sharp-dressed night crawlers, thinking about where they’d be glimpsed in the shadows of dimly lit bars or the back rooms of private members’ clubs. ‘There’s something dangerous about these characters and the places they go.’” —Sarah Mower

“As the designer acknowledged, it’s ‘kind of strange’ for Ann Demeulemeester to take inspiration from LA. But he said he’s fascinated by the darker side of the city. During his trip, Gallici watched Billy Wilder’s 1950 dark comedy Sunset Boulevard and started to see Los Angeles through a more sinister lens. ‘I was thinking about how LA is the ghost of a city that once was so florid. It’s almost a city worn to death,’ he said.” —Lucy Maguire

“As they were building out the theme, the pair watched any number of movies relating to Hollywood—Sunset Boulevard, Boogie Nights, Hollywood 90028, All That Jazz, They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?, Cabaret. The last is especially up August Barron’s alley; the designers are interested in the elusiveness or the decay of fame, the wearing away of its gold plating.” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“Yuka Kimura called this Mukcyen collection Low Energy. The designer, who is on her sixth season of the brand, had been watching Michelangelo Antonioni’s 1964 film Red Desert, which explores the psychological toll of industrialization, and was thinking about how it relates to our present reality.

Nowadays the grind of factories and machinery has been replaced by a ceaseless hum of digital noise. ‘A messy, overwhelming variety of inputs,’ as Kimura put it. ‘People are becoming increasingly sensitive to this kind of noise, or simply exhausted by it,’ she said. ‘I created this collection to express that feeling.’” —Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“Romance, ERD-style, has a dark undertow: The show notes evoked ‘a mysterious unnamed figure who destabilizes a wealthy bourgeois family by seducing every member of the household.’ Pasolini fans will recognize the late, great Terence Stamp in Teorema. There’s always a hint of trouble brewing.” —Tina Isaac-Goizé

“Leandro Cano is frustrated by how often Andalusia is underestimated. That frustration became the starting point for Le Chien Andalou, his latest collection.

Religion and flamenco traditions became two of the collection’s foundations, filtered through the same surrealist lens as Luis Buñuel’s famous film, which gave the collection its name. ‘This time I’m working from three ideas: hyperbole, beauty, and surrealism, which I accept as something completely natural,’ said Cano.” —Nuria Lui

“Francesco Murano went to Metropolis for his starting point (a particularly timely choice, given that Fritz Lang’s 1927 vision is set in 2026), and to the film’s two Marias for his central dichotomy: the virtuous woman and her seductive robotic double.

His response, a collection called Éidola, which is ancient Greek for ‘image,’ took the two and, sensibly, refused to choose.” —Tiziana Cardini

“Biga landed on Theodore Dryer’s black-and-white 1928 film The Passion of Joan of Arc as his spring inspiration. This martyr might be fashion’s favorite saint, and pop culture likes her too: Hlynur Pálmason released his own Joan of Arc film last year, and Baz Luhrmann is developing one as well. Biga was drawn to the he/she aspects of this historical figure who refused to give up her faith—and the menswear she wore.” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“The show melted two stories together, those of A Bug’s Life and the fairy tale of the princess and the frog—except ‘in this case it’s the prince and the frog,’ Browne said.” —Luke Leitch

“The designer explained that he had three points of departure: Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty; the Sylvanian Families he has been collecting with his young relatives (those inspired the tactile velvets, wide-wale corduroys, and lamés), and Alice’s mushroom-eating adventures in Wonderland. But he leavened the vibe with pointed commentary: ‘I figured since the world is so fucked up right now, we might as well turn everything upside down,’ Ortuño Perez quipped.” —Tina Isaac-Goizé

“For spring 2027, designer Louis-Gabriel Nouchi looked to America’s Pacific Northwest, specifically the David Lynch version as depicted in his cult-classic TV show, Twin Peaks. That not only gave the collection its desired outdoorsy feel (those Boy Scout shorts and ranger shirts!) but provided a cast of archetypes (the detective, the cop, the endangered ingenue) and a creeping sense of darkness, of strangeness. Add to that the navy/gray/brown/purple palette of Francis Bacon and a touch of Blade Runner’s dystopian futurism, and the broad contours of his collection started to coalesce accordingly.” —Max Berlinger

“‘[The Golden Girls] was not actually the inspiration for the collection, but in hindsight we realized that it has a lot to do with it and there are elements that feel very Golden Girls,’ added Lazo. ‘I would say 90% of that series is the women in their dressing gowns or bathrobes eating cheesecake, and that also became a talking point in the collection.’ ‘We put a beefcake in the cheesecake,’ Schmidl quipped.” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“In 1972 the Milanese musician Adriano Celentano conducted an experiment: He released a song without meaning, its lyrics written entirely in gibberish meant to sound like English, to see if it could still move an audience. At first the song bombed. But two nationally televised performances featuring group choreography and Celentano’s own distinctive dancing—his nickname was Il Molleggiato, or The Bouncy—saw it rise high in the charts, first in Italy and then in multiple countries across Europe.

One of those two TV performances featured another Italian pop progressive, Raffaella Carrà, whose immortal Italo-disco banger ‘Rumore’ was mixed into the ‘Prisencolinensinainciusol’-dominated soundtrack at Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi show. You could see Celentano’s experimental approach in 1972 as a mirror of Chiuri’s in 2026. Speaking at a preview, she said: ‘Fashion is part of our language.… Clothes give another sense to the body.’ She added: ‘Fashion is that. What do you like? What is your memory? Putting this together is like being a DJ. I think it is impossible to concentrate on only one aspect.’” —Luke Leitch

True Blue, presented by the Brodie Sessions, as the Skovgaardettes, from left: Lauren Glading, Sharleen Chidiac, and Maya Laner.

“Skovgaard, who grew up with the Spice Girls (and identified with Baby Spice) was turned onto the Supremes, The Ronettes, and the Shangri-Las while watching a Danish television series about the ’60s. He started researching them, ‘but instead of just reusing the vibe of those three girl groups, I wanted to create a fictional girl group instead because I couldn’t really see [the others] representing the collection I was dreaming of making,’ he explained. So ‘I decided to come up with this imaginary girl group called the Skovgaardettes.’” —Laird Borrelli-Persson

“The show had two phases, each delineated by music: Chaka Khan’s ‘Like Sugar’

and Michael Jackson’s ‘I Just Can’t Stop Loving You.’” —Luke Leitch

“It looks like goodbye at Saint Laurent. Ten years and precisely two days since his 2016 debut, Anthony Vaccarello took his last bow at the Kering-owned brand. At least, the signs pointed that way.

The music playing as guests filtered in was Miles Davis’s soundtrack to Louis Malle’s first film, the meaningfully named Elevator to the Gallows.” —Nicole Phelps

“The collection began with an assortment of images by photographer Trevor Hughes, whose bike-messenger series in 1990s Toronto captured an innate understanding of styling. Partly born from athletic and functional necessity, and partly from pure inherent fashion, such as a zip-up minidress styled over bike shorts, Hughes’s messengers captured what so many are trying to chase, becoming the basis for Attersee’s spring collection.” —Alexandra Hildreth

“‘I wanted to explore falling in all its forms,’ Kegels said. The runway included portions of stretch fabric, suspended just above the ground, to show the weight of each step. (It was inspired by a YouTube video of science educator Dan Burns, who used a similar setup to explain Einstein’s theory of general relativity.)” —Lucy Maguire
