#6716. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Celebration Begins Now

GQ’s December issue has arrived, and with it comes our annual Men of the Year blowout. Except, for the 31st year, we’re going bigger than ever.

We’re honoring the brightest figures in entertainment and culture with festivities as epic as their accomplishments. And for 2026 we’ll be celebrating across three nights in Los Angeles next week—GQ’s annual Men of the Year Party, as well as two new-for-2026 events.

A lucky few will join us Tuesday, November 10th at the newly opened, architecturally stunning Lucas Museum of Narrative History to honor Denis Villeneuve, GQ’s Director of the Year. Guests will get to hear GQ’s Zach Baron, host of the new show One More Question, in conversation with Villeneuve, followed by a screening of Dune: Part Two.

The GQ Director of the Year screening is presented by OMEGA.

Wednesday night, we’ll head into the Hollywood Hills for a house party at the breathtaking Sheats-Goldstein residence with our Breakouts of 2026: 13 of the actors, directors, comedians, podcasters, and more who stole the spotlight this year. The view from the terrace will be awe-inspiring; the vibe inside will be electric.

The GQ Breakouts party is presented by Hot Wheels.

Thursday, November 12th, GQ will host a private dinner honoring our Men of the Year followed by its annual Men of the Year party, at the iconic Chateau Marmont. The event will be hosted by Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, alongside co-hosts Chris Rock, Andrew Garfield, and Matt Damon.

The guest list, as ever, will be star-studded, and impeccably dressed. And the red carpet will be hosted Benito Skinner—tune into GQ’s Instagram for the biggest moments from carpet (and inside the party).

GQ’s Men of the Year Dinner and Party is presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label.

GQ’s Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi will co-host this year’s bash alongside three leading men: Chris Rock, Andrew Garfield, and Matt Damon.

We’re honoring the Creative Director of Celine, Michael Rider, as Designer of the Year, along with Dune’s very own Denis Villeneuve, as Director of the Year.

Benito Skinner, creator and star of Overcompensating and co-host of the podcast “Ride,” will bring his high-energy charm to the red carpet of the storied Chateau Marmont.

GQ’s annual Men of the Year party is presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label. The “Director of the Year” screening is presented by OMEGA, and the GQ Breakouts Party is presented by Hot Wheels.

#6714. Meet Melat Kiros, the 29-Year-Old Bringing Gen Z Politics to Congress

After losing her law-firm job over her stance on Gaza protests, she turned generational frustration into a historic win.

In 2023, Melat Kiros was fired. She was 26 and worked at a major New York law firm, but she refused to condemn an open letter addressed to dozens of law firms that had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on university campuses, at a time when students were protesting the slaughter in Gaza. Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned law firms, including the one she worked for, against confusing “bigotry with the geopolitical question of Israel’s legitimacy.” This cost her her job.

She, however, was not discouraged, as she belongs to a generation that is no longer willing to set aside its values for the sake of a career. “The right to question not only the legitimacy of a government but also its actions is the bedrock principle of a true democracy,” she said of her decision. Since then, Kiros has devoted herself more intensely to politics, and yesterday, in the midterm elections, she won as Colorado’s representative to the House of Representatives. Before her, only one other Gen Z representative, Democrat Maxwell Frost of Florida, had made it to Parliament in 2022, but she became the first Gen Z woman in Congress.

Melat Kiros was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, but moved to Denver with her family when she was still a baby and grew up there. She graduated from Washington College in Maryland in 2018, where she studied political science and economics, before earning a law degree from the University of Notre Dame in 2022. Today she is a lawyer and is pursuing a doctorate in public policy. In the meantime, however, she also works as a barista. It is not easy to balance a political career with her studies, but it is worth it.

After being fired, Kiros returned to Colorado and, in 2024, joined the election campaign of Democratic congressional candidate John Padora as communications director. It was excellent training for her, so much so that, two years later, she decided to run for Congress herself. On her side, she has strong political positions—she supports universal health care and child care, but also more politically controversial issues, such as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Her ideals openly align with her actions, and in fact during the election campaign she refused funding from corporate PACs and pro-Israel groups, while also sharply criticizing her Democratic primary opponent Diana DeGette, who had instead accepted donations from defense contractors as well as energy and pharmaceutical companies.

It is clear that Kiros's mark is different: She shows us what Gen Z can and will be able to do when it is given space. In this sense, her election also fits well into the climate of student protests, in Europe and around the world, by a generation that wants to make its voice heard. Yet it is still not easy: According to research by Future Caucus, more than 100 Generation Z candidates ran in the 2026 midterm elections for Congress, but the study found that young candidates were less likely to make it to the general election than other age groups, with only 24 of them appearing on the November ballots.

Kiros also had to face paternalism and dismissive attitudes from those who considered her unsuitable and inexperienced. “Now is not the time to gamble and send somebody with no experience to Washington,” DeGette had said during the primaries. Kiros, however, turned it into a strength, centering her congressional candidacy precisely on the theme of generational change. She emphasized socialist issues dear to younger people, such as affordability, social policies, climate change, countering the influence of multinational corporations, and support for students, families, and workers.

“People, I think, were really eager to see someone who is younger, who has lived experience with the economy that we're living through right now, the climate crisis that we are going to have to deal with the consequences of,” she said in an interview. For her, “socialism is about making it clear that we have basic needs for every single human being,” and she has promised to fight for this.

She also knows she has a lot to learn, but that does not stop her from walking through the doors of Congress with her head held high, without being overly intimidated by traditions and alliances. “Young people understand that we are in the fight of our lives,” she said. “We need to have leaders that are going to be fighting for the kind of bold policies that actually get something done, and they’re refusing to settle or wait for our turn or ask for permission.”

#6713. A '90s Prada Obsessive Picks Her Four Favorite Collections

To know Laia Garcia-Furtado is to understand that she’s obsessed with Prada. Indeed, it’s one of her most obvious traits. During her tenure as senior fashion news editor here at Vogue, she spoke at length about her expertise on Miuccia Prada on our podcast, “The Run-Through,” and wrote countless odes to her beloved brand. So when she was approached by an editor at Batsford Books with a proposal to write a book on Prada, it felt preordained. “I feel like I’ve been training my entire life for this,” she said. Still, as an editor herself, Garcia-Furtado had to gut-check herself. “I quickly remembered that there’s a lot more to ’90s Prada than those legendary collections that came in the second half of the decade.”

Her new book Prada in the Nineties comes at a great time for the new generation of Miuccia-heads, discovering the brand on social media. “I think everyone is still so obsessed with the ’90s because, looking back, we think of it as the last decade of a kind of freedom,” Garcia-Furtado explains. “The Internet was barely beginning, and people still dressed to their own spirit. But I think for Prada, especially, this is the decade where it went from a kind of fledgling label to the global behemoth it is today.” She adds that it was during this period that Mrs. Prada discovered her voice and encompassing vision for what the brand would one day become. “All those ’90s collections are still constantly referenced to this day.”

Even as a devotee, the research process yielded a treasure trove of information about Mrs. Prada, like the fact that the designer’s spring 1999 collection was actually her way of fighting back against the trends of the ’90s (trends, of course, she helped popularize). “The spring 1999 collection with mirror embellishments was her sort of ‘taking the piss’ to the hippie trend that was happening around the time,” says Garcia-Furtado. “I love when you see her humor peeking through, and that really reminded me of the lace collection from fall 2008—another one of my all-time favorites—that she said she made because she hated lace.”

Because the book is unauthorized and unapproved by Prada—as she wittily notes on her cover—Garcia-Furtado tapped illustrator Rachel Song to reimagine her favorite collections (think a chinoiserie look on page 133 or the spring 1999 bumbag on page 167). When asked if she’s sent a copy to Prada headquarters yet, she had a pithy reply: “You can’t just reach out to God like that.” Here’s to hoping a copy makes its way to Milan regardless.

On the occasion of the book being published, we asked Garcia-Furtado to share her four favorite ’90s Prada collections, and explain what makes them so special.

“I think spring 1994 is maybe an underrated collection, or maybe it was underrated to me, and now I love it. The strange sheer nightgowns layered over knitted separates and worn with little white socks and odd moccasins. The sudden Renaissance influence with the leather vests over the dreamy white dresses. It really captured the grunge spirit of the time yet in a purely Miuccia way, but I think it’s still really modern.”

“Spring 1996 is maybe my all-time favorite fashion collection, the root cause of my personal style. The mismatched prints, all the different shades of green that are supposed to be ugly but couldn’t possibly be. (It’s worth noting that my teen girl bedroom had two walls painted bright slime green and two opposing walls painted mint green—so I wouldn’t go totally crazy according to my mom.) But even beyond the prints, the silhouettes are pure Prada: a midi-length skirt ending in the no man’s land between knee and ankle, a simple slip dress worn under a car coat, strange sandals that expose entirely too much toe. Everything feels a little bit off, but it’s also perfectly feminine, perfectly balanced.”

“This was the season when Mrs. Prada started thinking about the future, like suddenly the idea of the new millennium became real. Everything looks a little bit tech-y yet also romantic, as if it came from a near-distant past. Beads look like the inside of a computer or maybe drops of rain? Her favorite little button-down shirts now come with latex insets. I also love the berry color palette, both in the ladylike suits with oddly-gathered skirts, and on the lips! Also, this season had those divine pink lucite heels that are definitely at the top of my wish list.”

“The early ’90s collections were my blind spot going into this project, but the more time I spent with some of them, the more I found things I loved. The clothes are deceptively freaky. I love Naomi’s loose-leaf bright white satin tunic and matching cigarette trousers, an odd red and white vertical striped dress with strangely sculptural shoulder lines. But my favorite look is Carla Bruni in a bike short twinset complete with pillbox hat. It’s so prim it’s almost totally demented.”

Prada in the Nineties will be available on November 10, 2026.

#6712. The 7 Best Nail Trends to Try Right Now

From “Winter Wine” to “Tiger’s Eye,” these looks are perfect for colder months ahead

It’s a little too early for holiday nail art manicures, and maybe even too late for a fall palette of maples, golds, and pumpkin polish shades. So, what to do in the weeks of November ahead when it comes to your nail look?

“November calls for rich, warming shades such as chocolate brown, mocha, espresso, and caramel, alongside deep cherry, oxblood, and olive green,” says Townhouse founder Juanita Huber-Millet. “Our Flawless collection captures the season beautifully, with coffee-inspired shades like Chai Latte and Mocha, and timeless reds such as Red Apple and Cherry for an effortlessly chic fall manicure.”

Huber-Millet also recommends burgundy, classic red, and deep plum for a timeless winter shade. “This season, expect modern twists with glossy chrome and cat-eye finishes, colored French tips and delicate gems that add a festive touch without compromising on sophistication,” the professional adds.

Below, discover our edit of the best nail trends and colors to wear this November and beyond, including gemstone-inspired cat-eye shades and modern, high-shine neutrals to suit any occasion.

A rich, high-shine black-brown shade is the new classic color for the season. The key is to opt out of milkier shades and lean into depth, with crisp, clean cuticles and a generously glossy top coat.

Dress up purple and burgundy shades with subtle polka dots, embracing the year’s most playful nail art trend with a sophisticated, grown-up edge. The key is to keep the dots spacious and minimal.

A clean, black manicure is as much a timeless winter staple as a gray layering piece or a pair of leather boots. The key is to keep your nails short and smart with a soft-square shape, and pay extra attention to hydrating and tidying your cuticles.

Trade cow print and leopard spots for a more elevated, minimal zebra print this November. The best method is to put a playful twist on the classic French tip manicure, using fine lines to create subtle definition.

November’s take on the burgundy manicure is the darkest, glossiest yet. Pair deep, shiny pinotage tones with a classic shape, like almond or soft-square, and embrace purple-leaning hues over classic reds.

“Chrome and cat-eye finishes are key trends this winter,” says Huber-Millet. “At Townhouse, we’re seeing brown chrome become a firm favorite, combining rich, chocolatey tones with a luminous finish for a manicure that feels luxurious, contemporary, and perfectly suited to the season.”

The result? A multidimensional finish evocative of the classic tiger’s-eye gemstone.

Skip natural pink chrome and cat-eye this season and embrace rich, dark bases, from black to brown to burgundy. For a wintry twist, opt for a reflective blue or silver sheer chrome that allows the depth to shine through while highlighting its unique shift.

#6711. Owen Wilson Breaks Down the World’s Best Golf Courses

The PGA Tour may be wrapping up in just a few short weeks, but this week marks the official beginning of Stick Season. No, not the Noah Kahan song, but Owen Wilson’s charming Apple TV+ comedy, whose second season premieres this Wednesday, November 4th. The show follows Wilson’s Pryce “Stick” Cahill, a former pro golfer who crashed out in a Kenny Powers-esque blaze of almost-glory a couple decades ago. Season one tracked his reentry into the game as the mentor of a talented but troubled young golfer played by Peter Dager. But in Season two, Stick has his eyes on a new prize: becoming the oldest player to ever win the U.S. Open.

Wilson himself might not be winning majors any time soon, but his experience filming the show has turned him into a real golf nut. He hadn’t played much beforehand, he told me, so the last couple of years have been a real crash course in one of the most difficult sports in the world. Still, it hasn’t taken much for him to compile a list of his favorite courses—and a bucket list of ones he’s dying to play a round or two on. Ahead of the show’s return, the 57-year-old actor hit the links with GQ.

“I have gotten an invite from a member to play, so I think that will happen at some point. What's always funny about that is that they close right after The Masters, so they're closed all summer. I’ve got to find a time that works for them where I could go play. That would be incredible.”

“My brother says St. Andrews and some of the other courses in Scotland are incredible. Out there the links style is pretty different from the courses in Dallas. And the people in Scotland, Luke says, are so knowledgeable about the game and friendly. I have not played link style and sometimes I wonder, Well, maybe my game would suit that because sometimes I'm not getting a lot of lift on the ball. And I am very comfortable with a putter. So yeah, maybe that's where I'll really prove that I'm good at the game.”

“Playing in Makena on Maui, that's a beautiful course that I love playing where you're getting to see the ocean and the beautiful Hawaiian features.”

“I played this one in Sydney that's kind of their [version of] Pebble Beach. It’s on the ocean, and there are some dramatic holes where you see waves breaking. I played lousy that day, but I'd like another crack at it.”

“I remember asking Collin Morikawa what his favorite course was and he said Riviera. Getting to play Riviera, I kind of feel like I've gotten to know more about the game. In the beginning, it was sort of lost on me—like getting a really good bottle of wine, and I couldn't really tell the difference. But now that I'm getting better, I can appreciate how incredible that course is. That first hole, where you're kind of teeing off from way up above. Just the other day, on number 10, I had a par four where I drove the green and just barely made it to the front of the green. But I was immediately on the phone calling to let my brothers and friends know that I had an eagle putt, which I missed. But that kind of kicked off a good little stretch where I birdied three out of four holes. That was a rare kind of day. More often, I'm kind of experiencing how challenging golf is.”

“I’ve stayed [at the Manor] and the course where they’re going to hold the Ryder Cup next year looked beautiful.”

“When I was training for the show, I learned how to play at Maui Country Club, a little nine-hole course kind of near where I am on the North Shore. [Maui] and Mākena, those were the two places that I really played a lot.”

“I played my best round at King Kamehameha with [former NBA coach] Don Nelson. I'd only been playing for a year-and-a-half where I was able to shoot in the low 80s, and everything just was very simple that day. Like, you hit your drive on the fairway, and then on the fairway you just hit it on the green, and then you two-putt and move on. I was with Nellie when he got his last hole in one. At that point I think he was maybe 83, and he was able to shoot his age and get a hole in one. I have not gotten a hole in one yet, but it's very exciting to witness one.”

#6710. Colin Jost Takes Gift-Giving Seriously

The Weekend Update co-host and Kay campaign star shares his approach to holiday shopping.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Finding the perfect holiday gift isn’t easy. Between the pressure to get it right, the endless wish lists, and the people who insist they don’t want anything, shopping for loved ones can feel like an impossible mission. Even Colin Jost, who has spent years navigating the pressures of live television, admits that the process is incredibly stressful.

This festive season, the Weekend Update co-host is putting his comedic talents to work with Kay by starring in the jeweler’s latest holiday campaign, “Love All In.” The cheeky ad follows Jost on an increasingly ridiculous quest to find the perfect present, poking fun at the lengths we’ll go to for the people closest to us. It’s a fitting partnership for someone who knows a thing or two about making people laugh but also takes gifting pretty seriously.

“I think I’m a good gift giver,” Jost tells ELLE. “Giving gifts is stressful because I do want it to be a meaningful gift. I hate the idea of just buying something because you have to give someone something.”

For Jost, the secret to getting it right has less to do with how much you spend and more to do with how much thought goes into it. “At every kind of price point for any gift, there [are] thoughtful and unthoughtful versions,” he says. “Something can be really expensive but not thoughtful.”

It’s a sentiment that aligns with Kay’s latest campaign, which encourages shoppers to go “all in” when expressing their love. And while Jost might not be the first person you’d think to turn to for jewelry advice, he’s developed an appreciation for it over the years, thanks to his very chic wife, Scarlett Johansson.

“Until five years ago, I didn’t own a watch,” he admits. That changed when the actress gifted him his first one, introducing him to an entirely new world of accessories. As for whether she’s influenced his personal style? “In that it’s exclusively managed by her, yes, I would say she’s influenced it.”

Despite his Staten Island roots, Jost’s jewelry preferences are surprisingly understated. “I don’t really wear a ton of jewelry, but I also am from Staten Island, so I do have to have certain pieces, or else they won’t let me back over the Verrazano Bridge,” he jokes.

While browsing Kay’s assortment, he found himself drawn to simple gold pieces, including a ring, bracelet, and necklace. “They were really nice, but also they weren’t gaudy or anything,” he says. His preference for gold also comes with some rather unconventional reasoning: “If we get into a post-apocalyptic situation, it feels like it’s better to melt down for trading.”

When it comes to shopping for the people closest to him, Jost admits that both Johansson and his Weekend Update collaborator Michael Che are difficult to buy things for, though he found a creative solution for the latter. “I got Che a really large and heavy, realistic statue of a velociraptor,” he recalls. “It was so heavy that he literally can’t get rid of it.” The real expense wasn’t the dinosaur itself. “The main cost was shipping,” he says. “It was a huge eyesore, and it’s prohibitively expensive for him to have removed from his property.”

The hardest person to gift on Jost’s list? His father, who insists he doesn’t need anything. “I think he actually means it, but it’s so unhelpful,” Jost says. After years of nostalgic gifts inspired by his dad’s past, he’s running out of ideas. “I’ve got to figure out something that breaks through his defenses.”

In terms of gifting etiquette, Jost has a few rules of his own. For starters, he’s big on surprises. While he understands the appeal of a wish list for children, he thinks adults should leave a little room for the unexpected. “For adults, it’s got to be ‘surprise me,’” he says. “The surprise is half the fun, three-quarters of the fun.” Regifting, on the other hand, comes with a few conditions. He’s open to the idea, but only if the gift is a perfect fit for someone and there’s full disclosure.

But perhaps the most surprising revelation comes when I ask what’s on his own holiday wish list. After spending much of our conversation discussing what to buy everyone else, Jost seems relieved to finally be on the receiving end. “Oh, thank you! Finally, someone asked me. What do I want?”

His answer? Nothing material. “At this point in life, I mostly want experiences,” he says. Whether it’s a trip or simply someone taking the initiative to organize an outing, he’s more interested in making memories than collecting more things. “Even if it’s just the plan of, ‘Let’s go do this at this time,’ I think that’s a great gift.” Or, when in doubt, a velociraptor.

#6708. Forget Arrakis, Zendaya’s Latest Look Comes From a London Auto Shop

If Ronan McKenzie called her spring 2027 collection for Selasi “Going Places,” this week it did just that when Law Roach enlisted the designer to provide clothes for Zendaya. (The image architect has been keeping himself pretty busy with his other very famous client, Kim Kardashian.)

Earlier this week, Zendaya appeared alongside her co-star Timothée Chalamet in a promotional video for Dune: Part Three, wearing look three from the show: a sleeveless halter-neck top and barrel-legged trousers in sandy shades of suede evocative of the movie’s desert landscape.

It’s always a thrill to see how far a collection can travel beyond the runway, particularly when it comes from a label with relatively modest resources. This was only McKenzie’s second runway presentation since joining the London Fashion Week schedule, staged in a mechanic’s garage and modeled by the designer’s inner circle, among them her mum, British Vogue contributing editor Zezi Ifore and entrepreneur Charlene Prempeh.

“Their presence underscored a central idea behind the collection: these clothes are intended to live beyond the runway,” read the show notes. “Going Places is grounded in pieces that can move through different bodies, ages, and lives.” Another headline-making moment from Selasi’s recent runways was the rediscovery of 59-year-old model Evelyn Effrim-Botchey, who has since gone on to make waves on Paris’s most rarefied catwalks.

Of course, Roach could commission custom looks from any number of luxury fashion houses—he has even been known to charter private jets to ensure Zendaya is dressed in just-seen-on-the-runway haute couture gowns—but he has made a concerted effort to champion emerging designers, too. The previous Dune press tour saw the actor wear Torishéju and Paolo Carzana, while she was an early supporter of Peter Do and Maximilian Davis’s Ferragamo before that. For a young designer, a co-sign of this caliber can make all the difference, offering a way through an industry difficult to break into.

“The energy you put into something won’t always lead to the outcome you imagine,” McKenzie told Vogue not long ago. “But you still have to fight, keep going, restart and pick yourself up off the ground.” It’s paying off.

#6706. The 77 Best Red-Carpet Looks of All Time (and What You Can Learn From Them)

What does it mean to truly own the red carpet? It means showing out the way that stars have at the biggest events on the planet for generations now: In the swankiest, swerviest, most spotlight-stealing fashion possible.

Maybe that’s stunting in a disco-tinged jumpsuit like a ruffled John Malkovich at the 2026 Venice Film Festival, suiting up in sumptuous red velvet like Gwenyth Paltrow in 1999, keeping things simmeringly subtle like Frank Ocean’s Prada look at the 2019 Met Gala, or popping out the big lapels on a suede tux like Tom Holland at GQ’s Men of the Year 2021. Whatever your interpretation, the best red-carpet looks need to feel unexpected, look unforgettable, and radiate confidence.

To help jumpstart your own legendary party ensembles, here are 77 of the greatest red-carpet moments ever—and what you can learn from each.

Don’t be afraid to lean into your sex appeal.

As one wise Twitter user once put it, “Colman Domingo always dresses like he's stepped out of a GQ Mag shoot.”

This lush Gucci velvet suit became so instantly legendary that Gwenyth herself recreated the look more than 20 years later.

Frank caused some consternation (though not around these parts) when he showed up to 2019’s camp-themed Met Gala in an understated, decidedly un-camp look. Four years on, though, his outfit remains a great reminder that sticking to the classics—in this case, black-and-white Prada from head to toe—is never a poor choice.

Ruffles have ridges, and so does this suit.

Leaning retro can sometimes go awry on the red carpet, but Stanfield managed to pull the ‘70s look off with funky ease when he pulled this giant-collared, razor-sharp Saint Laurent jumpsuit out for the Oscars.

This outfit looks like it comes with its own walk-in music, and it’s loud.

The right to rock bare-chested suit isn’t something you demand—it’s something you earn.

Keanu is no stranger to high-low tailoring—he’s been known to rock work boots with sharp suits and graphic hoodies with sport coats. But he’s never pulled that trick off better than he did here in ‘93, layering a badass leather motorcycle vest under a roomy three-button number.

Julia Effin’ Roberts in a Big Effin’ Suit. That’s it. That’s the caption.

Wearing Prada, like Wright at the 2023 Golden Globes, is a surefire way to get a lot of compliments. The brand makes you look stylish and smart. Don’t you just want to ask Wright which local art gallery to visit?

Gerber’s disco-ball gown is stunning, but it’s Butler’s silky, sumptuous, pussy-bow blouse—designed by Saint Laurent, as was his exquisitely tailored tux—that utterly steals the show.

#6702. Jennifer Lawrence’s Novelty T-Shirt Is an Archive Pull for the Ages—and All Ages

Jennifer Lawrence has a soft spot for a novelty item. Vintage Issey Miyake cats, Twilight merch, a litany of slogan-topped baseball caps have all found their way into the actor’s wardrobe. Her latest addition, however, is a particularly nostalgic one. A fashion archive pull for all ages, if you will.

Spotted out in New York City on Tuesday, the actor and now beauty brand founder leaned into her always colorful approach to off-duty dressing. The actor wore a white Sesame Street tee emblazoned with a scribbly blue portrait of Ernie, which she paired with slouchy, tomato-red Freecity Airjump pants, a blue-and-red plaid shirt knotted around her waist, and an oversized cobalt Auralee canvas jacket with a dark shearling-style collar. On her feet, a pair of lack-and-white Vans Authentic sneakers, and she added some small oval sunglasses. Her blonde hair was pulled into a loose and laidback braid—a little Katniss Everdeen-esque. There was another throwback in the mix, too. Lawrence flashed the three-finger salute made famous by her Hunger Games character for the cameras.

Lawrence’s fall wardrobe has been an ongoing exercise in getting comfortable without sacrificing character. Just last week, she took a sumptuous, floor-sweeping chartreuse house coat by New York designer Colleen Allen out for a spin, layering it over a lime Miu Miu cardigan and finishing the look with fuzzy black slippers. Elsewhere, there have been oversized knits, louche trousers, baseball caps, and all manner of unexpected color combinations. Cozy season is literal in the Lawrence household.

Lawrence’s more relaxed street style is often offset with her considered fashion eye. She might favor the quiet luxury of The Row, Khaite, and Phoebe Philo, but she’s just as likely to throw an irreverent graphic tee, a kooky accessory, or a flash of acid-bright color into the mix. Her wardrobe is expensive but never overly precious. And while her latest outfit might look like something borrowed from a pretty well-dressed child’s wardrobe, Jennifer Lawrence knows that approaching low-key looks require a certain beat of unseriousness—care of Elmo, et al, or otherwise.

#6701. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

It’s the skirt of the season. How will you wear yours?

#6699. All the Historic Firsts From the 2026 Midterms

The latest U.S. election saw history being made in states like Texas, California, Georgia, and more

On Tuesday, midterm general elections were held in the United States to determine all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, as well as 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate. Meanwhile, key governor races were held across 34 states, like New York, Texas, California, Florida, and Michigan.

These specific elections take place every four years during the middle of a presidential term, acting as a measurement of how happy voters are with the president’s current performance. More importantly, they help determine which side of the political spectrum will control Congress, the body of government that creates and passes legislation.

This time, Democrats ended up winning overwhelmingly, gaining seven seats in the Senate and 25 seats in the House, meaning the party is now in control of Congress and has significant power to buck many of President Donald Trump’s measures.

It was a joyous night for the left, it was also a night of many historic firsts for a U.S. election. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to ever be elected governor in American history, while Deb Haaland is the first Native American. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man ever elected to the Senate, while Abdul El-Sayed is the first Muslim candidate to join it.

Others made history in their specific states. Xavier Becerra is California’s first elected Latino governor. David Crowley is Wisconsin’s first-ever Black governor. Amy Acton is the first woman to ever become governor in Ohio. And that’s just the beginning.

Ahead, we break down all the historic firsts that happened during the 2026 U.S. midterm general elections.

Bottoms becomes the first Black candidate and first woman to ever be elected governor in Georgia. She also makes history as the first Black woman to ever be elected governor in the United States.

El-Sayed will become the first Muslim member of Senate in U.S. history, after he won his election in Michigan.

As a current House of Representatives member for New Hampshire, Pappas is the first openly gay man to ever represent the state in Congress. Now, with his Senate seat win, Pappas becomes the first openly gay man to ever be elected to the U.S. Senate.

Haaland is set to become the first Native American female governor in U.S. history. Previously, she was one of the first two indigenous women to ever be elected to Congress in New Mexico.

Acton becomes the first woman to ever be elected governor in Ohio, defeating Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. Previously, she served as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, and was also the first woman to hold that post.

Attorney and politician Xavier Becerra will become the first elected Latino governor of California. The last Latino to serve as governor in the state was José Antonio Romualdo Pacheco back in 1875, who ascended to the role when then-governor Newton Booth was elected to the U.S. Senate.

Montgomery becomes the first transgender state lawmaker in Alabama, in the state’s House District 25 seat.

Crowley is the first Black candidate ever elected governor of Wisconsin. Previously, he served as the executive of Milwaukee County and was the first Black person to serve in that position, as well as the youngest, as he was elected at age 33.

Hinojosa becomes the first Hispanic candidate ever elected governor in the state of Texas, and she also becomes the first Democrat to hold the post since Ann Richards won in 1990.

Flanagan, who is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe in Minnesota, becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate.

Ford becomes the first Black governor of Nevada, after previously serving as the first Black attorney general in the state.

Klobuchar becomes the first woman elected governor in the state of Minnesota.

Kiros becomes the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress, as part of Colorado’s first congressional district.

With her election to the Washington state legislature, Scott becomes the first out Black trans state lawmaker in the country.

#6696. Statement Scarves Are Fall’s Defining Accessory

Puffed, twisted, and totally oversize: Scarves are taking over as new statements.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The behemoth sculptural statement scarf is here, and it’s never looked better. Puffed, twisted, oversize, and opulent, these finishing pieces eclipse the coat and become a one-and-done look for winter weather. These are not your usual blanket scarves or faux fur creations. The new statement scarf is padded and sculpted, often done in fabrics like luscious leather. These XL scarves were seen on the fall/winter 2026 runway at Loewe, Celine, and Toteme. Elsewhere, Givenchy showcased the power of a smaller leather scarf done in brilliant cobalt blue. The main message with all of these outfit-defining scarves is that they do all the talking and create a strong visual impact with even the most simple of coats. Black leather jackets, neutral wool coats, basic blazers, and even beige trenches get a new look with a dramatic scarf. It’s no surprise the look is trending now. After season upon season of quiet luxury, we’re now firmly in the era of the statement coat.

But for those who don’t want to fully commit to the look, we have the statement scarf, which gives instant drama with ease. If you’re in need of styling inspiration, follow the runways’ lead. Keep it tonal and choose a scarf in the same color palette as your coat or jacket, or go the opposite way and pick up a primary hue like scarlet red or bright yellow to add contrast to a more subdued-hued jacket.

There’s also something beautifully haphazard about these pieces: On the runway, many of them are intentionally styled so that they look windswept or as if they were in motion and got frozen mid-moment. For designers like Michael Rider at Celine, that was part of it. The label’s fall/winter 2026 show notes presented the collection as “intuition over strategy. Feeling it rather than planning it,” and “contradiction, imperfection, character.” Adding to this, “I love when messy, complex, layered inner lives come through underneath great clothes,” Rider expressed in the show notes. “Thinking about people with style who wear beautiful clothes in a personal way.”

On a more practical level, the statement scarf adds a little bit of pizzazz with warmth. It acts as wearable sculpture. Tied tightly around the neck, styled with an over-the-top pair of sunglasses, it brings the focus to the face and creates an iconic look that is also strangely practical.

We’re all so bundled under layers in these cooler months that accessorizing (and wearing jewelry) can pose a challenge. Many of the big puffy scarves are editorial showpieces that may not have made it to the retail side of fashion, but the other side of statement scarves lies in embellishment. Think: embroidered wonders from Dries Van Noten, paillette triangle scarves from Zankov, or even just a classic scarf done with extra-long fringe. Just think of it as a warm version of a necklace.

#6693. Simu Liu’s First Favorite Brand Was Abercrombie & Fitch

Simu Liu is no stranger to fashion’s biggest night, so, when I met him at his hotel in SoHo Monday night, he figured the Council of Fashion Designers of America Awards show should be a cinch. “I think everything’s a little bit more chill than the Met Gala,” Liu says. “So I’m looking forward to having a little bit of a more relaxed environment to talk to fashion houses and meet people from the different brands and also just to see friends.”

We speak just a few hours before the 37-year-old actor is about to make his first appearance at the Oscars of fashion and it’s hard to tell that he just hopped off a plane from Los Angeles this morning. The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings actor has had a packed year, from making his Broadway debut in Oh, Mary! between February and April to getting married back in October. He’s preparing to start promotion for the highly anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’s set to reprise his role as the superhero Shang-Chi. Marvel fans haven’t seen him on the screen since his record-breaking film debut in 2021. “It’s been a long, long time,” he jokes.

For now, he’s clad in a robe sitting barefoot on the sofa, swiping a metallic device across his unblemished, glowing face. “I think it’s like a gua sha, but it’s cold,” he speculates. (His makeup artist, Alex Keating, confirms that it’s Shark Beauty’s Depuffi, a hot-and-cold contrast therapy gua sha that basically “gives you a full facial.”) A room service trolley is sitting inches away from him, allowing him quick access to a plate of chicken tenders and fries. And a Diet Coke. Don’t forget the Diet Coke.

Keating makes good use of Liu’s wavy locks, hairspraying a Superman-like curl into permanent place on his forehead as he sips his fridge cigarette. The actor’s dad cut his hair until he was 18 and he says it took him a while to learn what worked for his own mane. He envied the typical stick-straight Asian hair others had, but through his work with groomers learned the power of salt sprays to lean into his hair’s natural texture. It admittedly took a while for Liu to develop his own fashion sense as an adult, too.

“When you grow up working class and you grow up with parents whose purchasing habits were just the furthest thing from luxurious, I think it just takes time for you to learn about fashion,” he says. “The first brand that I remember really caring about was Abercrombie & Fitch.”

Tonight, though, Liu has moved far beyond the mall. He’s attending the CFDA Awards on behalf of White Rabbit Trust, an organization that supports AAPI creatives and entrepreneurs. It's hosting the award’s Emerging Designers Table, which allows industry leaders—this year, Jason Wu—to mentor AAPI designers who create custom looks for the muse of their choosing. In Liu’s case, he’s been dressed by Asian-Canadian designer Haoran Li of the brand Private Policy.

The look for the evening was a matching set made from black silk jacquard woven with bamboo paired with a shiny new silver wedding ring and a Rolex Batman GMT-Master II. His cropped trucker-style jacket, accented by hand-knotted Chinese buttons, sat over a crisp frayed-hem white button-down with wide-legged pants that draped over low-profile black shoes. “In Chinese culture, bamboo is one of the Four Gentlemen, a symbol of integrity and resilience,” Li says. “It bends in the storm but never breaks. That felt like Simu, who has spent his career pushing through doors that weren’t built for us.”

I ask if he’s ever bothered by the responsibility of representing the Asian diaspora. “Right around the time Crazy Rich Asians came out, it was the first studio Asian movie in 25 years,” he recalls. “Then Shang-Chi was the first Asian Marvel superhero movie. For a while it was just like first this, first this, first this. So I felt like innately the stakes were high and I put pressure on myself. I don’t regret doing that. I just remember looking around and not really seeing anyone doing that. So I thought, well it might as well be me.”

To that point, this isn’t the first time Liu has used his name to promote an indie AAPI brand. At the the premiere of Shang-Chi in 2021, he spotlighted Singaporean-British designer Chelsea Scott-Blackhall’s label Dzojchen, wearing the brand’s silk kimono tuxedo.

Prominence in Hollywood has meant more to him than giving him the opportunity to wear really nice clothes. He’s decided to take more agency in his career, he says. Last year, he starred and executive produced the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test, which despite favorable reviews was cancelled after one season. That hasn’t slowed his aspirations for new creative outlets: "I think actually right now I’m really excited by the idea of becoming a director."

But before we get to see “Directed by Simu Liu” on the big screen, the star has an awards show to attend—and a plate of tendies to devour. Just as quickly as he’s touched down here in New York, he’s off again to Hong Kong tomorrow.

#6689. Bikini Trimmers Are Painless, Easy, and Irritation-Free—if You Know Which Ones to Buy

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

“Bush on main,” “hot bush summer,” “don’t shave your bush!”—I see it all over TikTok and Instagram, and I’m all for this pro-pubes movement we’re in. But I haven’t exactly seen it anywhere, and none of my friends seem to be participating. In fact, I get more questions than ever about the best razors and shaving products. What I do think is happening, though, is a transition to trimming rather than a full Brazilian bikini wax. Which is where my endorsement (er, some might say campaign) for bikini trimmers comes in.

I ditched all the other at-home hair removal methods for a bikini trimmer in 2023, aside from the occasional wax or laser-hair removal device. Truly, nothing is as quick, easy, or painless as trimming my bikini line with an electric razor. Because I’ve reviewed so many bikini trimmers over the years, I’ve learned that the best one really depends on what you’re trying to do. My everyday electric bikini trimmer, my travel-friendly option, and my precision trimmer all serve different purposes—and each one does its specific job a little better than the rest. Here’s a peek at my faves:

Don’t worry, I’m getting into all the best bikini trimmers I’ve tried below. And if you need even more info to help you choose, keep reading for expert advice on how to trim your bikini line and which trimmer is best for you.

Why we love it: When I traveled to Miami to celebrate my birthday, this bikini trimmer from Bushbalm was one of the first things I threw in my travel bag. Why? Because I was able to charge it before my trip, then never had to worry about it dying on me in the middle of a pre-pool trim, thanks to the battery that lasts a full five hours. (TBH, I actually didn’t even charge it before—I’ve actually only needed to charge this once in the last six months, lol.)

And while I could wax poetic about the battery forever, I mostly love how powerful this little trimmer is while still feeling gentle against my skin. I rarely use it with the guard on, but I love having it as an option when I want a slightly longer length between waxing appointments. And it’s fairly quiet, which is great when you’re sharing a hotel room or have nosy aunts in the room next door at Christmas—ya know. Precisely, all the reasons we gave this a Cosmo Holy Grail Beauty Award in 2025.

One Cosmo editor says: “I’m so prone to ingrowns, it’s not even funny, so I’m always looking for a tool that can get me smooth and keep me smooth. The BushBalm is that tool. The trimmer gets pretty much as close to the skin as you can get without causing nicks and is so easy to use that I could do it with my eyes closed. It does the job and does it well, and I love that it’s waterproof in case you want to use it in the bath or shower. I’m also obsessed with the ingrown hair oil from BushBalm—it makes the perfect pairing.”—HANNAH CHUBB, FORMER LIFESTYLE EDITOR

Why we love it: For getting super close without nicking yourself, this Philips OneBlade device was made for getting into all the little crevices of your bikini line and intimate areas with precision. If there’s any straggling hairs after you shave, this is a great extra tool to have on hand for getting them. But don’t worry if you’re clumsy (like us), the blade isn’t too sharp. This waterproof trimmer is great for in the shower too, thanks to the lightweight handle.

Why we love it: IDK if a day passes when I don't see this trimmer on my FYP. I’ve seen a gazillion videos reviewing this, calling it the best hair-removal device for way, way, way cheaper than laser or wax passes. It’s double-ended: One side is a classic blade trimmer that takes off the hair, while the other is a precision trimmer that you run along your skin in circular motions to get the closest possible trim.

One Cosmo editor says: “Having the two options for trimming really helps get my skin smooth and reduces any stubble whatsoever. It’s also a huge plus that this device is super easy to use.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: If you usually end up with nicks in your bikini area because razors or trimmers aren’t contoured to your body, you’ll love the V-shape of this bikini trimmer, which easily trims all the lil folds and crevices of your bikini line. Not to mention, the three comb attachments give you choices for how much hair you want to remove in each area. And don’t worry about cuts, because the rounded blade glides across your skin without getting caught.

One Cosmo editor says: “I use this electric razor to trim my dad’s neck hair (sorry for blowing up your spot, Dad). But!! With that said, it proves just how simple this is to use. My dad would certainly screech in pain if I even remotely knicked him, and I never have with this (others, not so confident).”—BG

Why we love it: My battle with ingrown hairs is essentially what led me to try a bikini trimmer in the first place. And the first one on my list was this tool from Meridian, which went viral on TikTok because it’s got a strong, sharp blade that cuts through super-thick and curly hair without causing irritation (i.e., ingrown hairs and razor burn). I usually pop on one of the two included trim guards, which keeps the length a lil longer but helps further prevent inflamed bumps.

I’ll just exfoliate in the shower, rinse, then lather up a moisturizing, fragrance-free shaving cream and run the trimmer along my bikini line. I also make sure to avoid going over each area too many times to reduce irritation. Afterward, I’ll pat my skin dry and smooth on a gentle body lotion to keep my skin soft and smooth.

One Cosmo editor says: "Of all of the bikini trimmers I've tested—which is a lot, btw—this is definitely the most gentle. I've never, ever worried that I would nick myself, but it's been especially helpful for cutting down on ingrown hairs."—BG

Why we love it: One of the most necessary situations for a quality bikini trimmer is while traveling to quickly clean up any unwanted hairs without pain or irritation. Enter: This travel, touch-up trimmer from Bushbalm that won a Cosmo Holy Grail Beauty award. The stainless steel blades help pick up teeny-tiny hairs (including even peach fuzz on your face) in only a few minutes. But the best part is that it really doesn’t nick or irritate skin—a must for quick use.

One Cosmo editor says: “I love how easy it is to quickly touch up my bikini line with this, and it’s entirely painless. Best part: It’s waterproof, so I can use it in the shower to save time.”—BG

Why we love it: Fur reimagined their best-selling trimmer to do the work of both a trimmer and a razor, meaning you really only need one device to get it all done. Say you want a super smooth, hair-free bikini line but just wanna trim everything else? Run the trimmer along your skin, then pop on the razor head to get a close shave. This tool is also really helpful on the precision front, thanks to an LED light on the head of the device that makes it way easier to get in all those little hard-to-reach crevices that you can't see super well.

One Cosmo editor says: “I’ve used this tool for years, but I really fell in love when they relaunched this year. Yes, it’s expensive, but it feels fancy. The tool is weighted, but not too heavy, and made of a sturdy plastic that feels really good in my hand. And it also looks nice in my bathroom. I just keep it in my shower and charge up the pedestal once a week.”—BG

Why we love it: Just because my bikini line is covered in razor bumps after a less-than-stellar shave doesn’t mean I’m fine with the overgrowth. In those moments, I reach for this gentle Gillette Venus trimmer, which comes with a removable guard that helps me lightly trim my hair without irritation. “Using a comb attachment with a trimmer can prevent the blades from touching the skin at all, which helps avoid irritation and nicks and cuts,” says Katelyn Liston, associate scientist for Gillette Venus.

One Cosmo editor says: "When I found myself suddenly en route to pool party in Miami with a bikini line I hadn't touched in months, I ran over to Target and snatched this up in a pinch. Shockingly, it was so freaking easy to use. The guard helps reduce the potential for cuts and bumps, so I could quickly clean up all the stray hairs without worrying it would irritate me."—BG

No, a bikini trimmer is not necessarily better than shaving; it just comes down to personal preference and the look you're going for. “You should consider a trimmer if you experience irritation after shaving your bikini area, or if you prefer to maintain, but not fully remove, all of your pubic hair,” says Liston. Shaving, on the other hand, cuts the hair off at the surface, meaning you’re left with smoother skin afterward—but also with a higher risk of bumps, ingrown hairs, and irritation.

Do you need to use shaving cream with a bikini trimmer?

Yes, you can use shaving cream with a bikini trimmer if you want more moisturized skin, but you don’t have to. You can also trim your hair dry without any cream or lotion, which is why bikini trimmers are so versatile and easy to use. Check the instructions on your specific trimmer though, as some with extra-sharp blades might require shaving cream to help prevent friction that can lead to irritation.

Bikini trimmers do leave some stubble because your hair isn’t actually removed from your follicle like with plucking or waxing, or cut close to the skin like with shaving. Some trimmers have a strong, sharp blade that can get really close to your skin, leaving you with little to no noticeable hair, while others (generally best for sensitive skin) just trim your hair to a shorter length. If you prefer a totally hair-free finish, you can shave or wax and then just use a bikini trimmer to clean up any hairs as they’re starting to grow back.

A couple of days before you want to trim your bikini line, exfoliate your skin with a chemical exfoliant or body scrub to get a smoother shave, advises board-certified dermatologist Mona Gohara. Then, once you’re ready, lather up your skin with a hydrating, fragrance-free shaving cream or oil to avoid irritation and bumps when shaving or using a trimmer in the shower (you don't need cream when you're trimming on dry skin though, fyi).

The easiest way to prevent bumps and ingrown hair when trimming your bikini line? Make sure you’re shaving with the grain (i.e., the direction your hair grows), says Dr. Gohara, because shaving and trimming against the grain (or switching up your direction) is basically a recipe for irritation. “Take it slow and don’t rush,” she says.

Every bikini trimmer is different. “Using your trimmer incorrectly can cause discomfort, or even worse, cut your sensitive bikini-line skin,” says Liston. Some trimmers require that you use shaving cream, others need to be used dry; so, make sure you’re following the directions on the packaging of your trimmer (aka read it before tossing it out).

As soon as you’re done trimming, follow up with a generous layer of fragrance-free cream safe to use on your sensitive, external skin to keep your skin soft and bump-free, says Dr. Gohara. P.S., It's never a bad idea to dab on an ingrown hair toner while maintaining your bikini line—just dab one on every few days post cleansing.

Shaving or trimming with a dull, dirty blade is not ideal and can often lead to irritation or infections. Clean your blades with antibacterial soap and water after every single use, and make sure you're replacing your blades every few weeks for a more painless experience (you can even put a reminder on your calendar!). Also, never share your tools—even if your roommate asks nicely.

How do I prevent ingrown hairs when using a bikini trimmer?

Bikini trimmers don’t generally cause ingrown hairs because the hair isn’t removed from your skin, which means it's unlikely to get trapped as it grows. This is why bikini trimmers are a great option for anyone who’s prone to ingrown hairs, razor bumps, and razor burn.

Though a bikini trimmer is less likely to give you ingrown hairs, adhering to the following practices will help reduce your risk:

History and hair type: If your skin is sensitive, you have a history of ingrowns, or you have curly or coarse hair, your chance of developing ingrown hairs increases. Though there's nothing you can do about this, if you follow the tips below, your chances can significantly decrease.

Preparation: You should ideally wait until your pubic hair has grown back out to around 4mm, as any shorter can lead to irritation. You also need to exfoliate beforehand, and if your trimmer/razor works with it, add shaving cream or oil.

Direction of shave: Despite razors or trimmers claiming you can shave whichever way and not have any irritation, it truly is best to shave in the direction of your hair growth using short, small strokes.

Aftercare: Trimming is a form of exfoliation, so natural oils and moisture may be stripped away during the process. Layering on a post-shave moisturizer (that's fragrance-free and is applied only on your external genitalia area!) will provide moisture and soothe your skin.

Blade: Surprisingly enough, you should be changing your blades after five to 10 shaves. A dull blade can lead to more nicks and can increase bacteria buildup, which is a recipe for infection.

And, the most important rule: If you have a significant amount of ingrown hairs (or even just one!), let them heal and prevent picking. If you try to remove them yourself, you can risk infection.

Are you determined to get rid of razor burn or ingrown hairs? A trimmer is probably the better option. A bikini trimmer is also great if you don’t want to completely get rid of hair in an area. Need a completely smooth shave? You’ll probably want to shave or wax first, then use a trimmer to touch up between.

If you want to create precise designs or just touch-up your bikini line between shaving, you’ll like having a smaller bikini trimmer that can easily maneuver across your skin. However, if you like trimming your lower stomach, inner thighs, or other larger areas, opt for something that has a bigger blade (and if it comes with a bikini attachment for precision-work, even better).

Some trimmers are a little bit more ~advanced.~ Choose a trimmer that’s waterproof if you want to save time and trim in the shower. If you want a super-close shave, look for a razor/trimmer duo, or an electric razor that has a trimmer attachment.

If you trim, like, all the time, grab one that comes with replacement heads to make sure you’ll always have a sharp blade. I also live for a trimmer that has a light to help me see what the heck I’m doing down there (because there is nothing worse than going in there blind with a sharp object, right?).

#6687. 25 Great Gifts for New Dads, According to GQ

Becoming a dad changes a lot of things. Your sleep schedule, for one. Your relationship with a clean shirt, for another. But just because a guy has entered his daddy era doesn't mean he's stopped caring about the things he cared about before.

With that in mind, we've rounded up the best gifts for new dads, with a little something for him and the little one. Some are practical things that'll make those early days of fatherhood a little easier. Others are simply things that'll make him feel good, look good, and a little more like himself.

Nothing doing? Check out the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

At some point, he'll emerge back into the world, and there's nothing like a great shirt to ease the reentry. This swaggy checked shirt from Beams has all the layering built right in, so he can look like he hasn't missed a step.

There's a lot to be said for clothes that don't require much thought, especially when you've got a new bundle. Take this double-faced merino wool bomber from Quince: warm, unfussy, and easy to throw on with just about anything.

Some brands really are thinking of the children. Everybody.World makes its Trash Zip Hoodie from 100% recycled cotton waste, giving discarded material a second life as a very good sweatshirt.

A good pair of sweatpants is nonnegotiable. From the true masters of the category, these midweight terry sweatpants from Reigning Champ come with a relaxed silhouette, an open hem, and a nicely lived-in patina.

The undisputed king of dad shoes has entered its seventh generation, with its first major redesign since 2022 bringing a sleeker suede-and-mesh upper, softer cushioning, and all the Made in USA pedigree you'd expect. For a guy who's just become a dad, the timing couldn't be better.

He's a dad now. A man of refinement, responsibility, and a pressing need for a do-it-all boot. Enter Blundstone's new Heritage boot, a top-shelf take on its legendary shit-stomper, upgraded with premium leather and Goodyear-welted construction.

The baby's developing a sense of sight, and there's no reason for dad to sacrifice his. Lalo's Play Gym II is a far better-looking alternative to what's out there, with plenty to keep little hands and eyes occupied, including sensory toys, teethers, and a bell. The brand's set of high-contrast art cards wouldn't hurt, either.

If they've already got a Tripp Trapp, this one's a no-brainer. The iconic high chair is part of MoMA's permanent collection, and now the museum's Design Store has a set of colorful cushions to go with it.

One thing new parents can never have enough of is a good place to put the baby down. Part quilt, part playmat, these organic cotton numbers from House of Noa are among the most handsome we've seen, with an heirloom quality that makes 'em worth holding on to long after the baby has outgrown tummy time.

The problem with BabyBjörn? Too many good things to choose from. But for new parents, the gift of a few hands-free minutes is hard to beat. The new Bouncer Begin is designed specifically for newborns, with a shallower seat than the brand's wildly popular Bouncer Bliss.

Bottle-washing is a dad duty. We don't make the rules. Baby Brezza's Bottle Washer Pro 360 makes the job considerably less miserable, washing, sterilizing, and drying bottles in one go.

Two things you can never have enough of with a newborn: muslin and blankets. Coyuchi's wonderfully soft muslin quilt takes care of both.

New dads live by the clock. Three hours between feeds, 20 minutes until the next nap, two minutes to themselves, if they're lucky. Braun's Time Teacher, with its clean, easy-to-read dial, colorful hands, and markings for phrases like "quarter past" and "half past," makes keeping track a little easier. And when the little one is old enough to tell time, it'll come in handy all over again.

Apple's finally getting into the smart display game. The new HomeView is the company's first dedicated smart home hub, bringing home controls, FaceTime, and the usual Apple ecosystem conveniences to one ittle screen. Its 12-megapixel camera should come in especially handy for keeping the grandparents supplied with baby sightings.

A sleeping baby is a beautiful thing. Hatch's portable Go sound machine is a little godsend, with soothing sounds, a rechargeable battery, and a handy clip for attaching it to the stroller or car seat.

Bose's new sport-minded open earbuds let him enjoy his music or a podcast without tuning out what's happening around him—like, say, an actual human baby. And on the rare occasion he gets out for a run, they'll be just as useful for logging a few miles.

For the dad with his hands full (read: all dads), Ray-Ban's Meta Zena glasses pair a snazzy cat-eye silhouette with the ability to capture first steps, film stroller outings, or video-call the grandparents, all without reaching for his phone.

Tiny Vinyl's miniature record player and four-inch records are pure novelty, but there's something rather charming about a tiny turntable for a tiny human. Start building the little one's record collection now, and they'll have something to grow into.

Fujifilm's new Instax Pal 2 gives dad another way to document his little one, packing a digital camera into an adorable, palm-sized package. He can send shots straight to his phone, or pair it with an Instax printer for a few keepsakes the grandparents can stick on the fridge.

there's something to be said for having a few memories you can actually hold in your hands. This new 35mm point-and-shoot from Kodak lets him capture the little one on film, with actual prints to show for it.

Coterie diapers really do live up to the hype. And the brand's skincare lineup is pretty terrific, too. This set brings together full-size bottles of its hair and body wash, all-over moisturizer, and diaper and dry skin balm.

Dad's going to need all the help he can get in the sleep department. No surprise there. What might surprise him is how much magnesium can help, from supporting normal muscle and nerve function to regulating the body's stress response and potentially improving sleep quality.

The Fitbit Air might be the sleekest screen-free fitness tracker around, and at a price that makes it an easy sell. For the new dad who just wants to keep tabs on his sleep and daily steps without getting too deep into the fitness-data weeds, it's a straightforward proposition.

A little time for some om-ing is a fine idea for any new dad. Walden's meditation set gives him a dedicated place to find his center, and the accompanying mat doubles as a nice spot for the little one to stretch out.

#6682. Ralph Lauren’s 17 Best Outfits of All Time

On Monday night, the Council of Fashion Designers of America crowned Ralph Lauren as its menswear designer of the year—his 12th win since the show’s inaugural ceremony in 1981, minting him as the most decorated designer in CFDA history. The council even has a tradition of creating awards in Lauren’s honor, as they did with the Fashion Legend Award in 2007 and the CFDA Members Salute in 2018.

At age 87, Lauren is the consummate businessman of American fashion, and he’s still producing masterclass-caliber collections that build upon his label’s established codes. In addition to his business savvy and keen eye for tailoring, the designer remains as relevant as ever in 2026 because of something far more ineffable: a deep-rooted sense of personal style. For Lauren, clothes aren’t just a wardrobe; they are identity. His own relationship with getting dressed, from his deep and abiding love of Westernwear to his knack for blending Waspy blazers with rugged workwear and military pieces, has always been at the core of everything he does. Here are some of his best looks from the last 50 years.

Technical hiking gear was a relatively late addition to the RL oeuvre, but the man was wearing hikers in the city long before hipsters discovered Salomons.

Like a skilled party DJ, Ralph Lauren has an uncanny knack for combining unlikely elements—like a yachtsman’s sweater and a pair of worn-in blue jeans—with complete ease.

There’s black-tie, and then there’s RL black-tie. There’s no doubt that Lauren can wear a pair of tuxedo pants and patent leather shoes as well as anyone, but he is much more himself in jeans and cowboy boots.

A two-year stint at Baruch College in Manhattan was the closest Lauren came to the Ivy League, but that didn’t stop him from adopting repp ties, Oxford collar shirts, and other hallmarks of the East Coast elite. The juxtaposition of oversized aviator shades with this solidly trad look is quintessential Ralph.

Think a funky belt can’t be the defining element of an otherwise understated fit? Lauren would respectfully disagree.

Few people will ever look as good in a biker jacket as Ralph Lauren did at age 70. The difference is in the details—the flannel shirt unbuttoned and tucked, the crisp white henley—and the confidence.

Lauren is a master editor, but the magic of his greatest looks is in details like a vest tucked into trousers, a knotted belt, and a pair of precisely rolled sleeves.

Yacht club up top, honkey tonk downstairs. Another Lauren signature.

Ralph Lauren never learned how to sew, but he has an instinctive understanding of tailoring. By blending the stiff silhouettes of Savile Row with the breezy swagger of American ivy style, he created a look that was all his own.

Style is all about understanding the rules before you can break them. Lauren certainly does, and that’s why this ensemble—from the wide-spread collar and slim tie combination to the double-down on stripes—works as well as it does.

There’s perhaps no more challenging look to pull off than “office cowboy,” but Ralph Lauren makes it look easy.

Leather pants and a denim shirt under a tweed jacket is another decidedly advanced maneuver, but (if executed correctly) a potentially powerful one.

In recent decades, Lauren has increasingly swapped his signature cowboy boots for La Sportiva hikers, anointing gorpcore in the process.

Lauren has always revered the look of traditional British tailoring, from safari suits to Savile Row, but he’s just as likely to pair his flannel suits with cashmere turtlenecks and cowboy boots as neckties and Oxfords.
