#6681. All About Alexandra Leclerc, Charles Leclerc’s Wife

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Alexandra Leclerc has become one of Formula 1’s most recognizable fashion figures, but she built a public identity far beyond being Charles Leclerc’s wife. The Monaco-based influencer, art history student, and fashion collaborator first appeared alongside the Ferrari driver in 2023, and since then, she’s become a regular fixture at race weekends, fashion shows, and luxury brand events.

In February 2026, the couple officially tied the knot during a civil ceremony in Monaco after nearly three years together. They welcomed their first child in November 2026.

Here’s everything to know about Alexandra and her relationship with the Formula 1 star.

Alexandra was born in Calais, France, in June 2001 and has Mexican, Argentinian, and French heritage. She later studied art history at L’École du Louvre in Paris, specializing in 20th century art.

Her interest in the art world extends beyond school. Before becoming a full-time creator, Alexandra worked as an art assistant at Hôtel Des Ventes De Monte-Carlo auction house and also worked with Monaco Art Week.

She still shares that side of herself online, too. Alongside her main Instagram account, Alexandra runs a separate page dedicated to art, exhibitions, and artists she loves.

Fans first began speculating that Alexandra and Charles were together in early 2023 after she appeared in the background of social media videos during Paris Fashion Week.

A few months later, Alexandra attended the Monaco Grand Prix as an official Ferrari guest, further fueling rumors.

Their first major public appearance as a couple was at Wimbledon in July 2023, where they were photographed together alongside fellow Formula 1 driver Pierre Gasly and his girlfriend, Francisca Gomes.

Since then, the two have appeared together at NBA games, fashion events, Formula 1 races, and red carpets around the world.

As Charles’s Formula 1 career reached new heights, Alexandra regularly supported him throughout race weekends.

She has attended several races, including the 2024 Monaco Grand Prix, where Charles earned his first hometown victory, and the Italian Grand Prix later that year.

Following the Monaco race, the couple attended Formula 1’s annual gala dinner alongside Prince Albert II and Princess Charlene of Monaco.

Alexandra’s online following has exploded as she stepped more into the limelight in 2024. She now has millions of followers across Instagram and TikTok, where she shares beauty tutorials, fashion content, travel photos, and glimpses into her life in Monaco.

Her style especially helped distinguish her online presence. Rather than leaning into louder trends, Alexandra became known for minimalist silhouettes, neutral palettes, and polished styling.

In a May 2026 interview with The Cut, Alexandra explained that she genuinely enjoys planning outfits and building looks around references or locations.

“I love when there’s a story behind a look,” she said. “I love when the reference is right and it doesn’t feel random. It makes the whole look feel more personal.”

She also addressed navigating visibility online while keeping parts of her life private.

“I’m very selective about what I share,” Alexandra told The Cut. “I don’t feel the need to share everything.”

As Alexandra’s following grew, luxury brands quickly took notice.

She has collaborated with Rhode, Meshki, Nina Ricci, and Jacquemus, among others.

She also appeared on the cover of ELLE Mexico in October 2025.

In April 2026, Alexandra launched a capsule collection with Frame inspired by her day-to-day style in Monaco.

The collection featured denim, structured separates, leather pants, fitted dresses, and matching sets designed around what Alexandra described as her actual everyday wardrobe.

“This isn’t a collection I designed for a version of myself,” she told WWD. “It’s pieces I actually reach for, in a city that’s actually my home.”

She added that the collaboration felt especially personal because the campaign was photographed around places she regularly visits in Monaco.

Charles announced the couple’s engagement in November 2025 through a joint Instagram post featuring their dachshund, Leo.

The engagement announcement quickly drew congratulations from several Formula 1 drivers, including Lewis Hamilton.

Charles and Alexandra officially tied the knot on Feb. 28, 2026, during a civil ceremony in Monaco.

Alexandra wore a custom Paolo Sebastian fishtail gown, while Charles opted for a beige suit.

Their dachshund Leo attended the ceremony too, wearing a tiny tuxedo.

The couple later shared photos from the wedding on Instagram, including shots of them driving through Monaco in a vintage red Ferrari.

“A day we’ll forever remember,” Charles wrote in his caption, revealing that the pair plans to hold another larger celebration in the future.

After the wedding, Alexandra, whose maiden name is Alexandra Saint Mleux, updated her social media name to Alexandra Leclerc.

A few months after their wedding, Alexandra and Charles attended the Cannes Film Festival together for the premiere of A Woman’s Life on May 13.

The appearance marked one of their first major public outings together as a married couple outside of Formula 1 events.

Alexandra’s fashion choices generated almost as much attention as the racing during the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

On June 5, she arrived in the paddock wearing a white halter-neck Jacquemus minidress featuring a voluminous silhouette and an asymmetrical hemline.

The following day, Alexandra opted for a strapless red-and-white polka-dot column dress, accessorizing with a white handbag.

On June 7, she chose a look from Oscar de la Renta’s spring 2026 collection. The ivory gown featured intricate floral-inspired embroidery across the bodice and delicate fringe detailing throughout the skirt. She completed the outfit with Oscar de la Renta’s mini Poppy handbag and wore her hair pulled back into a sleek ponytail. The fashion house later confirmed the look on Instagram.

During the race, Alexandra was also photographed with Kim Kardashian while cheering on Charles.

Alexandra was seen in a flowing white and pink summer dress on July 25 during the weekend of the Hungarian Grand Prix.

She wore a similar spaghetti-strap look the following day.

She arrived in a blue and white dress with a cowl neckline and a skirt with a slit up one side.

Alongside her fashion work, Alexandra also launched the Corazones Unidos Fund through the King Baudouin Foundation.

The initiative supports Mexican children through education, music, and arts programming while also helping female artists.

“This fund is the realization of a dream I’ve carried in my heart for years,” Alexandra said on the foundation’s website. “Social networks have given me independence, and this chance immediately made me want to give back.”

In her October 2025 ELLE Mexico interview, Alexandra reflected on how quickly her public profile grew.

“For me, it’s about what you do with the attention you receive,” she said. “If people are looking at you, you can use that platform for something positive or to bring visibility to something you’re passionate about.” She added that she approaches both her art account and her charitable initiative, Corazones Unidos, with that mindset.

Alexandra also discussed the connection between fashion and her background in art history. “Fashion can definitely be art, that’s how I see it,” she said. “They share a creative process, a meaning.”

She explained that traveling has also shaped the way she dresses. “When I travel, I love observing the culture of each country and taking time to find local pieces or designers that reflect the cultural identity of each place,” she said.

Alexandra also opened up about staying grounded amid her rise online. “I think everything comes down to staying authentic and humble,” Alexandra said. “Social media can be very noisy, but if you really know who you are, you won’t lose yourself.”

During the interview, Alexandra also spoke about her connection to Mexico through her family and her philanthropic work. “The warmth of the people, definitely,” she said when asked what makes her proudest of her Mexican side. “And what I enjoy most? The food. I love the food!”

She even shared her favorite dishes: “Chilaquiles and mole. My mom makes the best mole.”

Alexandra sparked pregnancy rumors during her summer appearances at her husband’s Grand Prix competitions. Though the influencer never made a formal announcement, she subtly addressed the chatter when she shared photos of herself lounging on a yacht in a crop top on Instagram. She kept her caption focused on her bag’s ladybug details, posting a series of ladybug emojis.

On September 11, Alexandra wore an archival Dior newspaper dress to watch her husband at the AF1 Spanish Grand Prix’s first practice. Their dog, Leo, joined her:

Alexandra gave birth to a baby girl on Nov. 3, 2026. She and Charles revealed their daughter’s name, Bianca, and first photo on Instagram.

In the unending trend cycle, there’s one fall manicure that has been trending every year for almost half a decade: chocolate chrome. “I think the secret behind the popularity of chocolate brown shades with chrome powder is how they give a familiar color palette a completely new look,” Los Angeles-based nail artist Vikki Swan says. “Chrome creates a beautiful wet-look effect with delicate shine and soft reflections.”

Our Lady of Unending Nail Inspiration, Hailey Bieber, has been a fan of brown chrome nails for years: She went with more of an iced latte shade in September 2022 (the same month she wore the cooler taupe version in the photo below) and I found evidence of her wearing a deeper chocolate glaze in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, and, most recently, about a month ago. Bieber is known for her clean-girl aesthetic, which brown chrome definitely can fit into, but when done with a dark base polish the look can feel almost edgy—more glam rock than soft girl.

That’s all to say, chocolate chrome nails are versatile, with about a million variations that look great on every nail length and skin tone. Here, some expert tips for getting the look yourself, plus a handful of inspiration photos to bring to the salon.

“Chocolate chrome” follows the time-honored tradition of naming beauty looks after food, but these manicures are simply brown nail polish (usually gel) with chrome powder on top. Still, that basic combination can lead to some very decadent final results. “Chocolate chrome takes the richness of espresso and transforms it into the shine of molten jewelry,” says Tucson-based nail artist Max Estrada. “It's glamorous, seductive and beautifully indulgent.”

Estrada sees this year’s chocolate chromes as emblematic of a larger beauty trend. “I'm seeing a move away from apologetically understated manicures toward luxury that feels almost theatrical,” Estrada says. “Think New York or Paris in 1987 with extravagant faux-fur coats, vintage Schiaparelli, opulent dresses and a cloud of Dior Poison.”

With so many shades of brown and so many chrome powders to choose from, picking one for your own chocolate manicure can feel overwhelming. The first step is deciding what vibe you want. “Darker browns create a richer, more dramatic effect, while lighter shades give a softer, more delicate finish,” Swan says, noting that she generally prefers browns with a neutral or slightly warm undertone for this.

Whether you go with a nearly-black cocoa or a creamy caramel as your base, Estrada recommends chromes that lean more gold than silver: Think champagne, bronze, or copper (though “an airy pearl chrome adds a cooler editorial twist”). Regardless of which color you prefer, Swan says to look for a sheer chrome with a delicate pearlescent finish. “They enhance the depth of the base color without covering or overpowering the original gel polish shade,” she explains.

Brown chrome also works well in a mismatched manicure, another example of nails trending toward the theatrical. “Let's be extravagant!” Estrada says. “Mix chocolate chrome with black-cherry velvet cat-eye, deep oxblood French tips, tortoiseshell, baroque gold detailing, sculpted accents and tiny crystals.” Swan also loves brown chrome paired with tortoiseshell and gold. “The key is to stay within a cohesive color palette so the different designs complement each other without making the manicure look too busy,” she says.

While it is possible to do chrome over regular polish, the look is more commonly created with a gel set, since the base color needs to be totally dry before you rub the chrome on top. “I recommend applying chrome powder after curing, while the top coat is still warm,” Swan says. “After application, it’s important to seal the chrome thoroughly with a finishing top coat to minimize the risk of chipping and ensure long-lasting results.”

Both Swan also emphasizes the importance of having a smooth base under the chrome, which requires thorough nail preparation. “Chrome powder can highlight even the smallest imperfections,” she says. “Proper nail architecture and proportions are essential, along with a high-quality top coat that creates a perfectly smooth surface.”

While chocolate chrome can work on any nail length, Estrada thinks they’re especially luxurious on longer tips. “I love these colors on a long structured coffin, exaggerated almond or beautifully sharp stiletto,” he says, noting that long nails make the decadent finish even more striking. “This winter, I want excess, glamour and artistry. Too much is precisely the point!”

#6678. The 28 Best Hostess Gifts Guaranteed to Secure You an Invite Back

If one of life’s simple pleasures is going to a friend’s house for a home-cooked meal, one of life’s great conundrums is figuring out the art of the host gift. If you bring a dessert, should you poll for food allergies ahead of time? Does anyone really need more scented candles? And what about the much-maligned bottle of wine?

I host a pasta dinner nearly every Monday, and for what it’s worth, I’m always happy when someone shows up with a wine we can pour with the meal. I’ve had people bring a really great wheel of brie and I’ve had people bring a plant stand for a kumquat tree in my kitchen whose sad drooping they’d noticed at dinner the week before. Recently, one friend appeared with a calendar of Italian priests. Am I Catholic? No. Is it a newly prized possession, hanging prominently on the wall by the bread basket (it felt apropos)? Of course. The best hostess gifts don’t adhere to any strict guidelines; they’re the ones that show your friends know you, and put a little thought into what to get you when—to quote the cliché—they really shouldn’t have.

Whether your calendar is filling up with holiday parties or you’ve befriended someone with a weekend home Upstate, this time of year is rife with occasions that call for these sort of trinkets. And since there’s no such thing as a one-size-fits-all option, it’s worth taking a little time to pinpoint a present with a little personality.

The below is an assortment of the very best hostess gift ideas. If you’re looking for something small and sure to please, an edible treat is a safe bet; if you’re looking for a larger gift, say, for a birthday or a holiday, for your friend who loves to entertain, this is for you too. Herewith, a curated gift selection by type of host—and plenty of pieces you might want to earmark for yourself while you’re at it.

You love them not because they can whip up a multi-course meal on demand, but because they know all the best spots to order a multi-course meal on demand. Dress up pizza from the place around the corner with an infused oil, or zhuzh up the dessert course with resin ice cream spoons.

Bagged leftovers aren’t boring—they’ve just been missing a delightful fish clip to keep them secure.

Keep it short and sweet with four marbled resin spoons with which to scoop store-bought sorbet.

Dress up take-out boxes with the help of printed napkins. These, inspired by Byzantine mosaics, will make pretty much anything look fancy.

The host with the most—but the least amount of space—has mastered the art of the tiny apartment dinner party. Gift them something useful that won’t eat away at valuable cupboard space: a Japanese-inspired bento bag that moonlights as a makeshift bread basket and folds up when guests leave, for example, or a tiny espresso maker for after-dinner coffees.

Inspired by Japanese furoshiki, this linen bread basket folds up flat when not in use.

The original 1960s design needs no improvement: Here’s a compact, cheery solution to bulky coffee machines.

They’re a hazard in an Eataly; they’re one bad work day away from abandoning it all to make small-batch olive oil in the Italian countryside. The way to this person’s heart is a beautifully packaged specialty item—alongside an equally stylish serving vessel to let it shine.

If their pantry is a cabinet of curiosities, an army of multi-colored appetizer forks is the best way to serve it up.

#6677. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6671. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

#6669. After the Midterms, Millennial Optimism Makes Sense Again

None of us are the same people we were in 2008. But it's okay, just for a day, to bask in hope.

I have told this story many times in writing, but in 2008 I was so hopeful on election night that I stripped off my clothes with a bar full of people right before they called Pennsylvania for Obama, to take a picture and commemorate the moment. They took the photo; we got up off the sticky bar floor, pulled our clothes back on, and literally danced in the streets with the cops while the Obama reggaeton song played. This was peak millennial political optimism, and the rush of it could make you believe that all the contradictions of this country didn’t matter. That we were all moving forward together.

In 2008, I was a junior researcher at a Black history museum, a place where people thought deeply about legacy and historical sea change. I remember being so deeply excited, after seven years of political insanity post-9/11, that maybe the United States was finally waking up. It was a shock, then, to talk to my older coworkers, most of whom had been involved with or studied the Black radical tradition, and hear their cautious indifference to what felt like a coming revolution. “We’ll see,” was what most of them said—a pragmatism about this country that I didn’t fully understand back then. Back then I hoped, deep down, that what those older coworkers were experiencing was merely sour grapes.

In 2026, of course, we are all living through the political backlash that they were sure was coming, and the missteps of moderation during the Obama years that set the stage for Trump. I don’t really hope about politics anymore. Yes, I know, hope is a discipline. Hope is something that, by definition, you have to have when things are dire. But the way hope lives in my body—a frantic, desperate thing that plummets when it meets catastrophe—means national politics aren’t a good place for that emotion. When I talk about politics now with friends, it's mostly to see who can make the darkest joke about our current timeline.

But after last night, things are different. Like a lot of people, I’m allowing myself one calendar day to actually feel excited about the state of the world. I’m still saying “let’s see,” but for right now, every time someone tries to bring up why we’re still doomed, I keep scrolling. I can do bad all by myself tomorrow.

Since Trump entered the scene 10 years ago, there’s been an active disdain for sincerity in politics. The reasons for this are many. Trump and MAGA ran on the belief that becoming great could only be measured by how badly the people you hated were suffering. Those who would oppose Trump grew cynical about the national Democratic Party’s dance of fearmongering about the state of the country and steadfastly refusing to do anything meaningful about it when given the power to do so. Between these two extremes, it felt foolish to care. It felt smarter and safer to view politics the way a consultant or a pundit might, with the distance of someone who keeps telling you he has no skin in the game. As if that position was a superior one. As if that distance could save you any heartbreak, keep the threat of a layoff or a medical bill or an eviction at bay.

To care is to be cringe, and in the last few years, being cringe has been one of the greatest cultural sins, a devastating social faux pas. But last night was such a seismic shift in American politics that the idea of cringe is currently, blissfully, irrelevant. Being cringe enough to care brought millions to the polls and a historic midterm turnout. Being cringe enough to care meant that people like James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, and Angie Nixon launched campaigns even as everyone told their potential base that voting was irrelevant, that nothing could ever change about their states.

I’m not the same person I was in 2008—hopefully none of us are. And this is not the same country. But to make sure this country is one where I want to be present, I have to believe on some level that it’s possible. To change anything in this world, you first have to care enough to want to do it.

#6667. The Best Early Black Friday Clothing Deals 2026 Are Here

Before you start questioning your own reality, Black Friday is still a ways away. But it's not too early to start taking advantage of some early Black Friday clothing deals that already sprouting up. Retailers seem more eager than ever to get the sales started early this year, and at this rate, Black Friday will be here before you know it. And some of the hardest-hitting discounts land before the official day even kicks off.

And it’s not just like the stalwarts like Gap, Banana Republic, Abercrombie and J.Crew in the mix, although they are heavily in the mix. Killer indies like Lost & Found and Haven also have a host of discounted goods, and outdoor behemoth REI is feeling especially generous for early November. So, if you’re trying to shop away the daylight savings blues or just feel like getting a jump on holiday shopping, you’re in the right spot.

Abercrombie doesn’t have any specific promotions that are live at the moment, but the sale section was recently stuffed with some ideal fall building blocks—most notably some baggy cords—that will make a refresh as easy and affordable as you’d ever hoped it could be.

Banana Republic has been on a heater recently, and the perfectly-curated Archive Reissue collection is leading the charge this season. It should also be noted that anything on the site that is on sale also gets an additional 20% off.

Don’t tell anyone at Gap that Black Friday is a ways off, because there are a ridiculous number of in-season pieces up to 50%—sweaters, flannels, cords, jeans, jackets, and more—and it feels like raising too much awareness to that might cause some reconsideration and none of us want that.

Haven isn’t promoting a sale anywhere on the site and you might have to dig a little bit depending what size you wear, but if you’re looking for some of the sickest IYKYK brands on the planet at insane discounts, there aren’t many places I’d rather start.

If you’re not familiar with Huckberry, they preside over one of most thoughtfully curated assortments of menswear, footwear and gear anywhere, whether that’s IRL or URL. They haven’t kicked off anything Black Friday specific yet—again, it’s early—but if you haven’t gone through the sale tab in a while, you’re missing out on some preposterously good deals.

Nearly all of J.Crew’s spring-summer collection is on sale at the moment, over 300 pieces up to 40% off through May 26—including a whole bunch of heat-beating shirting, lightweight pants, archive classics and basically anything else you’d want to be on sale.

The first name in denim has a pretty nifty “buy two, get 30% off” promotion going on site-wide, so if you’re searching for some jeans, you might just want to buy a couple pairs. (Or maybe a trucker. Or sherpa-lined trucker. You’re in charge.)

Diving into Lost & Found’s sale section is one of the more enjoyable shopping experiences one can have online right now: the selection is great, the brand list is a top-five worldwide and there’s plenty of inventory, which puts it in stark contrast with some of the less rewarding sale sections.

One of the most quietly great, easy-to-wear brands in the game recently reloaded the sale section, and basically no category was left unturned. Of particular note, are the killer sweatshirts currently available with a healthy discount applied.

Mr Porter’s sale section is the kind you can lose an hour in without realizing it, even months after a seasonal sale has ended. Case in point: there’s roughly 500 pairs of shoes and 900 jackets on sale at this very moment, and while sizes might be hit and miss, the deals aren’t.

REI’s Deals section always lives up to the billing, but right now it’s about as good as it’s ever been. Hundreds of pieces from heavyweights like Arc’teryx, Patagonia, The North Face and more are discounted up to 50%, including plenty of winter-specific gear for anyone lacking in that department.

Todd Snyder presumably won’t be partaking in the Black Friday festivities this year—they announced a new sale structure a while back—but that doesn’t mean the already-on-sale fare doesn’t hold up to the promotions sure to fire up across the board.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of clothing deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6665. All the Exciting Ballot Wins You May Have Missed From Election Day

The 2026 midterms featured a number of key issues on states’ ballots

The midterm general elections held this Tuesday marked a major shift for the United States. A historic “blue wave” reflected the country’s overwhelming support for the Democratic Party, which now has control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. And a number of Democratic candidates won their elections for governor too, in swing (and even non-swing) states like Texas, Georgia, Iowa, and Ohio.

Many of the surprise wins also brought about historic firsts for the nation. Keisha Lance Bottoms has become the first Black woman ever elected to governor, while Chris Pappas is the first openly gay candidate elected to the Senate. Other notable firsts include the first-ever Muslim Senate-elect (Abdul El-Sayed) and the first-ever Native American female governor to be voted in to the post (Deb Haaland).

But with so much excitement around the candidates, it can be easy to forget that yesterday also saw a number of important measures featured on ballots across all 50 states. And a few of the results were quite uplifting.

Virginia saw a complete victory for voters on the left, with citizens of the state voting to codify marriage equality, even in the case that the Supreme Court ever decides to overturn Obergefell v. Hodges; and Loving v. Virginia, which protects interracial marriage, was also codified. Virginia voters also chose to protect reproductive rights, and to restore voting rights to those who have been previously incarcerated.

Nevada citizens voted to protect abortion rights too, while those in Washington voted not to repeal a millionaire wealth tax. (The key issues that many of the ballots centered around this year included abortion rights, taxes, drug policies, voting, and transgender rights.)

There are still some ballot measures that have yet to be called, and votes will continue to roll in throughout the next few hours, meaning a few major issues remain hanging in the balance.

Be sure to revisit this page as more results come in, and check out all the historic firsts from the 2026 midterm general elections here.

#6664. Exclusive: The All’s Fair Cast Held Court in Couture at the Season 2 Premiere and After-Party

“This season is just more of everything,” Kim Kardashian told Vogue, as Sarah Paulson shrieked “Yes!” in agreement, adding, “More drama, more sex, more fun, more fashion, more shenanigans.” They were talking, of course, about All’s Fair, Ryan Murphy’s panache-packed Hulu series following high-powered divorce attorneys with silver tongues, scores to settle, and exceptionally good wardrobes to do it in. On Monday, the cast gathered on Manhattan’s West Side for the New York premiere of season two, the third installment of their whistle-stop publicity tour.

Much like in the series itself, there was no shortage of drama at the Highline Studios: white velvet ropes, marble, and an infinite amount of gold. Add to that the parade of couture emerging from black cars, and suddenly the first Monday in November seemed as glamorous as a certain Monday in May. “This is All’s Fair! You either go big or go home,” quipped hairstylist Sharif Poston while giving Niecy Nash-Betts’s hair a final once-over with a shiny metallic comb.

The show’s costuming certainly sets the precedent for such excess. Fred Leighton brooches, Balenciaga gowns, and no shortage of Birkins. “The show’s wardrobe has the biggest budget I’ve ever seen,” revealed actress Denise Richards. “I was actually quite impressed by it.” (And that’s coming from a former Bond girl.)

For this red-carpet outing, some went the lawyerly route, while others dialed up the haute factor. Teyana Taylor managed to tick both boxes in an architectural Nicholas Oakwell Couture pantsuit, festooned with a giant bow below the waist. Her summation of the evening was the same as hers of the second season: “It’s drama and suits!” Similarly, actor Nyle DiMarco nodded to the legal theme in a Paul Smith suit, “straight off the runway.” And Nash-Betts’s Louis Vuitton look had multiple acts. “This dress turns into three or four different things—so keep your eyes on me.” Sure enough, the next time I saw her, the gilded halo that initially framed her was nowhere to be seen.

“She looks so good,” director and executive producer Anthony Hemingway said as Kardashian arrived in a lace-up Ashi Studio gown with a sweetheart neckline and a snatched bodice, accentuated with lace, croc embossing, and ribbons. Everyone seemed to stand a little straighter as Kardashian walked in—but sure enough, as soon as she started chatting, the room relaxed.

“I’m excited for people to see how funny we are,” Kardashian said. “There’s a lot more comedy this season,” Paulson added, hooking a thumb toward Kardashian, who leaned right into it. “I’m the funniest,” she teased. Paulson had her own theory: “Kim did a movie with all these comedy geniuses in between seasons one and two,” she said, explaining that her co-star came back to set brimming with notes. When Paulson said she’s still waiting for Saturday Night Live to call, Kardashian chimed in with an idea of her own: “Should we do it together? Please!”

Though there were photos to take and interviews to give, the cast still stopped mid-carpet for a catch-up. Glenn Close, in Matières Fécales, had missed the first two stops on the press tour. “I’m excited to see my friends,” she said, holding hands with Kardashian through an entire interview. Taylor, who’d been busy wrapping up another project as director, felt much the same. “You have to understand the FOMO I’ve been having.”

“We had long TV days that lasted up to sixteen hours sometimes,” Naomi Watts added. “It’s a grind, but we somehow find a way to laugh in between takes.” She credited Murphy with putting together a group that clicked. “There’s not an outsized ego amongst us.” For Taylor, that sisterhood mattered especially on the days she turned up feeling less than her best. “Everybody’s got their silent battles,” she said. “Come to work with them, and with this cast, you just know that you’re going to be surrounded by love.”

For reality TV regular Dorinda Medley, who plays Loni and worked mostly with Glenn Close, taking on a scripted role was a chance to try something new. “All these little steps in your life move you a little closer to who you are,” she said. “For so many years I was Dorinda someone.” She ticked off the surnames she’d gone by and the roles she’d played offscreen. “Mother, wife, widow. Now, for the first time, I’m just Dorinda. There’s incredible freedom in that.” Medley, in an embellished Gucci dress that she jokingly called “very casual,” already had a pitch for her next collaboration with Murphy. How about setting American Horror Story at Blue Stone Manor, her home in the Berkshires?

“We rarely get a chance to rock together. We’re always working,” Hemingway, the director, said. He was looking forward to a chance to “hang out, have a cocktail, even do a little two-step, and just laugh.” And at Crane Club nearby, there was ample opportunity for all four. Around the red velvet-draped dining room, servers made the rounds with truffle arancini and caesar salads, a giant ice sculpture of the show’s initials presided over the raw bar, and the DJ was good enough to make you forget it was a school night.

If the carving station said wedding reception, the cocktail menu said divorce. Bartenders whipped up drinks named Contested Assets, with habanero-spiked mezcal number, and Alimony, which came with gin, vodka, vermouth, sake, and a little cucumber. Taylor had a special order in mind. “I need a real big margarita,” she told Vogue. Her favorite? “Passionfruit. Sugar rim. There—you’ve got sugar, spice, and everything nice,” she said, dancing as she delivered the recipe.

For a cast that had reserved tables ringing the room, they sure spent little time in their seats. And who could blame them? Ash Hodgkinson was doing magic tricks for a knot of guests, while Murphy, in ochre-tinted aviators, made duck faces for the camera with Paulson. When the DJ put on “Plain Jane,” there was Nash-Betts, dancing with her girls. “I love those moments,” Hemingway had said. “That’s living.”

As for any flak the show had received, Anna Delvey, who knows a thing or two about mixed press and courthouse fashion, had a thought. “It says a lot about people, how they take it,” she explained—stating that some people “are too serious about it.” In her view, anyone busy cataloging the show’s excesses was liable to miss the joke. “They obviously know what they’re doing,” she said of the silliness.

Department stores have plenty of gifts, but narrowing down endless options can be overwhelming. For a more streamlined search, fashion editors often stick to browsing a single trusted brand with a smaller, more thoughtfully curated selection, like Rails. Worn by celebrities like Taylor Swift, Beyoncé, Jennifer Lopez, and Hilary Duff, the California-based contemporary fashion label is one of our top picks for holiday gift shopping.

Rails built its reputation on casual plaid shirts, but its sweaters, jackets, dresses, and casual tops have kept fashion insiders coming back for more than a decade. From cardigans and coats to winter accessories, the brand’s pieces have a luxurious feel without being too precious. (Most are priced under $300, yet look like they cost double.) These aren’t cashmere and silk items recipients will save for special occasions; they’re pieces they’ll rely on for everyday wear.

Rails sweaters, beanies, scarves, and other cold-weather essentials come in a range of neutral colors you can mix and match into coordinating gift sets. Knit from a plush cashmere-silk blend, the Miranda sweater, Alps scarf, Moritz mittens, and Autumn beanie (or any combination of the four) make foolproof gifts for the stylish women on your list. The brand’s elevated fabrics and quality construction are enough to impress on their own, but its celebrity fans give you a fun tidbit to share with recipients, too.

Should anything catch your eye for your own wardrobe, we fully support treating yourself to a little something, too. The Franca dress that Taylor Swift recently wore to dinner in Kansas City is still in stock, so you might want to peruse the label for potential date-night and holiday party outfits, too.

#6661. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman Is the Scariest Thing You’ll See All Year

In 2009, Andrew Garfield found a thread. He was preparing to play Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a little-hyped film called The Social Network, and he had located the thing in Zuckerberg’s story that he could pull on—the through line that turns personal experience into empathic performance and on into universal storytelling. Then he lost the part to Jesse Eisenberg. Director David Fincher had seen what, today, is obvious: Humanity flows fast and deep through Andrew Garfield. Fincher cast him instead as Eduardo Saverin, the betrayed cofounder and emotional counterweight to Zuckerberg’s opacity, who cries, sneers, throws a feint, and smashes a laptop (that’s one scene).

The movie made him a celebrity, and he brought an unusual depth of emotion to this job too. While serving as Spider-Man, he begged the public, via a handwritten sign held up for paparazzi, to care about a more important cause than what’s up with famous people. While promoting 2021’s Tick, Tick…Boom! on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, he talked about the death of his mother; the clip still gets shared by grieving people.

Boxers by Hermès. Sneakers by Bottega Veneta. Socks by Jacques. Watch by Rolex.

Now, 15 years after The Social Network, Garfield has picked back up the tech-CEO thread to play Sam Altman in Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s film that covers the founding of OpenAI up to the coup that led to Altman’s firing—and his re-entrenchment. (OpenAI has an agreement with Condé Nast, the owner of GQ, which allows OpenAI to display its content in search results for a limited term.) The movie seems destined to occupy the same orienting role as The Social Network, helping us understand the technology and the men who are shaping our futures, almost in real time. But whereas that film was a legal drama about status (Harvard guy vs. hotter, richer-born Harvard guys), Artificial plays as a horror movie where the monster, AI, is real. (And it just learned how to do theoretical physics.)

Garfield brings Altman to life as a mad guidance counselor: rubbing the shoulders of engineers, taking security meetings cross-legged, and sucking green juice in the faces of his adversaries. Here, finally, is an ascendant tech overlord that makes unsettling use of Garfield’s famous sensitivity. When Garfield-as-Altman cries, you’re not sure whether they’re the tears of a true superintelligence believer or a duplicitous power-seeker. Or which one would be scarier.

When we meet in early October, Garfield is transformed by a beard and shoulder-length hair. He grew it all out to play the magician Roy Horn, of Siegfried and Roy, in next year’s show Wild Things, though they ended up putting a wig on him anyway. He was filming that limited series in Berlin immediately after wrapping The Uprising, a Paul Greengrass movie about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, which shot before Artificial was even technically wrapped. “I did these three things back to back last year, and I did have a bit of burnout, to be honest. I was kind of sleepless in Berlin for a while, and not in a romantic way,” he says. “It was rough, dude. I should have just gone to Berghain and just rode it out.” Now, though, Garfield is visibly buzzing, both from watching Artificial with an audience at the New York Film Festival the night before—and from the chatter coming out of Silicon Valley.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Andrew Garfield: I’ve listened to his podcast.

The walk was a key for me, and the clothes and the physicality. He’s a very slight, slim guy, Sam, and seems to be very image-conscious. Which is interesting to me, which is something that I felt compelled by. There’s a great video of Sam, in what looks like a diner, when he’s talking about Loopt [the company he cofounded before running Y Combinator and cofounding OpenAI], when he’s in his early 20s, and he was much freer with his physicality back then.

Sam did an interview with Vanity Fair [for the magazine’s New Establishment issue]. I think it came out yesterday, the day of our premiere, where he was very sweet about the walk as well. It’s a very generous thing for the boys to acknowledge that the walk was close, a good approximation of Sam and his vibe. I think that’s a very classy thing, to acknowledge the thing that seems to be working. But who knows what’s happening in their hearts and minds right now or within the family? I can project myself into that experience and imagine what it must feel like for an actor to be so presumptuous to play a character called Sam Altman in a major film. I can imagine that must be really strange, and I feel for…. I don’t know. In terms of taking it on, what outweighed that sense of responsibility for me was this sense of it is the defining inevitable invention of our times. It felt like a great responsibility to interrogate not just the machine, if you can even call it that, the kind of the consciousness or the technology itself, but to interrogate the people who are building it and who are putting their hearts and souls and life’s work into it, and where they may or may not be leading us.

That was deeply researched. This is what I gleaned. There’s a lot of people that know Sam. There’s a lot of people that are happy to talk about Sam. Some very, very protective; others, slightly more inside information. And I’m not going to name who these people are. But it was a kind of adding to the cauldron and through my lens of the interpretation of who this person is, combined with what was on the page and the specific cinematic story we’re telling and how we’re telling it, and Luca’s tastes and sensibilities. And, yeah, a lot of people said he would never sit conventionally. He was always sitting like a little boy.

Intimacy, but also ownership of a space—a kind of subtle, very soft dominance of a space. But also, as you say, a kind of, “Hey, we’re all just hanging out doing the coolest job ever. So why can’t we just sit like we’re in a dorm room?” It’s very psychologically interesting to me and smart. And who knows if it’s all calculated? Who knows if it’s not? I don’t know. What was interesting, in tracking his physicality in all the videos I saw is, at the beginning, he’s very free in how he twitches and moves. He’s just freer in his ability to be his true self maybe. And then as he starts to become more and more powerful, and ultimately becoming the face of the new world, this behemoth company that’s going to define where we are going—even if he doesn’t know where we are going, and none of them do—he becomes a slightly more homogenized version of a tech CEO. That was a really, really interesting kind of journey. And you can see, now, in [Altman’s recent interview with Vanity Fair], he’s very image-conscious, and I am too. I think we all are.

I mean, yes. One has to. This is the job. And this is why I wanted to do it: Because with The Social Network, I was getting ready to play Mark Zuckerberg, and then David Fincher calls me in and says, “We found someone that is just going to do it better. It’s Jesse, but we think you could also play this part. And you’re a very emotional actor, Andrew, so why would we waste all of that on someone who doesn’t seem to feel many emotions?” So Eduardo became my kind of guy, and I was very happy with that. But it left a little dangling thread, and I was like, “I need to understand.” Because I started to explore what it takes to win, to win on that level.

I think I’m a competitive person. I’m an athlete. I was raised by a swimming-coach father and, at that time, a proud capitalist. My dad has evolved his view of the world over the course of the last decades, which I find very moving and touching, as I have evolved my view of winning and losing and the beauty of losing and how humility is the only thing that actually grows us. It’s fucking awful. I hate losing.

No. It’s so much easier. Because you’re on this fucking false pedestal and it’s so much easier for the shit to get kicked out. It’s like, Oh, wait a minute. I forgot that I got above my station for a minute, and it’s a wonderful, horrible gift to be forced to crawl back down into the mud of what it is to be a human being. And actually I think it does relate to the story that we’re talking about, the film that we’re talking about.

When I was in my 20s, 30s, it was a time of slaying dragons and trying to plant flags and say, “This is who I am.” And then I think maybe as you enter middle age, a bunch of unresolved wounds from childhood that you kind of patched over with success just go, “Hey, we’re still here, dude.” And then it’s time to realize that there’s still a lot of work to do on maturation. I’m sorry, but to keep bringing it back to the film, I think what we’re dealing with is we’re in a very immature culture. We’re being still defined by this kind of adolescent impulse to win at all costs and that losing is weak and vulnerability is weak and that humility is actually not allowed.

What was that T-shirt in the fashion show that was happening recently? “Bring Back Shame” [in designer Conner Ives’s spring-summer show this past September]. I mean, people will respond to that as they do, but how I respond to it, positively, is, Bring back accountability. Bring back accountability for our inhumanity to each other. Humility is a surefire way to get us back to our collective humanity, I feel. But it’s hard. It’s hard. I love winning. It’s so much easier when things are going great, but I think it’s probably better for your soul when things aren’t going so great.

I’ve had a weird few years just in my own life, in a way that I don’t think it’s appropriate for me to go into, just because it’s my private life that I really care about protecting and holding on [to] for myself. But I think it is related to what I feel in the world in terms of the transition we’re in. It feels like we’re in a falling-apart culture, that there is no center anymore. It’s hard to find our own center within that lack-of-center in the world. A lot of people my age who I speak to are feeling a similar sense of a kind of falling apart, which feels right, because as a thing falls apart, the seeds of the future put back together start to get planted. Something else being born. I don’t mean to be glib, I don’t mean to be evasive, because I do like talking. I remember being a young person and wanting people I saw on magazine covers to say something real. So I feel a responsibility to that young person that is out there as well.

I think I was a real pain in the ass to my family because I was like, “What’s that? What’s happening there? That’s fucked-up.” And they’re like, “Shut the fuck up, Andy. Shut the fuck up.” I was that kid pointing out the stuff that wasn’t being said and was being felt, because I could just feel it all. It’s mysterious to me, but it was a hassle for me as well. I was like, “I don’t want to be so sensitive. I don’t want to hug my bully after he beats the shit out of me.” I could just feel his pain. It would be a lot easier to not have to see and feel all of these things that I may just be making up, but I’m pretty sure I’m not. It was a radar that I’ve had since I was a kid, I guess. I think my family would say the same thing, and I think they would also agree that it was a bit of a pain in the ass.

I need a place to go and express all of the most difficult shit about me to other people in private where they’re expressing their most difficult shit about them. I would venture to say, and this is a bit of a bold statement, that we all need that. I happen to have that in my life because I fucking sought it out and I searched it out and I crawled through the woods and into the dirt to find it. I have a really great group of people.

It really happened when I was doing Spider-Man, and I was like, Oh shit, I’m in danger of losing myself. It’s like what they say about famous, really, really famous people. They walk into any room and they’re like, “Everyone’s so nice.” And it’s like, no. I don’t know this person, but you could say, “No, you’re just Tom Cruise, and everyone wants to hang out with Tom Cruise.” I mean, I do know Tom, and I haven’t seen him in a long time. I only bring him up because he’s one of the most famous people in the world and I happen to know him a little bit and really have enjoyed and have a lot of admiration for him. But for me, it was a big danger that I would start to think that was a reflection of who I am. Do you know what I mean? And so I think in order to hold on to my ability to be messy, my ability to lose, my ability to be “weak,” my ability to be all of the things that our culture says a man should not be or even a person should not be, I sought out places and people and spaces and groups that would allow for me just to stay in touch with all of the messiest parts of myself, all the stuff that I’m not going to talk about here because it’s not safe to talk about them here.

Pleasantly. It was completely unintentional. Literally before I was going on to do the show, Stephen’s assistant came into the dressing room with me and my dad and my brother and said, “Hey, he might bring up this. Is that okay?” And I’m like, “Give me a second.” And I checked in with myself. I was like, “Yeah, sure.” Because I love Stephen, I trust him, and I know that he’s very good with those kinds of topics. He’s a really great container in that way. So it was very spontaneous. And then I think I said a prayer before I went on. I was just like, “Hey, Mom, whatever you got, just let me be the channel. Whatever you want me to say, whatever you don’t want me to say, just use me. I’m here to be used for the good, whatever that means.” And then the rest is just kind of a spontaneous moment that was lucky enough to get captured. I got texts about it yesterday, people who lose people, they get sent that clip. There’s a taboo around the subject in our culture—“No, come on, get on with it. Move forward, move forward, move forward”—and also people are just so scared of dying. We’re all so fucking scared of dying because we’ve somehow been led to believe that “Well, not me. I shouldn’t have to fucking die. I know we’re all going to fucking….” It’s this ascension obsession.

Well, it’s immature, and it’s deluded, and it’s a little adorable. It’s like, Oh, that’s so cute. You think you can outsmart the great mystery? Oh my God, it’s adorable. And it’s kind of sweet, but it’s infantile. And it’s cowardly. It’s the scariest adventure, and we’re all going to go on it. Every single one of us, every single one of us, and it doesn’t make sense. I think that’s the place that I find really exciting, is the not knowing. That’s when people get interesting. And I say that with some irony, I suppose, because we are being led by a bunch of younger guys right now who don’t know where this technology is taking us.

There was an overwhelming amount of reporting done about Sam having a specific relationship with the truth. And it was obviously a really vital ingredient in our story. And so I had to get into that for myself. Because he’s very charming by all accounts. There’s the quote in the movie that if Sam Altman was dropped into an island of cannibals, he would be their king in five years. All of these things were so juicy for me to imagine and to merge with and to interpret. I had to look at myself with my relationship to the truth, to universal truth, to personal truth, to objective truth, to subjective, someone else’s truth about me.

But my relationship to the truth, I try to be rigorous with myself. I try to do a fearless searching moral inventory of myself in every single moment of difficulty or tension. I try my hardest. I’m a human being. I’ve definitely not been a perfect human being. I sound like Sam right now. I think in that Vanity Fair interview, he was like, “I’m not a saint.” I’m the same. I mean, maybe this is a question better asked to people who are closest to me in my life, to be honest. I would say that I wouldn’t be a reliable narrator in terms of that. I think there’s a survival instinct in lying. There’s a self-preservation in the lies we tell each other and the lies we tell ourselves, but I wonder how that plays out in terms of the technology that it’s being baked into.

Yes, I do. I think at that time, before The Social Network came out, people were scoffing at the idea of a Facebook movie. No one was really onto the tech industry and the people that were governing it in the same way, because they didn’t consciously pose as much of a threat to our existence. Now we’re all a bit more hip to it. By the public becoming more hip to it, but also powerful people becoming more hip to it, realizing that that’s where the power lies, means that a company like OpenAI will have much more authority and power. For regular people like you and I, it’s higher stakes because we all feel like we have our eyes slightly more open now to the real-world personal consequences of these technologies. So we’re healthily more invested in shining light where that power lies and where we’re giving our autonomy, but also simultaneously there’s a much larger vested interest in protecting those people and their technology.

I feel afraid now. But it’s outweighed by a faith in humanity, but also a faith in the mystery of life. It’s the artist’s responsibility to reflect the times we’re in, and I think it’s getting harder and harder to do that without fear of consequences from those in power who you are rocking the boat for. I was excited the morning of the premiere yesterday. I woke up because I saw Sam’s interview on Vanity Fair and I was like, Oh shit, I’m playing that guy and people are going to see it tonight. And he’s just been named the most powerful man in the world by this publication. And it was kind of like, this is genuinely a cool thing to be a part of and feels courageous being led by Luca, because he says he’s not afraid, which I really admire and respect. I am afraid, but I’m still willing to put it on the line, but we’ll see.

That being said, there’s another part of me that’s like, “I don’t think this is going to touch them in a way.” You know what I mean? There’s a part that’s like, “I wonder if they’re too big to fail, they’re too big.” They’re able to go, “Well, they got the walk right, but everything else is kind of bullshit.” And then they move on because it’s small potatoes to them. I’m not sure. I’m not in their sphere, but I’m really, really, really curious to see how it all plays out.

But then there’s always people that come out and defend them. It’s so strange. Whether they’re bots or otherwise, I’m not sure, but there’s just an army of people that are like, “Leave those rich guys alone.” I’m like, “What?”

No, I didn’t have a body double. No, I saw that interview and I replayed it a few times to try and discern what he was actually saying, because I was very confused by that. I never had any interaction with him. I’ve never seen him in real life. We were shooting outside of his house. It was an eerie day, for sure. We were told that he wasn’t home and his security people were there. I think I saw one security guard. But, no, I never saw Sam, so he maybe mistook someone else for me. I have no idea, but I’ve never waved at Sam. I’ve never seen him. I was curious about that. [A representative for OpenAI told GQ that Altman was home during the filming and reiterated that he waved at Garfield.]

Yikes. That’s scary. It’s not scary in terms of the link. It’s fine by me. It’s more maybe I’m getting into some survival stuff for myself. I don’t want to make really powerful enemies. I don’t want to do that, but I’m not saying that that’s certainly what’s going to happen, but I don’t know if he’s going to feel warm towards me, and that’s okay. But there’s still a part of me that wants everyone to be okay all the time and therefore I’m okay. You know what I mean? It’s a slightly backtracking impulse, but it’s an interesting position to be in.

I’m not concerned about that. And I don’t think Jesse should be either. I think he’s such an incredible artist and an actor and director [and] writer. I feel safe in that I will make other things and this will be a part of my work and that’s that. And there’ll be other things that take away from that. I know the beginning of my obituary will be “Erstwhile Spider-Man.” You know what I mean?

I haven’t really considered it. My desire is to make work that I feel is speaking from my soul every time. That’s kind of where I’m trying to get to in terms of the feeling of relationship with failure and success. You know what something feels like for you, and you know what it means to you, and then the rest is kind of none of my business. So I’ll make a movie and I love it, and then it just doesn’t work for people or it just doesn’t hit in the same way that something that felt very difficult.

And I’m really glad I had the experience, because it was the ultimate version of fame and visibility. To taste that, and to know what that is, felt really healthy in all of its unhealthiness.

I think I’m the same as everyone else who’s even remotely cognizant of where we are and where we’re heading. I look at my friends who do have kids and the beauty of it obviously, but also the struggle of it and the inescapable agony of young people’s longing to belong to the screen rather than longing to belong to the real world. It gives me pause for sure, like any person, I suppose. That being said, there is that kind of biological imperative, and there is that just kind of instinct, and there’s an image that you live with for so long—I have, anyway—of the concept of being a dad and going on that adventure. It’s mysterious to me.

I know that all tech-CEO people, they’re very, very anti-technology in the house across the board. That just is objectively dark, because they know what it does.

It’s the most obvious cliché stuff. I went to an Ezra Collective gig at the Roundhouse in London. It’s a British kind of conglomerate of amazing musicians in the realm of Afrobeat, jazz-inspired. That was a night where you go, Oh, life and humans and arts and bodies and sweat and creativity. I was in Devon recently with my nephews, and we were surfing and swimming and playing American football on the beach. And eating fish and chips. We had a friends-and-family screening in London for this other film I did with Paul Greengrass called The Uprising, which I’m really proud of and I really love, and I love Paul…. And it’s moments like that when a bunch of friends and family come up, and I don’t care how they feel about the film, but the fact that they want to support and be there and that I can be vulnerable with them after the screening and they can be vulnerable with me. And my friends who I hadn’t seen in a long time, we can catch up and be like, “How you doing?” “I’m struggling a little bit.” “Me, too.” Just as simple as that. ✦

#6659. Blake Lively Gets Ready for the Holidays in Archival Midnight-Blue Chanel Sequins

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Blake Lively is making a grand return to the New York City scene. After nearly two years privately navigating her high-profile legal battle against It Ends With Us costar Justin Baldoni, the actor stepped out in a shimmering midnight-blue minidress that seemed to signal the start of a sparkling new chapter.

Last night, the Gossip Girl star, whose appearances this year have primarily been limited to major cultural events—namely May’s Met Gala and the summer’s World Cup games—attended NYC-based jewelry designer Brent Neale’s holiday capsule launch party. Full of smiles, she was photographed wearing an archival look from Chanel’s Karl Lagerfeld days: a strapless sequin number with a scalloped lace neckline and black satin bows. More specifically, the piece was designed for the Autumn/Winter 1994 collection, and walked the runway on Christy Turlington with a floral brooch pinned at the neckline.

Putting her own stamp on the vintage mini, Lively updated the ’90s look with a black bucket bag from a more recent Chanel collection. The accessory, introduced for the Fall/Winter 2026 season, was crafted from black leather, with a rounded shape and top closure. Gold hardware detailing and a matching chain added a little pop of shine, and for some contrast, Lively selected a pair of silver Brent Neale bow earrings and mixed-metal rings.

The actor added a pair of red-bottomed PVC Christian Louboutin heels with a black cap-toe accent, ankle strap, and ultra-high stiletto. And of course, she finished things off with her signature bouncy blonde blowout, parted at the side. ’Tis the holiday season!

#6658. Cemeteries Are the Unsung Hero of Travel

I was flipping through old journals recently and came across an entry dated December 31, 2017. I was in Todos Santos and had risen early to watch the sunrise over the Sierra de la Laguna mountains. There were scribbled goals for the new year, and reflections on what I wanted to leave behind. But the part that stood out most was a slice of the surrounding atmosphere—rooster crows echoing in the streets, and sunlight spilling onto a colorful cemetery in the distance. It reminded me that for as long as I’ve been traveling, I’ve always sought out the local cemetery. And it’s always left an indelible impression.

If you’re not a fellow taphophile, allow me to make the case. Spending time in cemeteries invites you to sink in. It sticks your mortality front and center and reminds you that you won’t always be here (stress!). It’s also a reminder to appreciate today, and remember those who aren’t around anymore. And as it pertains to visiting the dearly departed while traveling, cemetery strolls offer a distinct way to familiarize yourself with the local people. How a culture approaches death conveys a great deal. (In the case of Mexico, graveyards are not somber, but rather, awash in rainbow colors and elaborate decorations. Very lively!)

On a less morbid note, cemeteries are also really lovely for architecture and natural landscapes. History, too. And with the spooky season in full swing (which I’d argue lasts well beyond Halloween), there’s never been a better time to become a cemetery convert. Below, nine destinations worth planning a trip around.

I’m very lucky to live less than 10 minutes from this world-famous cemetery in Brooklyn. Green-Wood was founded in 1838 and is now a National Historic Landmark. Its paths stretch across 478 hilly acres, winding beside tombs belonging to iconic figures such as Jean-Michel Basquiat and Leonard Bernstein. It’s also a Revolutionary War historic site, and a haven for birdwatchers (over 260 species have been spotted).

When I lived in Los Angeles, outdoor movie screenings at Hollywood Forever Cemetery were a common occurrence. But despite being one of the trendiest ways to spend a Saturday night, this cemetery dates back to 1899. It serves as the final resting place for numerous Hollywood legends, from Judy Garland and Cecil B. DeMille to Eve Babitz. There’s even a cenotaph marker for Toto from The Wizard of Oz for fans to memorialize the adored cairn terrier.

Established in 1821, this breathtaking cemetery features an array of architectural styles, including Neo-Gothic, Neo-Maya, and even Art Deco. Its tree- and mausoleum-lined avenues are home to over 25,000 burial sites, including Felipe Carrillo Puerto (a progressive champion of human rights who was assassinated in 1924). Leading up to Día de Los Muertos, there is a festive procession called Paseo de las Ánimas that begins at the cemetery.

I’ll preface this with the unfortunate fact that Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 is currently closed to the public (reopening is still TBD). But that doesn’t stop me from declaring it my favorite in New Orleans. This 19th-century cemetery has appeared in films such as Interview With the Vampire and can still be enjoyed with a stroll around its scenic perimeter—which is punctuated by towering Spanish live oaks whose massive roots pry the concrete curb upward into a wonderfully spooky, uneven pathway. (If you’d like to go inside a New Orleans cemetery, don’t miss voodoo practitioner Marie Laveau’s tomb in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1).

This is the cemetery I’ve probably returned to the most over the years (and arguably the most famous in the world). It’s huge, so you’ll need to set aside an entire afternoon to explore its 110 acres that play host to thousands of burial plots. Also in the thousands: trees (about 5,000), making this landscape exceptionally beautiful as the leaves change colors. Don’t miss the highlights—Jim Morrison, Frédéric Chopin, Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf—but also give yourself time to wander without a destination.

This is one of my favorite day trips from New York City this time of year. Hop on the Metro-North and get off at Philipse Manor Station. From there, it’s about a 10-minute walk to this 19th-century cemetery where writer Washington Irving is buried. After meandering around 90 acres of landscaped grounds, join a special event like an adaptation of Irving’s Bracebridge Hall complete with traditional carols and holiday cheer.

This cemetery was designed to resemble a city (rather than a burial ground) and is world-renowned for its neoclassical gates and beautiful maze of tree-lined paths. There are just under 5,000 burial vaults (all above ground), which include imposing mausoleums made of marble. La Recoleta Cemetery is the final resting place for dozens of Argentine presidents, as well as Nobel laureates and cultural figures.

Located a quick stroll from Hampstead Heath—my most beloved green space in all of London—this legendary cemetery is home to a fascinating mix of cultural figures ranging from Karl Marx to George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, author of Middlemarch). Travelers can explore both the east and west sides of the cemetery without a guided tour, but why not book one for your first visit to get the full lay of the land? Highgate was modeled after Paris's Père Lachaise Cemetery and now operates as a historic park, nature reserve, and active burial site.

On a peaceful bluff of the Wilmington River, Bonaventure is one of the country’s most gorgeous cemeteries. Live oaks draped in Spanish moss hover above Victorian sculptures and timeworn tombstones belonging to famous figures such as John Muir. (Fun fact: during his thousand-mile walk to the gulf, Muir ran out of money and ended up sleeping in the cemetery, which he later wrote about in a famous chapter titled “Camping Among the Tombs.”)

#6654. An Expert Guide to Nail Health, According to Professionals

Here’s exactly how to keep them strong and healthy

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As manicure trends evolve with new lacquers, changing shapes, and viral techniques, beauty lovers often compromise nail health for aesthetics. While many nail formulas have improved over the years to prioritize strength, uniformity, and finish, experts say incremental habits—from lifestyle shifts to resisting the urge to peel off chipped polish—can ultimately play the biggest role in keeping your nails in excellent condition.

“The future of manicures isn’t just about the latest color trends or how long your gel polish lasts, but how well we care for the nails underneath,” Krisztina van der Boom, founder of DryBy, previously told Harper’s Bazaar. Hand, foot, and nail expert Margaret Dabbs agrees, urging nail enthusiasts to “Adopt a dedicated nail care routine and stick to it.” But what does an effective routine actually look like? Along with keeping your nails clean and hydrated with an emollient moisturizer, like Caudalíe’s Vinotherapist Hand and Nail Cream, professionals suggest keeping a cuticle oil, such as Dior’s Huile Abricot, in your bag for quick touch-ups.

“Cuticle oil is the one product I would never skip,” says Peach Bling founder Sandra Wei. “Look for a formula with jojoba oil, which has small enough molecules to absorb into the nail and surrounding skin.” Wei encourages her clients to apply it daily, ideally before bed, and to treat it as a small ritual. “A rich hand cream and gloves for dishwashing and cleaning also make a real difference,” continues Wei, “since water and harsh detergents are among the most common causes of dry, weak nails.” Maintaining nail and cuticle hydration is also key for mature nails, as they tend to grow more slowly and hold less moisture as we age, which can contribute to brittleness and vertical ridges.

Professionals have debated whether it’s safe to trim your cuticles, since cuticles guard nail beds against bacteria and infection; that's why they often advise pushing them back instead of removing them entirely. “As long as you're not cutting any live skin and damaging your cuticles, gently pushing them back and buffing away excess skin will actually help improve the health and the appearance of your cuticles and will help make your manicure last as long as possible while looking salon-quality,” says Olivia Van Iderstine, vice president of education and manicure trend expert at Olive & June. Prep your fingertips with cuticle oil or a soak in warm, soapy water before a manicure, then use a disposable orangewood stick or stainless steel pusher, such as JinSoon’s HyperCare Cuticle Pusher + Reducer, to improve polish cohesion and create an elongated nail look.

Consistent, gentle filing can also keep nails strong, regardless of your shape preference, because a smooth surface guards against unwanted splits, rips, and tears that can cause long-term damage. While there’s nothing wrong with a budget-friendly emery board, professionals say investing in the right tools provides the right resistance without compromising your nails' integrity. Dabbs is a fan of crystal nail files because they can help prevent micro-splits that lead to peeling and breakage, though the best results depend on not overfiling.

And if you usually opt for gel polish manicures, they don’t have to be a deal breaker for nail health. Several options, from builder gel to Japanese gel and more, provide longevity, durability, and style without weakening natural nails.

“Japanese gel systems are known for their precision and for their focus on preserving the natural nail,” continues Wei. “The prep is minimal and gentle, so we avoid heavy buffing of the nail plate. The gel itself is applied in fine, structured layers that are flexible and sit close to the natural nail.” Peach Bling prioritizes formulas that are free of HEMA and TPO, two ingredients commonly linked to gel allergies and sensitivities. “The result is a manicure that looks refined, wears beautifully, and treats the nail underneath with care,” explains the founder. Bazaar editors love builder gel, as it works like Japanese gel, supporting natural nails with a rounded apex to reinforce their sturdiness.

Experts advise keeping a gel set on for no longer than four weeks, as regrowth changes the nail's balance, ultimately causing unwanted stress and making breaks more likely. Once gel polish begins to lift or crack, it’s often a sign that removal is necessary—and that process can often be more damaging than simply wearing a gel formula in the first place. “What protects nail integrity is how the gel is applied and, even more importantly, how it is removed,” adds Wei. “With careful, gentle removal, there is no need to take a ‘break’ between appointments.”
