#6639. Silver Fox at 16. How Men Are Embracing Gray Hair at Every Age

At 16, James Chudley’s first gray hair was spotted by the girl sitting next to him in Biology. He thought it was a joke. She took a photo to prove it. There it was: one silver thread, just above his ear. “For the rest of the year,” he says, “every Biology lesson, it was: ‘Oh, there’s another one!’”

Chudley, now a personal trainer-in-training from Surrey, England wasn’t too bothered. “I thought I’d just pluck it out,” he says. By 19, though, there were too many to pluck. An anti-gray shampoo turned his bath blue; dye was another option, but he had reservations: “I didn’t want to end up looking like Dracula.”

Away from school, Chudley gradually got comfortable with his grays. Even so, he mentioned them before anyone else could, “almost as a defense mechanism.” Usually the response was playful roasting, sometimes even a compliment. But then someone would catch him off guard. Chudley, now 22, was recently working as a delivery driver when a customer looked him up and down. “Bit young to be going gray, isn’t it?” she said. Almost as an afterthought, she added, “Is it stressing you out?”

Gray hair is an inevitability for most men. Live long enough, and the color starts to drain. For many people, that begins in their early 30s and becomes more visible with age. By 50, suggests a study by the British Association of Dermatologists, up to 23% of us will have half a head of gray hair. The science is straightforward. Hair follicles contain melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing pigment. As we age, the stem cells that replenish them become less active, and the color fades. It’s like a printer cartridge running out of ink: the paper keeps coming, but eventually, there’s nothing on there.

Going gray in your teens and early 20s, however, is another matter. It’s relatively uncommon, although anecdotes are easy to find. Spend five minutes on TikTok and you’ll see plenty asking why they’re suddenly gray. Reddit has versions too, with users swapping stories and theories about why they—and seemingly everyone around them—are losing their color so young. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but people’s hair seems to be turning white really fast lately,” says one post. “How did we end up in the worst century where literally anything can go wrong?”

It’s hard to say if we’re actually going gray earlier, or if it’s just that more people are talking about it. The theories, meanwhile, keep on coming—from mineral deficiencies to heavy-metal exposure. There’s also an optimistic explanation: More people are open to embracing it.

Young men are spending more money than ever on looking good—even on their grays. Rather than shopping for cheap cover-ups, they are forensically researching science-backed cosmetics. Part of this also means a rejection of chemical-heavy products and a more skeptical attitude towards unnecessary cosmetics. Hair dye, after all, is not entirely harmless.

Online communities like “Gray and Proud” and “Silver Revolution” have tens of thousands of members. Paul Mescal and Jeremy Allen White have also done their part for gray-hair representation among young(ish) people: The Times dubbed them “silver fox cubs.”

Maybe things really are shifting. But if the demand for anti-gray products is any indication, the revolution is still a way off. Anti-gray serums are becoming big business. The global market is expected to jump from around $1.3 billion to $2 billion by 2031, according to Deep Market Insights. Cosmetics Business magazine calls it the “next men’s grooming trend,” with growing interest in peptide-based products. On the internet, you see both sides. On Reddit, a 26-year-old guy shares a photo of his gray head of hair, saying that he’s already got more than his dad. The top comment reads: “Do your due diligence, of course—bloodwork, diet etc.” Someone else follows up with: “[Guys] with gray hair are [hot].”

One person making the case for Gen Z’s grey-haired men is model and musician Charlie Jeer. The 24-year-old first found fame on the Netflix dating show Too Hot to Handle. He has the chiseled jawline and cheekbones of a conventional heartthrob, but there’s another feature viewers can’t seem to get past: his hair. “I feel like it gets brought up in conversation every single day in my life,” he says.

Jeer first noticed the grays as a teenager, and mostly shrugged off the comments. Online, it’s a different story. “Why are you going gray?”; “Can’t tell if bro is 15 or 60; ” “Err this old man.” “It’s relentless,” he says.

Now, Jeer sees the grays as an opportunity to stand out. They’ve helped build his profile as a model, too, partly because of the “age ambiguity” they give him. He’s picked up credits with brands like Davidoff and Adidas. “There’s a massive commercial potential for me to make a black hair dye and just start marketing that,” he says. “I never did because I was like, ‘No, I’m proud of my hair the way it is.’”

On TikTok, Jeer takes on his critics with captions like: “Joke’s on them when I’m a silver fox by 30.” He really likes it when he hears from other young guys going gray. “I’ve had a little gray-haired community of people come forward and present themselves,” he says. “It’s nice to hear someone else say that they’ve had people come at them for being gray-haired and that they’re going to continue to wear it with confidence.”

Jeer might be on the young end of the gray-hair population, but as a guy, he’s riding a well-worn track. Men have always been afforded the privilege of associating their grays with looking more distinguished. You don’t have to be George Clooney (or a Too Hot to Handle contestant) to benefit from that. Women, meanwhile, aren’t part of that deal: gray hair is more often simply read as old, an obviously unfair double standard.

It still come with baggage for men, though: age, lost virility, fading relevance. “The first gray” is practically a trope in its own right—a visual shorthand in films, books and TV for a character beginning to age, often followed by the inevitable midlife crisis. There are dozens of those scenes, in everything from The Simpsons to Vanilla Sky.

Matt Newman is a New York–based hairstylist who hates his gray hair. “There are so many examples of men with premature grays that people love and adore,” he says. “But in your 20s, that might not be an aesthetic you’re ready to dive into.”

Perhaps that’s why Jackass star Johnny Knoxville waited until 49 to finally embrace his natural hair color. He started going gray in his 20s and dyed it for most of his life. Then, during lockdown, he asked his wife to give him a buzz cut to reveal the silver underneath, on Instagram. “I should start a challenge but I don’t want to call anyone out,” he wrote on Instagram. Going gray, declared one Mr. Porter headline, was now a “punk power move”.

That’s not quite how Saavan Varambhia, 25, a data analyst from Buckinghamshire, would have described it. Not at first, anyway. Like Chudley, he was at school when a group of female friends spotted his grays and tried to pluck them out. “I was like, ‘Hmm, I don’t know how I feel about this,’” he says. A few years later, he had enough gray hairs on his head to “stop people in their tracks.”

For Varambhia, the contrast was hard to miss. He’s South Asian, with naturally deep-black hair, so the grays stood out. The Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology reports that people of Asian descent also tend to go gray later, often in their late 30s. According to Professor Desmond Tobin, a professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin, many Eastern cultures have traditionally been less accepting of grays than the West, with men and women both more likely to dye them.

“At first, I felt like I didn’t want to seem a lot older than my peers,” Varambhia says. Over time, though, he came to see the silver as something that set him apart. “I’ve always been one to stand out, and it was another attributing factor to that.”

When there are too many gray hairs to pluck, do you reach for the Just for Men, or join the silver fox cub club?

Turning gray at any age can make you wonder why it’s happening. According to Tobin, the answer is usually in your DNA. “The first thing to do is just to look at your [previous] generation of relatives,” he says. “They’re going to give you a road map for where you’re going to be. And if you have early grayers—teens, early 20s—then that’s really mapped out quite starkly in the family.”

Other things can speed up the process, too. Stress is a big one. Tobin says it can damage the cells responsible for producing hair pigment, acting like a “sledgehammer” if the process has already begun. Just look at Barack Obama’s hair before and after his time in the White House. Nutrition can play a role, too, and a blood test can pick up any deficiencies. But Tobin says the nutritional deficiencies linked to premature graying tend to show up in countries where malnutrition is more widespread.

Crucially, though, Tobin says he hasn’t seen hard evidence that young people are going gray earlier across the board. Modern life might come with its share of chronic stressors, he points out, but humans have been enduring trying times since long before social media, climate change, and cost of living crises entered the picture.

Tobin is skeptical of the “overstated claims” made by supplements and serums that promise to “tickle your stem cells.” If you want to slow the process, he says, your best bet is the boring stuff: less stress, plenty of sleep and an antioxidant-rich diet. That might hold things off for a while. But for anyone genetically predisposed to graying, it might not make that much of a difference.

“Would maximum antioxidant intake really stop somebody from graying who’s genetically headed that way? It’s not likely to be a very significant contributor,” Tobin says. “It might, in a multi-prong way, add up to something, but if you’re graying significantly in your teens, that is probably the die that’s being cast for you.”

The good news? Going gray early doesn’t mean the rest of you is aging at the same rate. In fact, there may be a silver lining. People who go gray prematurely are more likely to keep their hair; “nearly all people who bald [do so] with their natural hair color,” says Tobin.

But for anyone who doesn’t want to live with their grays, the hunt for a treatment is on. Research into gray hair has surged alongside the wider boom in longevity science. Tobin says the past five years have felt like a return to the 1980s, when the topical hair-regrowth drug Rogaine first shook up the haircare world. He has consulted for startups developing anti-gray treatments aimed at reducing oxidative stress or extending the life of melanocyte stem cells. The science is promising, but so far, nothing has produced evidence strong enough to satisfy regulators.

Researchers are beginning to understand that graying may not be irreversible, as once thought. Melissa Harris at the University of Alabama has studied the melanocyte stem cells behind hair pigmentation, and immunotherapy as a way to reverse graying. Other research has shown that some hairs can spontaneously regain their pigment, with changes appearing to track periods of stress. It hints that some aspects of aging may be less linear than we assume.

Dr. Greg Williams, a hair restoration surgeon at the Farjo Hair Institute, has watched the field develop. He hosts conference sessions on gray hair and, a couple of years ago, set up a WhatsApp group where specialists around the world could swap ideas and compare notes. “Gray hair is very poorly understood,” he says. “There’s not a lot of research in humans around it.” Maybe that’s surprising, given how universal it seems to be. But commercial fallout is huge. The global hair-and scalp-care industry is worth nearly $9.4 billion, and Williams thinks anyone who figures it out “would be a Nobel Prize winner”.

As for Varambhia, the science seems to fit his experience. Genetics are clearly part of the picture: his dad’s hair has been white for years, and he still has a full head of it. Varambhia also suspects stress sped things up. His grays arrived rapidly as he settled into corporate nine-to-five life. Since hitting the gym regularly, he thinks the process may have slowed.

Knowing other people going through the same thing has helped. “I know eventually I’ll go fully gray. I hope it’s a bit later on than sooner,” he says. But when the time comes? “I’ll embrace it.”

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “Gray Ahead of Schedule”

#6637. A Night of Firsts: The History-Making Victories Across the 2026 Midterm Elections

It took 94 years for Kansas to elect another Democratic U.S. senator. It took the entire history of the United States for a Black woman to be elected governor. Both happened on Tuesday night—two significant milestones amid a night of major triumphs, firsts, and history-making moments.

The 2026 midterm elections delivered a political earthquake, with a series of candidates and statewide contests drawing national attention. Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seven Senate seats—including in Republican strongholds where the party had not won in decades. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in American history. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected to lead a state, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. Michigan elected the country’s first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed, and New Hampshire its first openly gay male senator, Chris Pappas. And longstanding political barriers fell elsewhere—from Texas electing its first Latina governor to Florida electing its first Black governor, Republican Byron Donalds.

And it was true that the gubernatorial races sent shockwaves from state to state. In California, Xavier Becerra, the former U.S. secretary of health and human services, became the first Latino ever elected governor of the state. And both Nevada and Wisconsin elected their first Black governors: Attorney General Aaron Ford and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, respectively. Minnesota elected its first woman governor in Amy Klobuchar, who will leave behind her seat in the U.S. Senate after two decades. And in Ohio, former state health director Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor in the state’s history.

The Democratic gains were impressive across states where Republicans have dominated for years. In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand became the first Democrat elected governor since 2006. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Roger Marshall to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state since 1932. South Carolina delivered another seismic upset as pediatrician Annie Andrews became the first Democrat to win a Senate election there since 1998—and the first woman ever elected to represent the state in the upper chamber. Former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper ended an 18-year Democratic Senate drought, and in Texas, state representative James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988, defeating Republican Ken Paxton.

There were significant victories further down the ballot, too. In Alabama, Democrat Allison Montgomery defeated Republican incumbent Phillip Rigsby to become the state’s first openly transgender lawmaker. The software engineer and LGBTQ+ rights advocate campaigned on issues including public education, healthcare, and affordability, despite facing dogged attacks on her gender identity from her opponent. In Indiana, 30-year-old Beau Bayh, the son of former governor and senator Evan Bayh and grandson of former senator Birch Bayh, became the first Democrat to win statewide office since 2012, defeating Republican Max Engling in the race for secretary of state.

Across the country, people voted in the midterm elections to significantly expand who holds power in America, all over a single night in which decades of political precedent were overturned.

#6636. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6635. The Only 9 Pieces You Need for a Chic Winter Capsule Wardrobe

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Getting dressed is hard enough on an ideal day, but add frigid temps and icy conditions into the mix, and I’m constantly on the verge of canceling my plans to stay in bed all day. As a fashion editor, one thing that I’ve found immensely helpful in this struggle is having a winter capsule wardrobe, replete with versatile staples that lend themselves to mixing and matching. It really takes the guesswork out of my mornings.

In case you can relate, I’ve decided to share my winning formula here. To maintain style while staying warm, you’ll need foundational pieces like a good coat and boots, plus a few winter accessories and, of course, a healthy dose of shearling. You’ll notice this list doesn’t include a pair of pants. This isn’t an invitation to go pants-less this winter, but rather a reflection of the fact that there aren’t any seasonal staples in the category. Utilize your jeans, trousers, or a pair of satin pants for a more holiday-friendly look.

Below, find nine key building blocks for all your wintery outfits and shoppable options that transcend trends. Good luck out there, friends.

Out of all the available outerwear options, I’ve decided that a wool coat is the first and foremost necessity. Every winter, I’m reminded of the importance of stylish jackets that can make or break my cold-weather ensembles. One of these will keep you warm, and if you shop smart, it will last for years.

The entrance to my high school was a long, uphill ramp, and I have many embarrassing memories of near or total wipeouts. I shudder at the thought of walking on an icy sidewalk. So, as an adult, I’ve traded my boat shoes for lug-sole styles (though they would not have been uniform-compliant) that offer more traction. I recommend a weatherproof option that can withstand rain, snow, and ice. As hard as it may be, avoid suede.

Turtlenecks are the heroes of winter layering. Whether you’re bundling up before hitting the slopes, adding warmth under a sweatshirt, or shielding your skin from that scratchy sweater, your winter capsule needs at least one of these bad boys.

I know cashmere can be costly, but it really is worth it. Plus, getting dressed for work during the colder months is so much easier when you have a trusted lineup of sweaters and knit tops.

A personal favorite, I confess! I adore a full-length, long-sleeve dress for the winter months. At a time when I can hardly be bothered to change out of pajamas, slipping into a dress can have a transformative effect. And there are so many delectable options to be had.

Everyone has their own opinion on furs—faux or real. Regardless of where you stand, this is the one time of year when you can lean into this look. Here at ELLE, we have a policy against real fur, so you can rest assured that these options are all faux.

Balaclavas, hoods, or ushankas—I’m not picky. Better yet, why not have a few options on hand? By avoiding them to steer clear of hat hair, you’re only hurting yourself. These make such a difference in staying warm.

Be it a scarf coat or a homemade take on Lenny Kravitz’s giant wrap, your arsenal isn’t complete without one.

If you want to do après-ski correctly, you’ll need a bag with a touch of shearling. Options abound this time of year, so feel free to be selective. I’ve rounded up a few favorites here.

#6633. Why Do We Keep Coming Back to Godzilla?

Like most people born in the western world after 1954, I knew of a monster named Godzilla before I’d heard of a country called Japan. It’s not a rare perspective. For as long as nearly any living person can remember, Godzilla has been hugely popular, far exceeding the global recognition afforded most leaders, athletes, and certainly his human co-stars, those men and women whose dramatic dealings are the universally agreed-upon bargain for apocalyptic havoc that millions upon millions have gladly paid to see for over 70 years.

What Godzilla hasn’t been is prestigious. The irradiated dinosaur of very few words—mainly deafening screams—is a beloved figure more in the key of Harry Potter, Batman, or James Bond than the loftier fare that typically gets recognized by major festivals or awards bodies. But exceptions to the rule do exist. The Criterion Collection issued Ishiro Honda's 1954 original on a deluxe Blu-ray in 2012 and marked their 1,000th release with a lavish set of Godzilla’s Shōwa era (1954-1975), which both documents film history and calls to mind John Huston’s Chinatown line about sticking around long enough to become respectable. Writing an introduction to Honda’s biography A Life in Film, from Godzilla to Kurosawa, Martin Scorsese deemed the series’ first director "an extraordinary artist and craftsman" and placed Honda’s 1954 film (alongside spin-offs Mothra and Rodan) among “pictures that haunted the imaginations of young moviegoers like myself and millions of others for years to come.” Kiyoshi Kurosawa—perhaps Japan’s greatest living filmmaker, and certainly its finest practitioner of austere horror—deemed Honda’s film an early lesson in national trauma. Thomas Pynchon, too, had ambitious plans to write a novel about the insurance adjuster who responds to Godzilla’s wreckage (the idea never fully materialized, though it did become a nice tangent in his 1990 novel Vineland). We can look at the films and countenance such appreciations from geniuses. In the meantime, good luck to anyone counting the exact number of action figures, coloring books, sticker packs, and lunchboxes boasting Godzilla and friends.

A critical shift started somewhere in the last decade. Toho ostensibly shelved Godzilla with 2004’s Final Wars, a grand finale that was the big-budget equivalent of a child smashing toys. (That is a compliment.) Godzilla LLC boasts enough films and ancillary products to be financially solvent until the sun burns out (or an indomitable monster rises from the sea), but that retirement was short-lived. Toho resurrected the franchise in aggressive form with 2016’s Shin Godzilla, both a complete series reboot and (across several stages, each grotesque and terrifying) character reinvention that dispensed with typical monster-movie hijinks. An unholy experiment that would make the series’ many mad scientists proud, Shin Godzilla fused the hilarious bureaucratic hallway-rushing of In the Loop or Veep with cosmic horror befitting its director, Hideaki Anno, whose contributions to Japanese culture are nearly Godzilla’s equal on the strength of Neon Genesis Evangelion alone. With time, it’s downright eerie to see Anno’s foreshadowing of the global unrest of Trump, Brexit, COVID, and our endless misinformation era. But rather than keep the great filmmaker on retainer for any number of sequels or spin-offs, Toho regrettably followed Shin Godzilla with an anime trilogy produced for Netflix, a rare class of films I’ve been too embarrassed to even log on Letterboxd.

Whether genius or dreck, none of these films quite anticipated 2023’s Godzilla Minus One. It’s one thing to become the highest-grossing Japanese-language release in U.S. history—any Godzilla movie that doesn't at least aim for such a distinction isn’t worth its salt. It’s harder to imagine anyone, even or especially the franchise’s most ardent fans, anticipated lavish public praise from a quintet of Best Director winners in Steven Spielberg (who claims to have seen the film at least three times), James Cameron (who offered to work on a sequel), Christopher Nolan, Guillermo Del Toro, and Bong Joon-ho. In a recorded conversation with Yamazaki, Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie credited the film as an inspiration; the actor went so far as to call it “perfect.” Which is to say nothing of the fact that Godzilla Minus One earned the series its first Oscar, a VFX prize awarded to none other than writer-director Takashi Yamazaki—a nice encapsulation of the film’s balance between spirit and spectacle.

Because Godzilla Minus One resonated more than anyone could have anticipated, Godzilla Minus Zero, which arrives in theaters this weekend, shoulders the burden of expectation. The first shot across the bow was its world premiere at last month’s New York Film Festival, where Zero debuted alongside prestige fare like Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial and Tony Gilroy’s star-studded Behemoth! There, NYFF’s artistic director Dennis Lim introduced the movie to a sold-out crowd at the Alice Tully Hall, praising Yamazaki for exemplifying "the endless possibilities of creative VFX and genre filmmaking." Minus Zero indeed thrives on spectacle: its opening sequence blazes a merciless path of carnage aided by an elegant long take, while subsequent scenes centered on one of Godzilla’s classic foes, the three-headed Ghidorah, inspire genuine terror more than cheap thrills. This is the first Japanese film shot for IMAX, a large-scale exhibition that’s often torqued for discomfort. Yamazaki’s centerpiece battle pitting the monster against a squadron of fighter planes is dogged by fatalistic doom: a mother and child screaming as their house crashes to the ground don’t get the last-minute salvation we’ve come to expect, and even the sentimental-seeming inclusion of a pilot named Honda is complicated by his eventual fate.

If not quite so grave as the visions of death that imprinted upon a young Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Yamazaki’s narrative—including a face-melting sequence that U.S. distributor GKIDS have asked not be spoiled—provides a stark contrast to the bloodless carnage of American blockbusters. It’s quite the cultural coup, too, that a film this brutal and generally skeptical of American imperialism has secured a simultaneous international release: every English-speaking actor (none recognizable, each portraying arrogant allied military) bears an amusingly off-market quality à la the nefarious white time-travelers of 1991’s altogether underrated Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.

Nearly all Godzilla films are a total restart. Minus Zero is immediately notable as a direct sequel. The results suggest that Yamazaki overestimated his initial project. Godzilla is not much of a presence in Minus Zero, first appearing around the 50-minute mark and then again in a suitable, albeit brief climax. Far more time is spent with those we came to know and like during Minus One, each reprised by an entirely competent ensemble that fails to elevate interest higher than a certain co-star’s 50 meters. (The protagonists’ adopted daughter from Minus One returns here for the sole purpose of standing in place and crying.) Whatever its pretensions towards grandeur, this is still a film where a scientist explains his master plan by smashing together two monster figures. It takes little to delight in this moment, a literal and figurative collision of serious storytelling and childlike abandon. More of that spirit might’ve served the final picture.

My mild disappointment is nothing compared to the agony Godzilla has wreaked on the district of Ginza, which last week hosted the first public screenings of Minus Zero through the Tokyo International Film Festival. Godzilla’s annihilated the city’s landmarks enough times that when we think of all-out destruction on the sprawling megalopolis that is Tokyo, we’re probably picturing its uber-fashionable shopping sector laid to ruins. When he emerged from the sea in 1954, he wrecked the district’s historic Nichigeki Theater, which was again destroyed (in real life, of humans’ accord) and reopened as the Yurakucho Mullion building in 1984—the same year as The Return of Godzilla, where he inflicted yet more damage on the brand-new structure. Godzilla Minus One recreated the Nichigeki Theater in loving detail only to destroy it again in a sequence that deployed modern visual effects to cause maximum tactility and human misery. That Hiroshima-like site is revisited in Minus Zero, leading one character to declare that “Ginza is again the battleground.” Time’s healed those wounds, however. The night before Minus Zero’s Japanese premiere, a small crowd gathered outside the Yurakucho Mullion’s Seiko watch for an extravagant display: the clock lifted, and out came a small set of Godzilla puppets that strike chimes while Akira Ifukube’s iconic theme plays.

Ginza’s Wako Clock Tower has fared no better: it was torn to ribbons in the 1954 original, 1995’s Godzilla vs. Destoroyah, Shin Godzilla, and Minus One. After a time you must wonder what keeps bringing Godzilla back to the neighborhood. Is it animal instinct, or mere coincidence, or an atomic hatred for its glowing consumerism? The Wako Annex, a nearby pastry shop that Google not-inaccurately describes as “chic,” currently advertises a Christmas-themed cake recreation of the oft-doomed Clock Tower with Minus Zero’s monster looming over it; accompanying text informs us that “Godzilla strikes Ginza’s Wako once again.” The nearby Toho cinema is within Hibiya Godzilla Square, featuring a small but impressively detailed statue and a plaque reading, “The human race must coexist with Godzilla.” Immediately adjacent is a three-story shopping mall hosting a Toho store selling numerous Godzilla ephemera. (I bought the tea cup.)

Even Americans accustomed to the fetishization of disaster would be impressed by Japan’s ability to marry suffering and spectacle to great financial gain. Perhaps it’s the same haunted fascination of a young Martin Scorsese or Kiyoshi Kurosawa cast unto the world at large; Godzilla might be scary as he destroys Ginza, but he’s something to admire when shrunk down to human size and displayed inside the Yurakucho Mullion’s lobby. (The photo-snapping crowds that gather every time I walk past suggest that bit of marketing paid off.) Even as Minus Zero’s first reviews show a less rapturous response than Minus One, this series’ viability—and its newfound prestige—shows little indication of flagging. Ginza’s residents were beyond happy to see Godzilla, at least in ossified, action-figure form. But who's to say they wouldn't be just as excited if, one day, his path of destruction broke through the screen?

#6631. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6629. 35 Gifts for Boyfriends Who've Been Very Good This Year 2026

The internet has some peculiar ideas about what constitutes a good gift for a boyfriend. Search long enough and you'll find yourself in a purgatory of ergonomic footrests, rechargeable headlamps, novelty T-shirts, and footwear that seem designed to extinguish whatever romantic spark remains. Surely the person you love deserves something a little more inspired.

So we've assembled a collection of gifts that reflect what we hope is a more generous understanding of the guy you're actually dating: the things that'll actually tickle his fancy. Because whatever the gifting occasion, it doesn't call for another set of monogrammed rocks for his bourbon.

Still on the hunt? Explore the rest of our gift guides, and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a steady supply of gift ideas that have our seal of approval.

A mainstay of Antwerp label Howlin's knitwear lineup, the Birth of the Cool is made from 100% Scottish Shetland wool. A very good sweater with a very good name.

A rich shade of green, a great collar, and that little pony perched on the pocket. This cotton corduroy chore coat from Polo Ralph Lauren is just the layer for the cooler months.

The first step in closing the swag gap is a first-rate white tee. Merz b. Schwanen makes them in all manner of cuts and styles, but the 215, famously worn by Jeremy Allen White in The Bear, hits the sweet spot.

Buying pants for a guy can be a delicate business, but Buck Mason makes it easy. The brand's Big Chino, with its generous, full-legged silhouette, is a safe bet for just about any wardrobe. Worth browsing the rest of the lineup, things tend to sell out quickly.

Earlier this year, a patchwork Shetland sweater from a 1996 J.Crew catalog became an unlikely object of obsession in certain stylish corners of the internet. This one isn't quite the same, but it's got enough of that vintage J.Crew magic to scratch the itch without having to scour eBay for the original.

Colbo and Sperry are on a roll. Their latest collaboration, the Sirah loafer, is an new-new silhouette that lands somewhere between a vintage dress shoe and a ballet flat, with a low-slung profile and Sperry's signature grippy sole.

This Timex and Todd Snyder watch takes its cues from the watchmaker's 1960s Marlin, with a slightly smaller case, a classic dial, and a handsome suede leather strap. A lot of watch for the money.

It wouldn’t be a GQ gift list without a nice tie. This silk-jacquard number from mfpen fits the bill, and won’t set you back too much, either.

Tekla and Auralee are back for their second collaboration, and these checked pajama pants sit right in the middle of the Venn diagram of cozy and covetable. Definitely a pair he should wear out of the house.

Handsewn in Maine, Easymoc’s Cozymoc pairs a full-grain leather upper with a 100% shearling lining for shuffling around in comfort. A Vibram sole makes it fit for trips outside, and it’s resoleable, too.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

When it comes to skincare, sometimes it takes a tool to help a guy take care of himself. This one from Korean skincare brand Abib packs retinal to help reduce the appearance of under-eye bags, with a built-in metal rollerball that makes application a breeze.

The whole point of a gift set is to give him something he wouldn’t try himself. Fortunately for you, after using this Mojave Ghost body wash, lotion, and hand cream, he’s never going to want to go back to whatever he was using before.

The Gap '90s nostalgia machine is running at full tilt, and this year the brand went digging through its fragrance archives, bringing back the scents that once perfumed an entire generation of mall-goers. T

Big news in sunscreen: BEMT, a UV filter long used in European formulas, has finally made it stateside. It offers broad-spectrum UVA and UVB protection and helps make those lightweight formulas we’ve long envied across the pond possible. Sunscreens containing it are starting to hit shelves, and one of our office favorites is from French pharmacy staple La Roche-Posay.

Couldn't care less about BEMT? Fair enough. If convenience is what he's after, Freaks of Nature's SPF 50 stick makes a strong case for keeping things simple. It's pocket-sized, glides on without a fuss, and offers 80 minutes of water resistance. No excuses for skipping sunscreen now.

Shaving with a safety razor is a lost art, and we say it's high time for a revival. Bevel's shaving kit has everything he needs to get acquainted with the old-school ritual, and maybe even start looking forward to his morning shave.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

The new Beats 360 headphones sound great and look the part. Swappable performance-knit cushions let you customize the look, while a sweat- and water-resistance rating makes them a rare pair of gym-worthy over-ears.

Ray-Ban’s Audio Clubmasters pack open-ear audio and six built-in microphones into a classic frame. Best of all, he can enjoy the latest tech without making everyone wonder if they’re being filmed.

Because you deserve more attention than his algorithm does, there’s the new Brick Night, which automatically blocks distracting apps whenever his phone comes within range. Unlike the original Brick, no physical tap required. Just park it on his nightstand and let it do the rest.

Teenage Engineering's Pocket Operators are calculator-sized music machines with a cult following. The PO-12 Rhythm packs 16 drum sounds, a sequencer, and a slew of effects into one tiny device, and syncs with other Pocket Operators to build out a whole little setup. Don't be surprised if he starts collecting them.

Keychron's new K3 Ultra is one dapper keyboard, with a low-slung profile, metal-and-wood frame, and three switch options to choose from. A fine introduction to mechanical keyboards, and plenty to geek out over for the already converted.

UAG’s ultra-thin tracking card might be the most practical gift in this guide. One of the few that plays nice with both Apple and Android, it lets him pinpoint his wallet’s location on a map or make it chirp when his scatterbrain misplaces it.

I picked up Nanu’s Arc earlier this year, and I’ve gotten way more joy out of it than I expected. It’s a well-built, thoughtfully engineered analog clock with a discreet digital display and a lovely mechanical chime. Not cheap, sure, but having one less reason to reach for my phone has been worth every penny.

If you're going to veg out on the couch with your better half, do it under something sumptuous. Brooklinen's Super Fluff throw is all plush faux fur and silky-smooth shag, made for the cold winter ahead. And yes, it's machine washable.

John Waters warned against going home with someone who doesn't own books. I'd say the same rule goes for wine openers. And this one from Craighill really is the best.

Our Place’s pans are take-it-or-leave-it, but the Wonder Oven Pro is the real deal. Yes, it’s an air fryer, but precise temperature and time controls mean it can bake, roast, grill, dehydrate, and even proof dough. With three rack positions and enough room for a whole chicken, it’s a serious little oven. Looks damn good, too.

You could get him a candle. Or you could get him this handsome little contraption: a glass teardrop set in a brass cradle. Fill the glass with fragrance oil, light the tealight underneath, and voilà: instant home aura.

Hoto’s sleek PixelDrive electric screwdriver comes with 30 interchangeable bits and a nifty pixelated display that shows exactly how much power he’s working with. That wobbly dining chair doesn’t stand a chance.

You’ve probably seen Satisfy’s hole-riddled MothTech tees everywhere. Those strategically placed perforations probably do wonders for ventilation, but let's be honest: they just look sick.

Cold-weather running is a lot more appealing when you've got the right gear. Lululemon's swishy Pace Breaker track jacket keeps the chill at bay without weighing down their stride.

Give the guy an excuse to take a load off. Lookout & Wonderland’s Magic Bath combines mineral-rich Japanese sea salt, French green clay, and nourishing oils with 500 mg of CBD for a seriously luxurious soak.

DedCool’s cult-favorite Xtra Milk scent gets the body scrub treatment, which means he can exfoliate his way to softer skin while smelling like the best version of himself.

Bowflex’s SelectTech dumbbells are about as functional as fitness equipment gets. A quick turn of the dial adjusts the weight, replacing an entire rack of dumbbells without turning his place into an Equinox.

The new Nike x Hyperice Air Zoom HyperSlide delivers targeted heat and vibration massage across the top of the foot, giving his hardworking dogs some well-earned R&R, rest day or not.

#6628. Book Breakfasts, Babysitters, and the Russian Tea Room: A Day With Author Tarajia Morrell

Forget 9-to-5. Mothering knows no schedule—often it feels more like 5-to-9 and everything in between. In this series, we look at the hectic, messy, sometimes beautiful, often frustrating enterprise of being a mother—and maintaining a life of your own. Consider it a “day in the life” for the forgotten hours.

Today, we’re following Tarajia Morrell, the James Beard Award–winning food writer, author, and communications consultant. Her new memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast, is out now. The book is a rich and lyrical telling of her childhood as the daughter of a dynasty of Manhattan wine sellers; her days on the New York City club scene of the late ’90s; her culinary studies, acting auditions, and restaurant jobs; and more.

A single mother, Morrell lives in her childhood home—a rent-stabilized Manhattan apartment that she fought for and won—with her five-year-old daughter, Viva. On a recent Thursday, she brought Vogue along for a busy day, which included everything from the school bus stop and a book breakfast to a podcast taping, a party, and the realities of mealtime. (“Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater,” she writes.)

My alarm goes off. Immediately, I recall that today is not a normal day at my desk at home, writing copy for the hotels for which I’m the communications director. Today is a day in which I must also focus on my book, and it’s going to be a doozy.

I go make myself some jet fuel. While the coffee pot is on the stove, I turn on my morning music: Alice Coltrane Radio on Spotify, which both soothes and invigorates me at once with its harp and organ. It’s still almost completely dark out, but, from the living room, I can see the first blush of light above a little slice of the 59th Street Bridge. This sight (and the coffee) has its usual effect: I have a jolt of how lucky I am to be exactly where I am—in this home with this child.

It’s been a challenge to pry Viva from sleep for her new kindergarten wake-up time, so I am delightfully surprised when I open the door to her tiny bedroom (the tiny bedroom of my childhood!) and she’s sitting in front of her dollhouse at play. Blaring Alice Coltrane and Éthiopiques is clearly an excellent, calming way to start her day too.

Viva colors while she eats her breakfast of a cinnamon-raisin English muffin with Nutella (I know, I know), berries, and juice. Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater. A predawn morning is not the hour to prove points.

I help Viva dress for school even though I am supposed to let her do it entirely independently. My excuse is that time is of the essence, but that’s true in more ways than one. I stare at her long, lithe limbs and wonder where my chubby baby has gone. Since having her, time has changed. It used to be something that haunted me with its slow creep; now I am always chasing more of it.

Our school bus is meant to arrive at 7:22 but is always outrageously early or late. I receive a text from the dad of an older girl who also gets picked up at our stop, saying “The bus is running early,” so I grab a coat and Viva’s things and we dash. As we make our way, I feel enormously grateful for this relative stranger whose tiny updates help my life be less stressful. As a parent in general, but particularly as a solo parent, supportive gestures that help the wheels stay on (and help me avoid a school run) are more appreciated that I can express.

We do a weird little dance while we wait, with Viva basically inside my coat for warmth and cuddles. The song I hum is vaguely reminiscent of the Beverly Hills Cop theme song. I don’t care what I look like in these stolen silly moments of just being her mother.

Back home and I hop in the shower. My literary agent, Andy McNicol, is picking me up to go to a breakfast hosted at Claudette by owner Carlos Suarez on lower Fifth to celebrate my memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast.

Andy is right on time and we head downtown. Twenty minutes into the ride, I ask the driver why we skipped our exit off the FDR, and it turns out that it’s because he has the wrong address. I tease Andy about typing without wearing her glasses. One of the many indignities of aging is that none of us seem to be able to see without our glasses.

We arrive at Claudette and I instantly feel more calm. Writing the book has been a very solitary experience—done after Viva falls asleep—and finally getting to squeeze my pals and feel less alone in it is a balm to my nerves.

So many people I love are here from many chapters of my life, and an adorable number of them are wearing red and black—a clear nod to my book cover—as am I. My friend Batsheva Hay clocks my dress and asks if it’s vintage Geoffrey Beene. We both laugh: She’d had her eye on the same one on The RealReal. I am the geek who enjoys matching my book cover. Plus there’s a great vintage Geoffrey Beene scene in the book (i.e., in my life), so it feels pleasantly full circle.

The breakfast ends and I prepare to depart for the rest of my day. I tucked jeans into my bag, but, unfortunately, I forgot to put in a shirt. Classic me to find myself in this predicament on a day that I am reporting to, ahem, Vogue. I put on my leather jacket without a shirt underneath and go hunting for a T-shirt before my next rendezvous. Save Khaki United on Greenwich Avenue seems like the best and closest option, and sure enough, I find a perfect simple long-sleeve T-shirt there.

I meet creative director Anna Polonsky at the new Santo Taco on Carmine, where she’s overseeing a photo shoot with Gentl and Hyers of the food and space. Anna and I have done branding projects together for both Troutbeck and Belden House & Mews, the sister hotels with which I work. We catch up over agua frescas and divine tacos and discuss branding for Firehouse—the soon-to-open membership and events space for Belden. We soon discover we will also both be at the same event later that night; love it when that happens.

I fly by The Strand, the legendary bookstore where I am launching my book on November 4 (!), and its events director greets me for a quick tour of the room I’ll be in. I am completely verklempt to see my book on little posters, including on the elevator. I’m pinching myself…even more so when I am taken to the greenroom and see the walls covered in photos of my literary idols who have read there.

I walk up Broadway to the Malin to meet Angela Ledgerwood of the podcast Lit Up to record an episode on my book. We also did one for Savor: A Chef’s Hunger for More, which I coauthored with Fatima Ali, and since our last recording session, Angela married a friend of mine from high school. They’ve become winemakers, launching Old Sound Vineyard on the North Fork. If insomnia and needing glasses are drawbacks of getting older, one of the enormous pleasures is this sort of happenstance: people you love finding love with people you love.

I take the R train downtown to meet Charlie Champalimaud, an owner of Troutbeck and Belden, at Thompson Street Studio, where artist Kiva Motnyk has her more commercial practice. Charlie has commissioned a work by Kiva for Belden, so we go to see sketches for it and discuss timing for delivery. I learn that Kiva grew up in the building we are in, which feels like another good omen, since my book is about unexpectedly finding myself in the New York City apartment in which I began.

I am properly zonked. I consider a taxi but despise being stuck in traffic and the absurd prices, so I get on the R at Prince Street and start to tackle my neglected emails. I am so distracted and fried that I forget to switch to the Q and accidentally go to Queens instead of 86th Street. Amateur hour. I take the train back to Manhattan and hail a cab to make up for lost time.

I pick Viva up and we head home. I ask her what she had for lunch at school, and she tells me “applesauce, french fries, and broccoli.” Super.

Home. Quick dinner of “crispy chicken,” which is hammered panko and egg-battered chicken breasts that I made the night before and is no longer crispy, blanched broccoli (Viva’s requested veg for the night, despite its presence at lunch), and avocado with sea salt.

The lovely sitter arrives and immediately engages Viva in an art project. Nothing is normal this month of book launch and tour, and it would be impossible without my mother and support system of other mom friends helping enormously. I am so tired that when I sit down for a moment of sunshine on the terrace, I consider bailing on my plans for the evening, but the sitter is already here.

I arrive at Le Monde Beryl’s new shop on 67th Street for a cocktail party cohosted by The Perfect. One of my oldest friends, Lily Hanbury, started LMB 10 years ago with Katya Shifrin, and they’ve just opened this stunning store designed by Silka Rittson-Thomas. I live in Le Monde Beryl shoes because I can walk everywhere fast in them (Viva calls fast walking “city walking,” which I love). I am wearing a long silk dress by DeMeric, really chosen for my next and final stop, so am a bit dressed up for the cocktail at LMB, but old buddies and immediate laughter (with me? at me?) make it irrelevant.

I arrive on that strange crest of 57th Street to the Russian Tea Room, which is celebrating 100 years. I’m in a room with my food world family…as well as the trademark bawdy ice sculptures, gilt details, and red patina. I try to recall the last time I was here. I think it was 1999, at a dinner with Paris Hilton before a wild evening at a nightclub.

My exhaustion hits me hard. We restaurant folk commence our usual conversation of where we can go to get food immediately, and I suggest Dim Sum Palace, around the corner on 56th. It is not a palace, but it is a great place to go when you’re starving with six friends and no reservation at 8:30 on a gorgeous autumnal Thursday.

Home. When you parent alone, a babysitter who puts things in the dishwasher is like winning the lottery. I climb into the loft bed that was once mine and kiss my child, pulling the covers she’s kicked off back over her. As I fall asleep in my own bed, I am thinking of how well our home fits us—a mother and child, just us. It’s still pretty unfathomable that I lived in this fabulous but not so large apartment with two parents until I was 15. My last thought is to marvel at the strangeness of it all, the gift of it, being here with her. All this searching, hunger, and marveling is what drove me to write the book. Good night.
